items.title: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament
paragraphs: A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.

Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.
“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said as she formally introduced the petition, according to Politico.
She called Donald Trump’s envoy “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada had ever seen.
The petition accuses Hoekstra of “undermining” Canada-US diplomatic relations through repeated statements about Canadian politics that its signatories say are “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol”.
The US state department said it was aware of the petition.
Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particularly for his response to Trump’s desire to annex the country and make Canada the 51st US state.

Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the president’s rhetoric as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”.
Hoekstra also previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election that saw a remarkable come-from-behind victory for the prime minister’s Liberal party as “anti-American”.
The US ambassador had suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans performed poorly in this month’s midterm elections.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney replied, when asked about the comments.
Democrats swept the November elections, including key Senate races in border states such as Michigan and Maine, where the bitter tariff war between Washington and Ottawa has hit residents hard.
Last month Carney said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.

“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

Hoekstra had also accused Canada of potential “political interference” in the US election, a claim Carney said held “no merit”. Speaking to reporters in Turkey, the prime minister said he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.
Even though the Canadian government is required to provide a formal response to the petition presented by May, the petition is nonbinding.
“I think the government will quite likely say, ‘No, we’re not prepared to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and strip him of his diplomatic credentials,’”, May said in an interview with CTV.

Despite this possibility, May expects the petition to signal to Trump that the Canadian government has the support of its constituents, and she hopes the government can use it as leverage against Trump with Democrats holding power in Congress for the second half of Trump’s term.

items.title: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow
paragraphs: Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.
According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.
Programa’s Schedules function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.
The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.
As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.
From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.
Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule “clean” as the design is fleshed out.
Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.
The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.
Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.
The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.
Designers can place saved 3D models directly into their designs, and use product images as material swatches to bring selected finishes into the model.
In this way, the products (and finishes) a studio has chosen can be seen in the visuals as well as listed in the Schedule.
The process also works in reverse, starting from the Schedule. A product with a compatible 3D model attached can be placed straight into SketchUp.
If there is no model, designers can choose a stand-in from SketchUp’s 3D Warehouse, or from elsewhere in the current model, to represent the product.
Once a component and a product are connected, supported changes can be reviewed and applied in either direction.
For example, adding another copy of a connected chair in SketchUp generates a quantity change, which the designer can then apply to the Schedule.
The company added that changes are presented for review “before the corresponding update is applied”.
This means the model and the specification can move together as a design develops, while the Schedule is only updated once the designer has chosen to apply a change.
Programa stressed that responsibility remains with the studio.
Designers stay in charge of “selecting the right product, checking its details and deciding when the model or Schedule should change”, the company said.
The aim, it explained, is to carry information between the model and the specification rather than make those decisions on the designer’s behalf.
The extension is aimed at studios that model in SketchUp and manage their specifications in Programa.
The Programa extension works with SketchUp desktop on Mac and Windows.
To learn more, visit Programa’s website or its extension setup guide.

items.title: Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'
paragraphs: Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cyber incident".
Downing Street has not ruled out an attempted hack but said there was "currently no evidence" personal data had been lost, adding an investigation was ongoing.
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it took the digital services down as a "precaution", and assured claimants regular benefit and pension payments would be paid.

But a number of benefits recipients say money they rely on has still not come through - and they fear being penalised for not being able to fill in an online journal that proves they are looking for jobs.
The UK's former Chief Technology Officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the incident was an attack.
"They've taken down some of the citizen-facing services which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door," he said.
Single Cardiff mother-of-four Samantha Reah told the BBC the technological disruption meant she was missing £1,600: "I rely on the payment today - it's my payday.
"I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop. I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."
Georgina Howarth, 30, from Plymouth, said she had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment.
"I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am. They said they can't even get on the system."
Claimants are also unable to fill in an online journal which shows the DWP they have been applying for jobs, a condition of their benefits.
Gemma Barnes from St Neots in Cambridgeshire told the BBC she was worried her payments could be cut as a result.
She said she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site.
"With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she said., explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.

The DWP says regular payments are not affected and if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline. They say they will not be sanctioned over missing journal entries during the incident.
There are also problems with Healthy Start, an NHS scheme for women who are pregnant or have young children to help them buy milk or fruit.
A spokesperson told the BBC the online application service was unavailable but there was no interruption to payments.

As of around 12:00 GMT on Friday, the online systems for pensions, universal credit and Pip applications, as well as the "Tell Us Once'" system to inform government when someone has died, could not be accessed.
It was not clear when the government expected services to be up and running again.

A DWP spokesperson said: "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption."
A statement continued: "As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links."
Tech disruption to major service around the world have hit the headlines repeatedly in recent months.
There was a major outage of Microsoft services, the grounding of all US flights, problems at the US National Security Agency, and disruption at major American banks.

The causes of these incidents have varied. Many were linked to upgrades going wrong but experts have also mentioned factors including outdated IT systems and the use of AI to potentially exploit tech vulnerabilities.

While the nature of the DWP incident is unclear, officials could not rule out the involvement of a "malicious actor", but added there was "no evidence" that other government departments had been targeted in this way.
The DWP outage follows warnings that AI technology could fuel attacks on UK digital infrastructure.
Earlier this month a National Cyber Security Centre report urged organisations to strengthen their defences against hackers as the technology becomes more complex and capable.
Its CEO Richard Horne said there was a "real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents".
Last month the government carried out inspections on several websites after a flaw was identified in a programming language used around the world.
The PHP security flaw prompted a global race for organisations to identify whether they were impacted and fix it before it could be exploited.
UK government websites have been impacted by other cyber incidents in recent years.
In April 2025, the government reported that cyber attackers had breached the Legal Aid Agency's online services.
It said the group responsible accessed a "significant amount" of personal data going back decades, including contact details of people who had applied for legal aid.
The agency took some services offline while responding to the incident.

items.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
paragraphs: A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.
The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.
Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.
Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.
Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.
More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

items.title: NHS Grampian publishes leaked report at centre of hospital scandal
paragraphs: Lawyer Aamer Anwar is representing whistleblower Dr Mohammed Habib, who leaked the 2022 report
NHS Grampian has published the internal report which revealed there had been 19 avoidable deaths of patients who had undergone liver and pancreatic surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.
It was leaked last week by surgeon Dr Mohammed Habib, who called for NHS Grampian to face a corporate homicide probe after the report said some patients bled to death on the operating table.
NHS Grampian has now released the report from September 2022, along with a redacted version of a follow-up from November the same year.
The health board said they were being published, external now "in the interests of absolute transparency".
Meanwhile, written submissions have also been published from witnesses who will appear at the Scottish Parliament's health committee next week.
These include two whistleblowers and Prof Caroline Hiscox, former chief executive NHS Grampian.
Separately, the health board has apologised after confidential papers containing sensitive medical and personal details of 22 patients were found discarded on a street near Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.
A passer-by found the documents near a bin on Raeden Park Road, near Foresterhill Health Campus, on Thursday.
NHS Grampian has been at the centre of controversy since a report from the health watchdog published two weeks ago highlighted "major deficiencies" in its leadership and culture.
Habib, a consultant surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), leaked the 2022 report the following week.
The Scottish government then announced an independent review into concerns around hepatobiliary (HPB) surgery at the health board.
A number of patients have come forward to raise concerns about their treatment.
On Thursday, Scotland's chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith, who had faced questions over his role, resigned on mental health grounds.
The September 2022 report was written by Prof Stephen Wigmore, regius professor of clinical surgery at Edinburgh University.
It looked at 45 patients in the care of liver and pancreatic services at ARI between 2015 and 2021.
It said 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.
The review criticised decision-making in liver surgery for occasionally being "overly aggressive", with surgery going ahead even if the disease was thought to be inoperable.
In pancreatic surgery, patients were regularly rushed into theatre without adequate planning or consideration of non-surgical alternatives, the report said.
Laura Skaife-Knight urged anyone with concerns about their care to contact the health board
A follow-up report was published in November 2022 where Wigmore was asked to review more HPB surgery cases which had not been within the scope of his original report.
It found unacceptably high mortality rates for some pancreatic surgeries, as well as "extremely high" blood loss for a number of pancreas and liver operations.
The professor said surgeons had low caseloads, which harmed their technical experience.
He offered to support the surgeons, then issued a letter in May 2023 which said HPB services at NHS Grampian had improved and was now safe.

The health board's chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight said that following the presentation of the Wigmore report in 2022, there had been Serious Adverse Event Reviews (SAERs) for patients where the circumstances surrounding their deaths warranted detailed investigation.
"These reviews included the offer of engagement with and psychological support for affected families," she said.

"We have welcomed the independent review into HPB at NHS Grampian and it's important we don't pre-empt the findings of this work. We will co-operate fulsomely and in a way that is nothing other than open and honest."
She said the names of patients and families had been redacted from the second report to protect their identities, and the health board was "contacting/re-engaging" them to offer support.
"I recognise the significant concern the events of the last week have caused our patients and local community," she said.
"However, I would encourage anyone who needs our care to come forward at the earliest opportunity.
"Please continue to engage with our healthcare services and attend appointments and operations as normal. Our priority remains patient safety."
Prof Hiscox, who was in charge of NHS Grampian when the reports were written, has submitted evidence ahead of the Holyrood health committee meeting on Wednesday.
She said the NHS Grampian board was fully briefed on the first Wigmore report at a meeting on 27 October 2022.

This was done to "protect patient and staff confidentiality", provide time for patients and families to be contacted, and "enable full and frank discussion of the issues and avoid causing undue public alarm that could potentially increase the likelihood of late presentation and possibly lead to poorer health outcomes".
Her evidence said this "communications approach was shared with relevant officials at Scottish government".
She also said the families of 17 of the 19 patients whose deaths had been avoidable were contacted, but contact details could not be identified for the other two.
A Scottish government spokesperson said the documents released to date had shown that a number of government officials were aware of the concerns raised by Dr Habib.
"It is a matter of public record that the Scottish government has engaged on the concerns raised by Dr Habib over a number of years," it said.
The spokesperson added that the independent review would deliver "clarity, transparency and accountability to patients and their families".
The committee will also hear from two whistleblowers who have raised concerns about patient safety at NHS Grampian.
In his evidence ahead of the hearing, Dr Izhar Khan - who currently works as a consultant pephrologist at ARI - said the roots of the problems dated back more than 14 years.
"For years senior management has not listened to clinical advice and on occasions when advice was given, often it was ignored," he said.
The senior clinician also said he believed Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin, Moray, was not fit for purpose to deliver acute services.
Dr Khan said the health board needed "strong and resilient leadership that listens to clinicians and staff".
Prof Zygmunt Krukowski, former consultant general surgeon at ARI, has also written to the committee ahead of his appearance.
He said it was "distressing" to see the reputation of the hospital where he worked for more than 40 years damaged by "inept management and clinical governance".
"If there had been effective clinical leadership and management the pattern of poor care which was clinically obvious as early as 2010 would have been addressed," he added.
The confidential papers found discarded on a street on Thursday are believed to consist of four crumpled pages, dated from the day before.
They are understood to have listed names, CHI numbers and medical conditions of 22 neurosurgery patients.

NHS Grampian's senior information risk officer, Shantini Paranjothy said: "We are making efforts to contact those patients whose data was contained in these documents and apologise for the distress this has caused.
"Investigations into how these documents ended up in a public place are under way and this incident has been reported to the Information Commissioner's Office.
"Patients have the right to expect their data to be stored securely. We take the issue of data protection very seriously."

items.title: Explainer: Why Beijing is watching Taiwan’s local elections, and what they could mean for 2028
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

When Taipei voters choose a mayor Saturday, they will decide who oversees housing and transportation in Taiwan’s capital. They will also choose who represents Taipei at an annual forum with Shanghai, one of the few places where senior officials from Taiwan and China still meet. One candidate, Puma Shen, is wanted by Chinese police on allegations of separatism.

The Taipei race illustrates why Beijing is watching elections fought largely over local concerns. Across Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties, the results could shape whom Beijing deals with and which parties enter Taiwan’s 2028 presidential campaign with the strongest local networks.

Nearly 19.6 million people are eligible to vote for mayors and county magistrates, according to Taiwan’s Central Election Commission. The “nine-in-one” elections cover nine categories of local office and will fill 11,051 posts, down to village and neighborhood chiefs. A separate national referendum asks whether Taiwan should use nuclear power to boost its economy and abandon its goal of a nuclear-free homeland.

Transportation, housing, and public services have featured prominently in the campaigns. The central government sets defense policy and manages relations with Beijing. Saturday’s vote leaves intact the legislative majority held jointly by the opposition Kuomintang, or KMT, and the smaller Taiwan People’s Party, or TPP.

William Brent Christensen, a former director of the American Institute in Taiwan, told VOA in Washington on November 17 that the campaigns had focused largely on domestic issues. He expected some impact on U.S. engagement with Taiwan, though he saw no specific implication for those ties.

“The United States “certainly interacts with both major parties,” Christensen said. “We believe that Taiwan is fully capable of conducting free and fair elections, and we look forward to seeing how things turn out this year.”
Why does the Taipei race matter to Beijing?

China considers Taiwan part of its territory and has refused to talk with President Lai Ching-te, whom it labels a separatist. Lai rejects Beijing’s claim, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide the island’s future. Beijing does keep channels open with the KMT, which supports closer ties with China.

In Taipei, KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an faces Shen, a lawmaker from Lai’s Democratic Progressive Party, or DPP, who has studied Chinese disinformation. Shen told Reuters he would be willing to continue the Taipei-Shanghai forum if Beijing imposed no political conditions and refrained from harassment. Chiang’s campaign has also said outside powers should refrain from pressuring Taiwanese voters. A Shen victory would raise a question for Beijing: Would Shanghai officials sit down with a mayor whom Chinese police are pursuing?

Two cities offer a test of each major party’s ability to win on the other’s turf. New Taipei, which surrounds the capital, has more than 3.4 million eligible mayoral voters, the largest electorate in Taiwan. The DPP’s Su Chiao-hui faces the KMT’s Lee Shu-chuan for an office the KMT holds. In the southern port of Kaohsiung, the KMT is trying to capture a DPP stronghold with more than 2.3 million eligible voters.

For Lai, who is eligible to seek a second term, gains in KMT-held cities could strengthen his standing within the DPP, according to analysts Emma Y. Liu and Edgard D. Kagan of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The KMT has yet to choose a presidential candidate. Outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen is considered a leading contender. Lai himself served as mayor of Tainan before becoming president.

Saturday also offers an early test of opposition cooperation. The TPP backs Chiang in Taipei while fielding its own candidates elsewhere. Its ability to win offices under its own name could affect its bargaining power in any talks with the KMT about a joint campaign in 2028.

Recent elections show how differently Taiwanese voters can judge candidates for mayor and president. In 2018, the KMT won 15 of Taiwan’s 22 city and county leadership posts. Two years later, voters reelected DPP President Tsai Ing-wen. In 2022, the KMT won 14 of those posts. In 2024, voters chose Lai.

items.title: Alun Wyn Jones urges men to talk about hair loss after transplant
paragraphs: Rugby legend Alun Wyn Jones has urged men to open up about hair loss, saying he was "very comfortable" talking about the fact he has had a hair transplant.
Speaking one year since his operation, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions captain said men typically do not talk about the issue, but said "a lot of people" had spoken to him about it.
"I think it's important that people know there's a lot of people out there they can talk to," he said.
Jones played 158 times for Wales and 12 for the Lions, making him the most capped rugby player in history before he retired in 2023.
Jones, 41, from Swansea, said he "wasn't conscious" about his hair loss until his playing days were coming to an end.
He spent most of his career playing for the Ospreys, before a stint for Toulon in France near the end of his career.
He said his playing career had prevented him from getting a transplant sooner because of the time off required after the procedure and then to "recover properly".
But after his retirement he said he began to learn more about it and had the operation.
He said he hoped his openness about hair loss would encourage other men to talk about the issue.
"Men in general don't talk, but I've had a lot of people talk to me about it," he said.

items.title: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
paragraphs: Four million people in Lagos, Nigeria may be exposed to extreme sea levels by the end of the century, a new study says
Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.
Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.

The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.
Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".
This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change.
Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.
In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.
But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.
Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days.
"[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".
The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.
More of Alexandria could be exposed to flooding than previously thought, the research says
The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.
If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.
Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.
Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.
The man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained.
One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking.
The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests.
In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence.
Hear from those trying to solve the problem
Methods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops.
"Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level.
The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.
The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.
Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

items.title: Rare panto programmes owned by 'Freddie Mercury of his time' sell at auction
paragraphs: A rare pair of pantomime programmes from the private theatre of a man dubbed "the Freddie Mercury of his time" have sold at auction for £3,600.
The 4th Marquess of Anglesey Henry Cyril Paget, also known as the Dancing Marquess, used his family home Plas Newydd, on Anglesey, to stage lavish productions free for local people.
His life was recently turned into a biopic, with Callum Scott Howells playing the aristocrat.
The programmes were for a production of Red Riding Hood and in the shapes of Little Red Riding Hood and Little Boy Blue.
Auctioneer Ben Rogers Jones said they were a "special piece of history" allowing people to look at text "Paget's audience held in their hands on Boxing Day 1902".
Rogers Jones added it was difficult to predict what "two bits of cardboard could make", but the backstory and film, nominated for six Bafta Cymru awards, helped with the sale.
"There is definitely hype around what is a very modern story," he said.
"He was a flamboyant character. A Freddie Mercury of his time."
Paget was declared bankrupt at the start of the 20th Century, and his 17,000 possessions were sold in a 40-day auction to pay his creditors.
He lived a life of excess before dying from tuberculosis aged 29 in 1905.

items.title: Police suspect criminals robbed fans at Manchester gig disrupted by ‘unknown substance’
paragraphs: A group of organised criminals are believed to have carried out robberies during Don Toliver’s Manchester concert, where an “unknown substance” was released, police have said, with similar incidents having occurred at another two of the US rapper’s gigs in Europe.
Greater Manchester police said they were working to identify the suspects and the substance involved during the incident at the Co-op Live Arena on Sunday evening.

No arrests have been made but mobile phone and CCTV footage is being reviewed by officers, a police statement said. The force is working with other law enforcement agencies across Europe after similar incidents at two Toliver gigs, which officers believe are “relevant” to their inquiries.

Eighty-nine people displayed symptoms believed to be linked to exposure to the substance during the performance in Manchester. The venue was evacuated and a major incident declared as those in the crowd described a “horrible smell”, which police initially believed to be teargas.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue, and medical officials urged anyone who had become unwell after leaving to get in touch. Some of the dozens assessed by doctors reported eye and respiratory symptoms.
Police in Switzerland said four men were arrested after thefts at a concert at the Hallenstadion in Zurich on 26 October.
Zurich cantonal police said the men were seen mingling with people dancing in the crowd in order to get close enough to steal their necklaces.
Several necklaces and a canister of pepper spray were found after the suspects were searched, the force said.
The men – two Moroccan nationals, 29 and 25, and two Italian nationals, 26 and 22 – were handed to the public prosecutor’s office after police questioning.

Tom Harding, Greater Manchester police assistant chief constable, said: “We’re working to identify those suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents. All of this work is ongoing at pace.
“There are similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our inquiries. We’re in contact with law enforcement involved in those investigations.

“No arrests have been made, but our detectives are working through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV. There are over a 100 people at the gig we are working to try to contact to assist with our inquiries. We thank all those that have assisted us so far.”

Harding said the force was aware some people had been affected psychologically during the Co-op Live incident because of the 2017 terror attack at the Manchester Arena where 22 people were killed by the suicide-bomber Salman Abedi.

He added: “We also know many more people were impacted on the night and afterwards, physically and psychologically. What happened on Sunday night and the imagery on our TVs and online will bring back painful memories of 2017.
“Thankfully, we are not dealing with an incident of such a devastating nature or motive; however, we understand the impact this is likely to have caused.”

items.title: Chicken Shop Date: The perfect end or a disappointing send-off?
paragraphs: After more than 10 years, Amelia Dimoldenberg announced Chicken Shop Date was shutting up shop
For better or worse, everyone recalls their first date. But how will the last one be remembered?
After more than a decade of serving up her awkward, off-the-wall questions, Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date is no longer looking for love, with the YouTuber calling time on her hit series.

From a youth club project to a full-blown media empire with A-listers asking her out, the series has influenced the interview landscape and carved a new path for the next generation of content creators.
"To start my next chapter, I have to close this one," Dimoldenberg told the BBC earlier this month.
"I'm focussing on making sure I say goodbye in the perfect way so I feel ready to do my next thing."
This article contains spoilers for the final episode of Chicken Shop Date.
After much speculation as to who would be the final date, fans were never going to be able to agree as to whether the farewell was indeed perfect.
Names like Harry Styles and Beyoncé had been floated around, but it was Drake who was the favourite with some bookies after Dimoldenberg previously described the Canadian rapper as her dream date.
So when the camera panned to psychotherapist Esther Perel, "everyone was a bit surprised", says fan Sarah Almond, who watched an early cinema screening on Tuesday.
Relationships expert Perel is also a bestselling author and podcast host
"I wasn't familiar with Esther Perel myself and I don't think anyone else in the cinema was aware of who she was," the content creator tells BBC Newsbeat.
And when the episode went live on YouTube, while most viewers reacted positively to the choice of guest, some said they did not recognise her and asked "where's Drake?!".
"I did hear a few people say they were disappointed, but I wasn't disappointed at all," Almond says.
"Even though I was expecting a bigger name to go off with a big bang, it was exactly what the show needed."
The episode played out like a counselling session, becoming emotional at points, Almond says.
"She's treating the end of Chicken Shop Date like it's a relationship break-up.
"It served her really well. It was a nice goodbye."
Sarah Almond says the final episode was "bittersweet" but a fitting end for the series
Signing off with an interview with a relationships expert is a sign of the journey Dimoldenberg has been on with her pioneering series.

With more than three million YouTube subscribers, Chicken Shop Date has climbed the pecking order to become a key stop on press tours for even some of the world's biggest names, including the likes of Cher and Sir Paul McCartney.
Rachel Adeolu watched the series from the very beginning, when Dimoldenberg would mostly date emerging rap and grime artists.
"A chicken shop is somewhere that's very familiar to a lot of people who grew up in London," the 21-year-old says. "It's kind of like a third space where a lot of us built friendships.
"So seeing content creators who also looked like us being interviewed in that same kind of setting with this unconventional interview style, which was also very funny, was unheard of."
Rachel Adeolu was a fan of how the series represented black culture when it first started
By 2021, seven years on from the first episode, the show was starting to look different.
As well as rappers and content creators, Dimoldenberg was bagging interviews with pop stars like Ed Sheeran and Finneas, as well as footballers Tammy Abraham and John Stones.
It was about that time producer Liv West joined the team, and her background at a major music publisher helped the series secure an impressive roster of guests.
"That summer we had a really big line-up," she says, with the likes of Keke Palmer, Charli XCX and Rosalía looking for love at first bite.
"It was then we started to think the tides are changing," she adds.
Liv West was a producer on Chicken Shop Date for almost five years
As the profiles of the dates grew though, so did their teams, with West saying it became a challenge to squeeze everyone in for shoots - with some being put into the kitchen.
The producer feels things ramped up after the episode with documentary maker Louis Theroux, as he was not a typical guest and of "legendary status".
For earlier fans like Adeolu, the take-off came at a cost.

"It feels like the audience who are more interested in seeing A-list celebrities be interviewed, they have definitely been favoured over the people who made the show popular in the first place," she says.
"In terms of just the initial charm of what the show was, I think that has probably had a negative impact on it."
Dimoldenberg has collaborated with Theroux multiple times since their date in 2022
As Dimoldenberg reached new audiences, her success started to balloon and before long she was appearing on major red carpets, in films and magazines - as well as a guest on other people's talk shows.
It also allowed her to work on a passion project: Dimz Inc Academy.
Launched in 2025, the scheme aims to upskill and mentor young people from underrepresented backgrounds who want to get into creative industries.
"It was Amelia's big dream to really make the creative industry, and particularly digital entertainment, accessible from every walk of life for every young person," West says.
Now in its second year, the scheme will be a legacy for the series away from screens - but as for what's next for the series' star, that's yet to be revealed.
"I really want to spend more time writing, that's what I'd like to focus on in the future," Dimoldenberg told the BBC.
"But who knows, the possibilities are endless."
Additional reporting by Naomi Clarke, Miya Chahal and Srosh Khan.
Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

items.title: Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil
paragraphs: Brazilian firm Estúdio 41 has completed Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that “explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete“.

Located in the seaside community of Prainha, which sits within the city of Guaratuba in southern Brazil, the holiday home was designed for a family to serve as “a refuge between the mountains and the sea”.

“One of their main requirements was, therefore, a strong visual connection between the interior spaces and the surrounding natural landscape,” said Estúdio 41, an architectural firm based in Curitiba.
Rectangular in plan, the 375-square-metre house has two floors. It is wrapped in folding screens made of perforated melamine panels.
The screens filter natural light and reduce solar gain on glass surfaces. When opened up, they reveal views of the scenic landscape.
“At night, the transparency and geometric patterns of the house’s skin give it the appearance of a lantern within the landscape,” the team said.
To protect against flooding, as the coastal site has been affected by storm surges in the past, the building was lifted up 70 centimeters (2.3 feet).
It has a prefabricated concrete structural system that was assembled in only six hours, with the concrete structural elements left visible.

The system consists of six columns, four beams and 20 double-tee slabs, also known as “π” (pi)-shaped slabs. The latter are pre-stressed concrete panels with a cross-section that resembles the Greek letter π.
“The project explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete,” said the team.
“The conception of a very simple and easily executable construction system reflects a concern for the realities of the local workforce,” it contniued.
“The construction technique, the modular arrangement of the structural components, and the ribs of the double-tee floor slabs are all clearly legible.”
Rooms feature artful decor and a neutral colour palette. The ground level contains an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room, along with service areas and a guest bedroom.
The communal area opens toward a garden, and beyond it, a sheltered barbecue terrace and a swimming pool.
“The social areas were conceived as one large veranda in direct contact with the beach sand, with views of both the sea and mountains,” the team said.
The upper level contains four bedrooms, including the primary suite, and a family room. A bridge passes over the garden below and connects to a concrete terrace with sweeping views of the sea.
Other projects by Estudio 41 include a small white house in Brazil with a roof garden, and a prefabricated, teal-coloured research station in Antarctica.

items.title: The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children
paragraphs: It sounds benign: the Com, short for the Community. But crime agencies around the world warn that it is far from that and the young cybercriminals involved are causing havoc and putting children at chilling, sickening risk.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed by a UK judge on Friday for his activities as part of the Com. He was one individual operating from his bedroom in north-east England, but there are probably thousands more like him and parents are being urged by police to be aware and to check their children’s devices.

The Com, crime agencies say, is a sprawling and fluid global network of online communities populated by young cybercriminals. A typical Com member is a boy or young man aged 16 to 25. They are primarily native English speakers. Their crimes are broad and may include data theft, crypto scams, bringing down IT systems and causing chaos through attacks that slow down networks.
Then there are young men such as Mensforth who targeted vulnerable young girls and encouraged them to harm themselves or sacrifice their pets.
Often the criminals coerce girls to take indecent images of themselves which they then share. They blackmail and threaten their victims with swatting and doxing, police say.

Swatting is the term used for reporting fictitious incidents at the victim’s address to the emergency services, so they turn up in numbers, sometimes armed. Doxing is threatening to put all of someone’s personal details online.

They operate on every platform, according to DCI Steve Brown of Northumbria police, who led the investigation into Mensforth. “They target people they know have vulnerabilities, people who need somebody to make them feel wanted, to feel valued,” said Brown. “They gain that trust and then they turn that trust against them by asking them to perform horrendous acts.”
In July 2025, the FBI issued its first big public alert about the Com under the headline: “Theft, extortion and violence are a rising threat to youth online”.

The FBI said the Com was a growing and evolving online threat, calling it “a primarily English-speaking, international, online ecosystem comprised of multiple interconnected networks whose members, many of whom are minors, engage in a variety of criminal violations”.
It added: “The FBI estimates thousands of individuals identify as current or recent members of the Com with varying levels of associated activity.”

The UK’s National Crime Agency has said reports of Com networks increased sixfold in the UK from 2022-2024, describing members as “usually young men who are motivated by status, power, control, misogyny, sexual gratification, or an obsession with extreme or violent material”.

The Molly Rose Foundation, a leading UK online safety charity, this year issued a stark public warning about the Com and called for a coordinated global response from governments, regulators, law enforcement and tech companies.

Andy Burrows, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The growing threat posed by Com networks is the most chilling and urgent threat to children online today and it requires a swift and comprehensive response.”
The motivations of Com members vary but, according to the FBI, often fall into one of these categories: “Financial gain, retaliation, ideology, sexual gratification and notoriety.”
They wanted to have control, said Brown. They got a kick out of getting people to do things they would never normally do.

Courts around the world are increasingly dealing with criminals linked to the Com. Sentences vary but there’s thought to be none longer than the 77-year jail term handed down in August, in Tennessee, to Kyle Spitze, 27, for abetting the distribution of animal crushing videos and child sexual exploitation material offences.
The US Department of Justice said Spitze’s crimes occurred as part of his association with an online network known for its “sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people around the world”.
Crime agencies such as the FBI urge people “to exercise caution when posting or messaging personal information, photos or videos on social media, dating sites or other online platforms”.
For parents it can be bewildering and scary but they do need to monitor their child’s online activity, police say.

After the gruelling slog of the Mensforth case, Brown said he now checked the devices of his own children. “Personally, since this investigation, I do that to my kids,” he said. “It’s simply asking parents: talk, know and act. Talk to your children, know what they’re doing and act upon it.”

items.title: 'Calculating predator' who blackmailed girls into self-harm jailed for 14 and a half years
paragraphs: A "cowardly monster" who blackmailed girls across the world into self-harming for the entertainment of others has been detained for 14 and a half years.
Beau-Jack Mensforth was 17 when he began forcing vulnerable girls to send sexual images, hurt animals and carve his assumed name into their bodies, Newcastle Crown Court heard.
One of the girls' mothers said he used the internet to breach the safety of his victims' homes and minds, causing lifelong devastation.
Mensforth, 20 and from Sunderland, admitted 17 offences. They included crimes against nine victims, the youngest of whom was aged 12, and having indecent images of children as young as five.
Mensforth was in online groups who made content for their "com", short for community, by victimising "vulnerable young girls", prosecutor Charlotte Hole said.
They often targeted girls in self-harm support groups and used apps including Telegram and Discord to befriend them.

Abusers convinced the girls they were in romantic relationships and coaxed them into sending indecent images of themselves, then threatened to publish the pictures unless they committed more "extreme" acts, the court heard.
If you are affected by any issues raised, help can be found through BBC Action Line
The girls would be forced to carve the names of their abusers into their flesh and write messages and logos in blood promoting the "com" groups.
They were also ordered to "sacrifice" animals under the threat their personal information would be released online or false reports would be made to trigger armed police raids of their homes.
Under the username Yuri, Mensforth targeted girls in the UK, USA and Australia, making them write "I worship Yuri" in blood among a litany of other abuses.
When one of his victims asked him why he was doing it, Mensforth replied "for content", the court heard, with the abuser seeking to rise to the top of the group's hierarchy.
A victim from the USA said she was 16 when she was "lured" into Mensforth's "online child predator group".
Having been forced to harm herself, the pictures of her "mutilated" body then got thousands of views online, she said.
She said she begged her abusers to take the images down but they refused, adding: "The more I cried about it the more amusement it seemed to bring them."
Her mother said she had no idea there were "cowardly monsters" like Mensforth "hiding behind a screen tormenting our baby girl".
A UK-based victim, who was 13 when Mensforth began abusing her, reported himto police.
"Instead of looking back at my early teen years and being filled with joy, I'm reminded of the fear and violation I felt," she said.
Her body was "covered" with scars inflicted at Mensforth's behest, she said, describing him as a "psychopath" who "feeds off the pain" of others.
Other victims said they had ongoing mental health issues and their trauma was worse because the images were still online.
Mensforth admitted blackmail, sexual communications with children, making and distributing indecent images of children and participating in an organised crime group between 2023 and 2024.

Judge Edward Bindloss said Mensforth was a "calculating predator" who groomed, manipulated and blackmailed girls for those who shared his "taste for sexual violence and enjoyed watching females self-harm".
Mensforth "rose to play a leading role" in the harm group and "thrived" on his status, the judge said.
Bindloss said Mensforth, who told probation workers he hoped to push a girl into killing herself, would have to serve six years on extended licence.
