items.title: Veruschka obituary
paragraphs: The aspiring model Vera von Lehndorff created “Veruschka” – little Vera – as a memorable alternative persona whose existence was performance art.

She used her natural resources: a 6ft-plus-tall body that, horizontal, could fill an entire glossy magazine spread; a face with magnificent bone architecture and feline eyes; and a long mane that was amenable to brutal short cuts and extraordinary coiffures. All were animated by her instinct for making shapes in air – not a model’s poses but a dancer’s movements that only a click of the lens could catch. Watch her seducing the camera of the photographer, played by David Hemmings, in Michelangelo Antonioni’s 1966 film Blow Up to see her original act in action.

These gifts made Veruschka, who has died aged 87, one of fashion’s greatest stars for 15 years, with hundreds of magazine covers (she did not keep count), many for Vogue. She was just what the new empress editor of American Vogue, Diana Vreeland, wanted in order to express the exotic aspects of 1960s culture. When first introduced to the young model, Vreeland pinned her photo to her wall and declared: “You’re going to hear from me.”

Veruschka was a big, and deep, enough “character” to sustain Vreeland’s wild fantasies, including a legendary 1966 sequence shot by Richard Avedon in Hokkaido, Japan’s “snow country”, a cinematic epic with Veruschka wrapped in a zoo’s-worth of furs plus an 8ft-long Dynel wig. Vreeland wanted it to be 20 feet. Veruschka could have carried that off too.

Nothing seemed preposterous with Veruschka in focus: for fun she attended Woodstock in 1969, in multiple necklaces and a minimal bra, and every camera gravitated to her. Vreeland went so far as to allow Veruschka and her then lover, the photographer Franco Rubartelli, to come up with their own mad ideas, such as a moonlit shoot on Christmas Day on the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas; he also snapped her adventuring in an Yves Saint Laurent safari jacket in 1968, an image that established the designer’s bold-woman credentials.

Besides Avedon, who thought her the most beautiful woman in the world, other Vogue photographers, from the old-school Horst P Horst and Irving Penn to Bert Stern and David Bailey, enjoyed collaboration with Veruschka, open to any experiment except smiling, though Steven Meisel did at last capture her surprisingly goofy grin.

It had been an Italian photographer, Johnny Moncada, who helped Vera create Veruschka. The photographer Ugo Mulas had spotted her beauty when she was studying art in Florence in 1959, but Paris turned her away for being too tall, and the New York agency chief Eileen Ford advised her to starve on hard-boiled eggs, then rejected her.

Back in Italy, she and Moncada did sporadic jobs together over a year, and when those pictures were published in 2014 as a book, From Vera to Veruschka, she remembered how he developed her on-camera persona by encouraging her to reveal her real feelings: “Having a look of sadness in my eyes is my biggest problem … he allowed me to be myself, even if that meant looking melancholy.”

Her life had had much to be sad about. She was born the daughter of Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, with a family castle on their estate in Steinort, East Prussia: he was executed in 1944 for his part in the July plot to assassinate Hitler. The Gestapo imprisoned his pregnant wife, Gottliebe von Kalnein, and sent young Vera and her sisters, Gabriele and Marie, to an SS-run children’s home in Bad Sachsa. They were reunited with their mother and new sister, Catharina, after the war’s end, but were homeless and shunned in Germany. They lived wherever a relative took them in, which meant 13 different schools in which the spidery, long and thin Vera was always an outsider.

None of this was known to the fashion world, which easily accepted the vaguely eastern European identity suggested by the pseudonym Veruschka, and took advantage of her metier for metamorphosis. The 60s were the era of the international “Beautiful People”, and Veruschka was the fairest of them all.

Yet even during her peak years, when she commanded an unprecedented $10,000 a day, she wanted to dissolve into the background, and on shoots camouflaged herself with shoe polish to disappear into a Kenyan landscape, or used body paint to match herself to a floor.

She finally gave up on fashion in 1975, after Grace Mirabella, who had deposed Vreeland as Vogue editor and was under orders to democratise the magazine, told her that she needed to be more ordinary, what we would call “relatable”. Veruschka interpreted that as more bourgeois and stalked away in her usual flat shoes.

Thereafter, she lived under her own name as the simultaneous artist’s model and artist she had intended to be, using her body for a canvas. She had worked with the photographer Holger Trülzsch from 1970. He painted her to blend into surrounding natural surfaces for fine art photographs, and then in 1978 for performances where she absorbed herself into old buildings. They also played with painting clothes directly on to her body, an exploration of, and revenge for, her years of exposure to fashion. Trülzsch and Veruschka published a monograph of their work, Trans-figurations, in 1986, with a forward by Susan Sontag.
As an artist she led a simple life in Brooklyn and, from 2005, in suburban Berlin, where she wrote an autobiography, Veruschka: Mein Leben, published in 2011.

Fashion asked her back occasionally, paying well for her to parade on a show catwalk, something she had not done in her glory years. She did not care whether the designers were unknowns or Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel, as she had never liked couture. Her personal style remained haute hippy, almost any length of cloth or exaggerated makeup looking elegant on her frame and face. In a late appearance, aged nearly 80, in denim and worn leather for Acne Studios, she was as cool and beyond it all as ever.
Her sisters Gabriele and Catharina survive her.

items.title: If you want a new TV, these Black Friday deals save up to 47%
paragraphs: If you've been holding out for a new TV, now's the time to take the plunge. Prices on everything from budget 4K sets to premium OLEDs have dropped sharply at Amazon, with some savings approaching 50%.

For creatives who spend all day pouring over visual work, looking for imperfections, a poor quality TV just isn't an option. Instead, even more than the average punter, we need accurate colour, deep blacks and high brightness to properly enjoy TV, movies and video games – and appreciate all these things when we have them.

To save you buying the wrong model, we've picked out three standout deals. The first is our top pick, balancing price and performance. The second is brilliant budget buy. And the third is a premium OLED for anyone who wants the very best picture. Of course, if you'd rather a smaller display, check out all the best Black Friday iPad deals.

It mostly comes down to how and where you watch. If picture quality is your priority, especially in a dimmer room, OLED is hard to beat. Because every pixel lights itself, blacks are truly black and contrast is superb, making the LG C6 is our premium pick. Mini-LED sets such as the Hisense U8 can't quite match that, but they get much brighter, making them a better fit for sunny living rooms, and they give you more screen for your money. If you just need a decent 4K TV for a spare room or studio, a budget set like the Amazon Ember will do the job nicely.

It's also worth thinking about size before you click buy. Measure your space and viewing distance, and remember that the price jump between sizes can be surprisingly small: on the Hisense deal, for instance, going from 55 to 65 inches costs just $150 more. Gamers should look for a high refresh rate and VRR support, which both the Hisense and LG offer. And if you'll use the TV to review your own photos or video, turn off any motion smoothing and switch to Filmmaker Mode or the most accurate picture preset.
Want expert-reccomended deals on top creative tech, tools and kit?
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: GTA 6 crashes into top end of music chart after its record launch
paragraphs: Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.
But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.
Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.
Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.
Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.
Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.
It originally peaked at number 58 in the UK 11 years ago, but has re-entered the charts at number 28.
Speaking to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage, Jepsen remembered feeling the track had "something special to it" when she recorded it.
While it's a favourite among some of the singer's most loyal fans, it has never reached the level of recognition as her hits Call Me Maybe and I Really Like You.
"It never got eyes like it's getting right now," she said.
"It's just so lovely to see that happening, it makes me believe in that special feeling that we had."

There are three elements of GTA 6's soundtrack, including an official, double-sided album containing tracks recorded for the game, and an original score composed by electronic duo Justice, due to be fully released in December.
The game also features hundreds of licensed tracks on its in-game radio stations.
Flower In A Hurricane was released as a single in October, giving it time to appear on playlists in the lead-up to the game's debut.
But Mat Ombler, head of partnerships at video game music label Laced Records, says GTA 6's impact on the charts is still impressive.
He says video game soundtracks entering the album charts "isn't unheard of" but "it's incredibly rare to see multiple tracks hitting the singles charts".
Ombler likens the spike in streams of Jepsen's track to the boost Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill got from its inclusion in Netflix hit Stranger Things.

"Both tracks are part of a huge cultural moment, but I'd argue that GTA's usage of Run Away With Me is more impactful... where the music responds according to what you're doing during a key story mission," he says.
Ombler thinks the chart impact of GTA 6 highlights "the growing importance and cultural impact of video game soundtracks as a whole".
"Over 40 million people will spend the coming weeks and months listening to more than 800 tracks featured in the in-game radio stations, possibly hundreds of times," he says.
"They'll discover new music in genres they might never have engaged with otherwise, and this music will stick with them for the rest of their lives."
Steven Ellison, better known as Flying Lotus, points out the GTA series was already an established cultural phenomenon.
Millions of players heard the US producer, DJ, film-maker and rapper hosting FlyLo, one of GTA 5's in-game radio stations.
He also curated its tracklist - a job he confesses was made easier by the series' profile.
"People just wanted to have any involvement at all," he says.
"It was like: 'Who do we want? Who don't we want?' It was incredible."
He says the role gave him an opportunity to "shine a light on musicians from LA", his hometown, and the inspiration for the game's fictional location Los Santos.
It also influenced his own musical taste, he says.
"I remember when I played GTA: Vice City and it was the first time I actually listened to Africa by Toto.
"I was like: 'Man this song is awesome'. I didn't really know it before."
That curated experience, according to Ellison, is a big part of the appeal, and why the game can generate surprise hits out of neglected songs.
"It's so hard to get an experience like that nowadays with the way we listen to music and find music," he says.
"So this is kind of like that experience from back in the day where you're actually being put on to something by hanging out with people and then someone plays a track.
"It's that genuine connection that I think is possible with this."
Additional reporting by BBC Newsbeat reporters Jordan Kenny and Naomi Clarke.

items.title: Taliban rule, security concerns challenge progress on $10 billion TAPI pipeline
paragraphs: Washington — Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Construction of a key section of the long-delayed Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India, or TAPI, gas pipeline is moving forward, but analysts say Afghanistan's political isolation under Taliban rule, tensions between Kabul and Islamabad, and persistent regional security concerns continue to cast doubt on the project's full completion.

According to a Reuters report, Turkmenistan expects to complete the 153-kilometer pipeline segment from Serhetabat to Herat by the end of this year, with gas deliveries to Afghanistan expected to begin in early 2027. The section is part of the broader TAPI project — a roughly 1,814-kilometer pipeline designed to transport Turkmen gas through Afghanistan and Pakistan to India.

The project, first proposed in the 1990s and formally launched in 2015, is estimated to cost about $10 billion. Turkmenistan has largely financed recent construction itself as international lenders and private investors remain reluctant to commit funds.

The Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021 has proven to be a major obstacle. With the exception of Russia, no country formally recognizes the Taliban government, making international financial institutions and investors cautious about backing large projects that rely on long-term engagement with Afghanistan.

The Asian Development Bank, once a key supporter of the project, told Reuters that it paused regular assistance to Afghanistan after the Taliban takeover. The bank said any future technical assistance or financing would depend on prevailing circumstances and required approvals.
Economic affairs analyst Ahmad Sear Quraishi and chairman of the Afghanistan Private Banking Association says the Herat section could still provide meaningful benefits for Afghanistan.
"If this gas is supplied to factories at a reasonable price, it will undoubtedly reduce production costs and create greater opportunities for business and industrial growth," Quraishi told VOA.

He noted that Afghanistan is expected to initially purchase 500 million cubic meters of gas annually from the pipeline intended to carry up to 33 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually to the much larger markets of Pakistan and India.
Quraishi cautioned, however, that political tensions could complicate those plans.

"The transfer of gas through the pipeline to Pakistan and India faces significant challenges," he said. "The existing tensions between Kabul and Islamabad, along with the long-standing disputes between India and Pakistan, mean that the continuation of the project will depend on agreements among Afghanistan, Pakistan and India."
Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have deteriorated in recent years amid border clashes, disputes over militant activity and disagreements over cross-border security.

items.title: The best cordless vacuum cleaners for a spotless home: 10 tried and tested favourites
paragraphs: Choosing a cordless vacuum is a big decision. Whichever model you go for, you’re likely to use it for years, relying on its ability to suck up dust, crumbs, mud, pet hair and any other dry spillages or sheddings. Choosing the right model can be the difference between an effective cleaner that’s a delight to pull out of the cupboard and a dud that you dread having to unblock, detangle and clean after every use.

In this review, I took 18 of the leading cordless vacuum cleaners from a range of manufacturers and at various prices and inflicted the same cleaning tests on each one. That takes all the guesswork out of picking your next cleaner: I can tell you exactly which ones picked up the most mess, and how easy and enjoyable they were to use.
Best cordless vacuum cleaner overallShark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251UKT
Best budget cordless vacuum cleanerHoover HF3 Pet DynamicClean
Best cordless vacuum for deep cleaningDyson V15 Detect Absolute
Best cordless vacuum for clean emptyingHenry Quick Pro
Best handheld cordless vacuum cleanerDyson Car+Boat

I’ve been reviewing technology and home products for more than 30 years. In the past few years, I’ve specialised in testing vacuum cleaners. During that time, I’ve tested more vacuum cleaners of various shapes, sizes and types than I’d care to count, from handheld helpers to heavy-duty dirt-shifters.

Most cordless vacuum cleaners are designed to work on carpet and hard floors, so I tested them all on both, where applicable. To do this, I weighed out spillages of flour, recycled wood cat litter pellets and pet hair. Flour and cat litter are easy enough to come by, but my dog doesn’t shed enough hair to test this many vacuums. So I’m also the proud owner of a box of sweepings from a friendly (but slightly bemused) local dog groomer.

I gave each of the 18 vacuum cleaners I tested a chance to pick up as much of the spillages as possible with a single push-forward and pull-backward motion, and weighed the collection bins before and after.

Most vacuums will collect more if given repeat chances to go over a mess, particularly from a different angle, but I wanted relatively tough tests that would truly differentiate one vacuum from another, so I allowed only a single sweep.

I also tested the batteries by seeing how long it took them to run down from a full charge – at full suction and in each one’s most economical setting. I performed these tests with the floor head attached, where possible.

Lastly, I tested the suction using a pressure gauge. While strong suction is useful, the cleaning tests were more important because other factors play a big part in the overall cleaning prowess. For example, a well-designed floor head can make a moderate sucker as good a cleaner as a more powerful model with an inferior brush or roller.
All the vacuums I tested have been sent back to their manufacturers or donated to the British Heart Foundation.
What we loveExcellent cleaner; empties into docking station

If there’s one thing that makes cordless vacuum cleaners a pain, it’s the emptying: taking it to the bin and jettisoning the debris after vacuuming. And, if your family is anything like mine, you may have to do it before you clean too, because someone else didn’t bother to empty it. That won’t be the case with this Shark vacuum, though: it empties itself. It’s also very good at cleaning.

Why we love itThe Shark IP3251 comes with a base station that operates as a stand and charging dock. When you rest the cordless vacuum cleaner on it, it springs into life, opening the base of the vacuum’s collection bin and sucking its contents into a larger container, leaving the cordless stick empty and ready for next time. The secondary bin has a volume of two litres, so it can take a few empties of the 0.7-litre stick.

That would all be pointless if the device itself wasn’t up to snuff, but it’s an excellent cleaner. Its floor head has a fluffy roller for hard floors and a brush bar for carpet, and it works well on both surfaces, performing a literal clean sweep in my tests.

It’s a shame that … I found it worked better if I held it lower while vacuuming on some carpets, with the fins on the base otherwise catching when I pulled it back. That may make it better for shorter than taller people.
Weight: 3.71kgSuction power (tested): 28kPaBattery life (tested): 43minsDust capacity: 0.7lAdditional filters supplied? No
What we loveExcellent cleaner; empties into docking station
What we loveGreat price for a powerful device that excelled in my tests
What we don’t loveIneffective anti-tangle, occasionally awkward dusting brush

While budget vacuum cleaners often compromise on features and accessories, the Hoover HF3 does a great job of balancing the scales. It doesn’t have all the bells and whistles of more premium vacuums, but it performed very well in my tests and comes with a good range of features and accessories.

Why we love itThe HF3 Pet DynamicClean is both capable and versatile. Its powerful suction gathered all the cat litter and pet hair from carpet and hard floor. My scales reported that it fell slightly short on picking up flour on both floor types, although I couldn’t actually see any left behind on my floors, so it may have got caught up in the brushes and tubes.

In use, it’s light and comfortable to hold. Controls are basic, with only three power settings (Eco, Standard and Turbo) and two buttons: one to switch it on and off and the other to cycle through the power modes. However, there’s a handy screen that shows you exactly how much battery power it has left as a percentage.

Alongside its strong suction, I was impressed by its ease of use. The floor head can support the rest of the vacuum when left upright, so you don’t have to find somewhere to lean it while taking a break. And for those smaller jobs, it comes with a useful crevice tool, a pet tool for upholstery and a dusting brush that’s built into the main handheld unit. This sits around the outside of the extension wand when the main floor head is connected.

It’s a shame that … the roller in the floor head trapped a lot of the hair from my daughter’s bedroom floor despite its anti-tangle design, and the built-in dusting brush is awkward to use in tight spaces.
Weight: 2.54kgSuction power (tested): 29kPaBattery life (tested): 48minsDust capacity: 0.7lAdditional filters supplied? No
What we loveGreat price for a powerful device that excelled in my tests
What we don’t loveIneffective anti-tangle, occasionally awkward dusting brush
What we loveSuperb cleaning on carpet and hard floors
What we don’t loveExpensive and messy to empty

Although the V15 Detect Absolute was usurped at the top of Dyson’s range by the V16 Piston Animal, it remains widely available. That’s good news, because this older model did a much better job of cleaning up in my tests than the V16.

Why we love itThe V15 Detect Absolute is as close to vacuuming perfection as I’ve seen to date. It comes with two interchangeable floor heads: one with a brush bar for carpet, the other with a fluffy roller for hard floor. They blitzed my tests, with the anti-tangle brush bar leaving only tiny fragments of cat litter and a light trace of flour on carpet after a first pass, both of which were easy to deal with on a return visit. On hard floor, the fluffy roller is king, picking up every last morsel of mess that I dropped. Its dust-detecting green glow is a genuine help, highlighting just how effective it is at collecting even tiny particles.

Remove the extension wand, and the Dyson converts into a useful handheld. The included crevice tool is good at getting into tight corners, while the combination upholstery and dusting tool copes with most other problems. Sadly, it doesn’t come with the hair screw tool, which is really effective at removing pet hair from upholstery and also handy on stairs. It’s well worth seeking out as an optional extra if you let your pets on your furniture (and suffer the consequences).
It’s a shame that … Dyson hasn’t managed to solve the conundrum of messy emptying, with this model creating quite a dust cloud when you release dirt into the bin. It’s also really expensive.
Weight: 2.96kgSuction power (tested): 31kPaBattery life (tested): 50minsDust capacity: 0.77lAdditional filters supplied? No
What we loveSuperb cleaning on carpet and hard floors
What we don’t loveExpensive and messy to empty
What we loveDirt collects in bags, eliminating emptying mess
What we don’t loveDisposable bags cost money and are part plastic

Most cordless sticks create a dust cloud when you deposit the contents of their collection bins into your dustbin. With the exception of the newly added Haier I-Pro Clean M5, which has a bag inside its external docking station, the Henry Quick Pro is the only cordless vacuum I’ve reviewed here that uses disposable dirt-capturing bags.

Why we love itWe can’t emphasise this enough – it’s frustrating to vacuum the floor only to have the dust billowing out of your bin and back into the air when you empty it. With the Henry Quick Pro, you push a lever on the top, and the base opens, jettisoning the bag of collected rubbish out of the bottom. It leaves no mess and has the added benefit of no filters to clean.

In my tests, the Quick Pro performed decently enough, other than on hard floors with the cat litter, which it pushed ahead instead of sucking up. That job would be better tackled by removing the extension wand and using the device with a handheld attachment. It comes with a comprehensive selection of accessories, including a motorised mini head for stairs and upholstery, a flexible hose and a useful handle extension for taller users.

It’s a shame that … the bags have a plastic top that holds them in place inside the collection bin. Henry manufacturer Numatic claims to offset the carbon cost, but it would be better environmentally if it didn’t use any plastic at all. They also cost about £1.30 per one-litre bag.
Weight: 3.2kgSuction power (tested): 10.75kPaBattery life (tested): 1hr 11minsDust capacity: 1lAdditional bags supplied? Yes, six pods (bags)
What we loveDirt collects in bags, eliminating emptying mess
What we don’t loveDisposable bags cost money and are part plastic
What we loveAs powerful as a regular Dyson
What we don’t loveA fully equipped Dyson V8 doesn’t cost much more

Dyson doesn’t manufacture a vacuum purely for handheld use, instead opting to repackage an existing cordless stick without the extension wand. The result is a handheld device so powerful that you may wish you could also use it on the floor.

Why we love itThe Dyson Car+Boat is a cunning repackage of the Dyson V8. That model is now the bottom of the range of Dyson’s regular cordless stick cleaners, but it makes for a handheld unit that performs above and beyond expectations.

It comes with three key attachments: a mini-motorised tool for upholstery and stairs; a crevice tool for gaps; and a combination dusting brush and funnel. It’s a powerful combo that cleaned up my test messes with aplomb. I had to use the funnel rather than the motorised tool to collect cat litter, though, because there’s no way this smaller device wouldn’t just push them ahead.

It’s a shame that … you can still buy the V8, with the extension tube and attachments, for a similar price. It also comes with Dyson’s old mini-motorised tool. Newer models come with a better-designed tool, which has a tapering roller that doesn’t trap longer hairs. It would have been a nice addition to this repackage.
Weight: 1.9kgSuction power (tested): 21kPaBattery life (tested): 38minsDust capacity: 0.54lAdditional filters supplied? No
What we loveAs powerful as a regular Dyson
What we don’t loveA fully equipped Dyson V8 doesn’t cost much more
PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty Pet Pro IA3241
What we loveEffective at cleaning on carpets and hard floors
What we don’t loveUnclear messaging when the battery was running out

The second self-emptying Shark in this list, the IA3241, is a smaller and sometimes cheaper version of my favourite, the IP3251, reviewed above. It performed slightly better on carpet and almost as well on hard floors, despite the fact that this model’s floor head doesn’t have the distinctive dual roller that’s typical of Shark’s best cleaners. It’s lighter and easier to push around than the IP3251, though the collection bin has a smaller capacity of 0.47l.

In my battery tests, it appeared to last a good length of time, almost making it to the 50-minute mark. However, in use I found that it couldn’t quite manage a full cleaning circuit of my detached home, and the information screen doesn’t provide enough warning when it’s about to conk out.
It didn’t make the final cut because … the display doesn’t give enough warning when the battery is about to run out.
Weight: 3.2kg; suction power (tested): 24.5kPa; battery life (tested): 49mins 55secs; dust capacity: 0.47l; additional filters supplied? No
PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty Pet Pro IA3241
What we loveEffective at cleaning on carpets and hard floors
What we don’t loveUnclear messaging when the battery was running out
For more, read our full Shark PowerDetect Speed Clean & Empty Pet Pro review
I-Pro Clean M5 cordless vacuum cleaner + docking station
What we loveSelf-emptying into a bag is a clean, dust-free process
What we don’t loveAnti-tangle floor head doesn’t work as well as some rivals

Shark’s self-emptying PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251 is a better all-round vacuum than this Haier alternative, but this model empties itself into a bag instead of just a container you have to empty directly into the dustbin. It’s a double-edged sword, though, because the consumable three-litre bags are an ongoing extra cost (£14.77 for four), but the process of emptying the dust from the unit is far cleaner because all the dirt and dust is contained within the bag.

The vacuum’s main multisurface floor head performed very well in my tests, rivalling the Shark IP3251 in most areas. However, its floor head didn’t cope as well with long hair, quickly getting clogged on my daughter’s bedroom floor. There’s a second floor head supplied with two fluffy rollers for hard floors. It didn’t perform as well as the regular floor head, though, and I was disappointed that it doesn’t spin and glide over the floor like the Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones.
It didn’t make the final cut because … its performance fell short of the self-emptying Shark IP3251.

Weight: 3.24kg; suction power (tested): 27kPa; battery life (tested): 1hr 20mins; dust capacity: 0.7l (vacuum), 3l (base); additional filters supplied? No, but supplied with two bags: one installed and a second spare
I-Pro Clean M5 cordless vacuum cleaner + docking station
What we loveSelf-emptying into a bag is a clean, dust-free process
What we don’t loveAnti-tangle floor head doesn’t work as well as some rivals
What we loveAffordable, effective and easy to use
What we don’t loveBest on carpet, as there’s no soft roller for hard floors

The Vax HomePro Pet-Design is good value for money, coming with a decent selection of accessories for the price. It’s comfortable to hold and use, and simple to operate, keeping the controls to two large buttons and an illuminated ring to show how much power is left in the battery.

Emptying it is straightforward, too. It has a button to open the collection bin, while a sliding action pushes trapped dirt out of the container, so you don’t have to poke your hands in. It also performed well in my cleaning tests, including those for pet hair.
It didn’t make the final cut because … the floor head has just one brush roller, which is unsophisticated when compared with alternatives from Shark and Dyson.
Weight: 3.5kg; suction power (tested): 19kPa; battery life (tested): 34mins; dust capacity: 0.7l; additional filters supplied? No
What we loveAffordable, effective and easy to use
What we don’t loveBest on carpet, as there’s no soft roller for hard floors
What we loveGlides across hard floors, superb in tight spaces

Dyson’s PencilVac Fluffycones is a hard-floor expert designed for a quick, regular sweep of kitchens, dining areas and bathroom floors. It doesn’t work on carpets and is best with dust, crumbs, fluff and light scatterings of pet hair, rather than clumps or chunks of dirt.

While that limits its usefulness, it’s fantastic at what it does. A clever floor head design makes it feel like it’s floating on air, and it can be pushed in any direction, manoeuvring around chair and table legs with ease. As a secondary device just for hard floors, it’s hard to beat.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it only works on hard floors, so can’t replace your existing carpet-friendly vacuum cleaner.
Weight: 1.8kg; suction power (tested): 21kPa; battery life (tested): 23mins; dust capacity: 0.08l; additional filters supplied? No
Read our full Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones review
What we loveGlides across hard floors, superb in tight spaces
What we loveMore affordable self-emptying model than the Shark
What we don’t loveFluffy roller isn’t great on carpet

If you like the idea of the Shark PowerDetect Clean & Empty IP3251 but are put off by the price, Tower has a more affordable alternative. This uses a similar self-emptying base that sucks the dirt out of the collection bin and doubles up as a charging station.

The vacuum cleaner is less sophisticated than Shark’s, with fewer features. It still performed reasonably well in my tests, but it only comes with a fluffy roller. That makes it ideal for homes with mostly hard floors, but it lacks the ability to dig deep into carpet.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it left too much flour and pet hair behind in my carpet cleaning tests.
Weight: 2.6kg; suction power (tested): 26.5kPa; battery life (tested): 43mins; dust capacity: 2l (self-emptying base); additional filters supplied? Yes, one spare
What we loveMore affordable self-emptying model than the Shark
What we don’t loveFluffy roller isn’t great on carpet
What we loveOne head for carpets and hard floors
What we don’t loveRedesigned floor head not as good as the old system
Best for: a Dyson that doesn’t require you to switch floor heads

The V16 Piston Animal is a significant change for Dyson, using a single floor head for both carpet and hard floor. Previously, Dyson’s top-end cordless vacuums came with two interchangeable floor heads, which needed switching over as you changed surfaces.

The redesigned floor head has several design tweaks, but basically uses a brush bar with both bristles and fluffy strips so that it works with either surface. By detecting what it’s cleaning, the vacuum adjusts its spin speed and suction to get the best performance.

Eliminating the requirement to switch makes using this Dyson less of a faff. The downside is that, in my tests, the redesigned floor head wasn’t as effective on either carpets or hard floors as the V15 Detect Absolute above.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I’m used to Dyson’s vacuums producing near-perfect results in my tests, but the redesigned floor head in the V16 fails to deliver, making the V15 a better option.
Weight: 3.4kg; suction power (tested): not applicable; battery life (tested): 1hr 11mins; dust capacity: 1.3l; additional filters supplied? No
For more, read our full Dyson V16 Piston Animal review
What we loveOne head for carpets and hard floors
What we don’t loveRedesigned floor head not as good as the old system
What we loveStands without support, picks up small particles
What we don’t loveStruggled with cat litter; uncomfortable long-term

A constant source of annoyance with cordless vacuum cleaners is that you have to find somewhere to lean them when you want to put them down. The AirFox is light and well-balanced enough to stand on its own, so you can leave it in the middle of the room while you do some dusting, and it won’t fall to the floor.

The trigger needs to be held down to keep the vacuum running, and while there is a trigger lock to keep it in place, it’s fiddly to use. It cleaned well in my tests, though, only really struggling with the cat litter, which seemed to get stuck in the floor head.
It didn’t make the final cut because … I found it uncomfortable to hold for extended periods because the back extends out over the handle, getting in the way of my wrist.
Weight: 2.9kg; suction power (tested): 31kPa; battery life (tested): 1hr 9mins; dust capacity: 0.4l; additional filters supplied? No
What we loveStands without support, picks up small particles
What we don’t loveStruggled with cat litter; uncomfortable long-term
What we don’t loveShort battery life, basic features

Despite being a high-end brand in most categories of domestic appliances, the Miele Duoflex HX1 sits in the middle of this gathering in terms of price. That’s largely thanks to the lack of additional features you get when compared with the likes of Shark and Dyson. It performed well in my cleaning tests but generally proved better on carpets than on hard floors.

It operates in either floor or handheld mode. The floor head is basic, with a simple brush bar and no anti-tangle features. It comes with three handheld attachments – a crevice tool, a basic upholstery nozzle and a dusting brush.

It didn’t make the final cut because … emptying relies on gravity alone, so you end up having to poke your fingers into the collection bin to clear it out. Most disappointing was the battery, which didn’t last long with the floor head attached, even on the weakest suction setting.
Weight: 3.1kg; suction power (tested): 12.5kPa; battery life (tested): 13mins; dust capacity: 0.3l; additional filters supplied? No
What we don’t loveShort battery life, basic features
What we loveSolid build quality, good cleaning performance
What we don’t loveUnnecessary features drive up the price

With the Unlimited 10, Bosch has gone all in on the bling. It has a very flashy screen, which informs you visually when you’re changing floor surfaces, and lights up in a different colour depending on what power setting you’ve got the suction on. It’s useful, but possibly not useful enough to justify its higher-than-average cost.

The overall build quality is excellent, though. I loved the spring-loaded filter-clearing lever on the back, which means you can empty the collection bin in a smooth single-push motion rather than the banging and poking you have to do with most other vacuums. This lever can also compact the rubbish as you clean to reduce how often it needs emptying. The Unlimited 10 also had the best battery, which made the unit heavy but lasted an astonishing hour and a half on its Eco setting.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s a bit expensive without there being enough of a cleaning benefit to justify it.
Weight: 3.8kg; suction power (tested): 13kPa; battery life (tested): 1hr 34mins; dust capacity: 0.4l; additional filters supplied? No
What we loveSolid build quality, good cleaning performance
What we don’t loveUnnecessary features drive up the price
What we loveExtremely affordable and a fair performer
What we don’t loveProne to getting blocked by larger particles

If most of the other reviews left you thinking you were going to have to take out a second mortgage to get a new cordless vacuum cleaner, the budget-friendly price tag of the Beldray Airgility Pet Plus+ should be a breath of fresh air. It’s light and petite but has small attachments, too, which aren’t large enough to pick up larger particles. It doesn’t collect dirt as well as the best vacuum cleaners here, but for a fraction of the price, it does a reasonable job.

The biggest problem was cat litter, which was sucked up OK from the floor but caused a blockage after only a tiny amount had entered the collection bin. It was surprisingly proficient at removing flour from hard floors but failed to agitate my test carpet enough to replicate that success. It also left a bit of pet hair behind during testing, either on the floor or stuck to the rollers.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it didn’t perform as well as more expensive rivals, though it does still impress for the price.
Weight: 2.2kg; suction power (tested): 9.25kPa; battery life (tested): 41mins; dust capacity: 1.2l; additional filters supplied? Yes, one
What we loveExtremely affordable and a fair performer
What we don’t loveProne to getting blocked by larger particles
Cordless vacuum cleaners are vastly more convenient than corded models. There’s no cable to unwind and no need to find a power socket – you just take the vacuum to the mess and get started.

The downside is that they run on battery power. The batteries can last anywhere from an hour or so on light settings and down to a few minutes on full blast. They should last long enough to get around an average-size house in one go, but larger spaces might need a mid-clean charge, which can take a few hours (or an expensive extra battery).

Suction powerGenerally speaking, a vacuum cleaner with powerful suction will be better at cleaning than a model with weak suction. However, other factors also come into play. A well-designed floor head, for example, can help a less powerful vacuum outperform a more powerful rival.

I tested the suction on the models reviewed here using a vacuum gauge, which measures suction pressure in kPa (kilopascals). A suction of 25kPa or above is good. Anything less than 10kPa isn’t ideal for picking up larger debris, though it may still be good at vacuuming dust, particularly if it’s paired with a decent floor head.

WeightCordless vacuum cleaners are perfect for transporting around the house, as you don’t need to worry about plugging them into a wall socket and managing a cable. It makes weight a key consideration, though, as you want a unit that’s light enough to carry around.
The weights I’ve quoted are the actual weights of the vacuum cleaners in their standard configurations, including extension wand and carpet floor head.

Vacuums that weigh less than 3kg are relatively light, while those approaching the 4kg mark are likely to feel quite heavy. A weighty vacuum will be less problematic in use, though, because a good portion of the weight is usually found in the floor head, which will be resting on the floor during cleaning.
Vacuums will be lighter in their handheld modes without the extension wand and floor head attached, but a model that’s heavier overall is likely to be weightier in this configuration, too.

Battery lifeHow long your cordless vacuum’s battery will last is important, particularly if you’re expecting to clean an entire house between charges. I test batteries by keeping the device running on a section of carpet, from a full charge until they cut out. Generally, this tends to be shorter than the battery life quoted by manufacturers, though the difference can vary from model to model.

A runtime of less than 20 minutes or so may not get you around the whole house clean. Longer life is a bonus, particularly if you live in a large house. If the battery life on your chosen model isn’t that long, you may still be able to buy a secondary battery that you can swap to extend cleaning sessions. You can only do this if your model has a replaceable battery, so check before you buy if you’re likely to want that feature.

Bagged vs baglessMost cordless vacuum cleaners are bagless, which means they collect all the dust and dirt directly into their collection bins, and you empty them by releasing or tipping the dirt into the bin. A few models use bags, however, which provide a cleaner emptying process, as all the dust and dirt is contained in a sack that you dispose of when you empty. If you suffer from allergies, this cleaner emptying process could make life more pleasant.

Vacuum bags can vary in price, though popular models often have third-party bags available, as well as those supplied by the manufacturer. They tend to be single-use only, and you dispose of the entire bag and its contents when you empty.

Of more concern is what the bags are made of. While some can feel papery, most are made from synthetic plastic fibres, which often use recycled plastic but may still take a long time to break down in landfill. Bagless vacuum cleaners are significantly kinder to the environment.

Carpet vs hard floorAlmost all cordless vacuum cleaners will have a good go at your carpeted areas, and most work on hard floors, too. Basic models will use the same brush bar floor head, but may spin it slower when cleaning hard floors for a gentler approach.

Some models come with a soft, fluffy roller, either built into the main floor head or in a separate unit that can be swapped as required. These are even better at picking up dirt from smooth surfaces than a standard roller brush.
If you don’t have much hard flooring, you probably don’t need a soft roller, as carpet vacuums work here too, or you may just prefer to do a quick sweep with a dustpan and brush.
AttachmentsCordless vacuums can be broken down into a handheld device if you remove the extension wand and add an attachment. Check that the model you want comes with the attachments you need.

Almost all vacuums come with a crevice tool – a narrow funnel that’s useful for getting into small spaces and nipping around skirting boards. Also useful are dusting brushes and upholstery tools with wider nozzles. Look out for motorised upholstery/pet hair tools. These look like miniature versions of a regular floor head, complete with a mini brush bar. They’re ideal for vacuuming smaller areas, such as stairs and furniture.

Yes, manufacturers quote high levels of filtration for cordless vacuums, with some claiming to trap even the tiniest of particles, such as pollen. However, emptying cordless vacuums that don’t use bags can create a messy dust cloud, so these may not be the models for you if you’re allergic to dirt particles. Filters also need regular cleaning, which is something you won’t be used to if you’re moving away from a vacuuming system that uses disposable bags.
Maintaining your vacuum cleaner doesn’t stop at emptying the collection bin. There are a few other areas that deserve your attention if you want top performance and a long life from your vacuum.

The first is keeping the filter clean. This doesn’t need doing after every use, but it’s worth keeping an eye on how dirty it’s getting and cleaning it before it gets too clogged up. Dyson recommends doing this once a month. With Dyson vacuums, you remove the filter by twisting it and lifting it out of the body of the cleaner, then rinsing it in cold water to remove the dirt. Let it air dry for at least 24 hours and check it’s completely dry before refitting.
The filters on most other brands can be cleaned in a similar way, but some don’t like getting wet, so check your vacuum’s instruction manual if you’re not sure.

The other problem area is the brush bar. Anti-tangle floor heads have improved things in recent years, but even these can be clogged up with hair, fluff and dirt over time. The brush bar can usually be removed from the floor head, and you can attack entangled hair with a pair of scissors. If the bristles are loaded with fluff, you can tease it out with your fingers or use an old comb.
For a really deep clean, you can dismantle most vacuum cleaners and wash any non-electrical parts with a damp cloth. Make sure it’s all properly dry before putting it back together.

While you might have decided to move on from your old vacuum cleaner, a working model could still hold value for others. It’s worth seeing if you can sell it locally or donate it to someone who can still get some use out of it.

Alternatively, when you buy your new vacuum, ask the retailer about its WEEE (waste electrical and electronic equipment) recycling scheme. The UK’s WEEE Regulations state that companies selling such items must accept the device you’re replacing and responsibly recycle it.

Lastly, you can always recycle it yourself. Your local recycling centre should have a section for electricals, and you can find your nearest at Recycle Your Electricals. Alternatively, check your local council’s website to find out about its recycling services and opening hours.

Andy Shaw is a consumer journalist and technology addict. Having reviewed tech products professionally for more than 30 years, his favoured working environment is a small desk surrounded by big boxes. His greatest weakness is that he never, ever remembers how things came out of their packaging, so they rarely fit back in again when it’s time to return them.

items.title: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit
paragraphs: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF.

Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities.

Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air to water cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests. The company has appealed and a ruling is due early next year.

The vast building, which occupies about 3 hectares (7.4 acres) of a 50-hectare business park on the site of a former coalmine at Aiseau-Presles, about 15km (9 miles) west of Charleroi, is one of three originally planned by Google on the site.

Nicolas Yernaux, a regional government spokesperson, told Agence France-Presse on Friday that a report was being submitted to public prosecutors alleging “a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering 3 hectares”.
The environmental group Greenpeace earlier this week published a report including drone footage that showed Google was carrying on construction work at the site despite lacking the correct permits.

“The tech giant is continuing work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this datacentre was revoked,” Greenpeace said, adding that it had filed an emergency appeal with local planning authorities.
“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region,” the environmental group said. “Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”

Google’s 2024 permit was to construct three smaller air-cooled datacentres, but in 2025 applied instead to merge two of them into one much larger facility and switch to liquid cooling by drawing 600m3 of water an hour from the nearby Sambre River.

The regional administration initially approved the amendments in April, but residents and protest groups appealed and in August the Wallonia infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, revoked the modified permit over drought concerns.

Google appealed against that decision to Belgium’s council of state and a ruling in the case is expected on 7 January. The legal row is the latest confronting the company in Europe as large tech companies push to build datacentres to support the AI boom.

In October, Finland opened a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of environmental ⁠laws ​at a planned Google datacentre in the rural north of the country. Work has been halted until environmental impact assessments are completed.
