items.title: Jess Wilson’s plan for Melbourne sewage plants risks water and wetlands without bringing debt down, experts say
paragraphs: Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants, which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.
The lease is estimated to be worth $9.2bn, with Wilson saying there would be “no change” to water bills or the Essential Services Commission’s regulation of prices across the sector.
Experts are concerned the move could lead to worse services for Victorians, and compromise vital wetlands in Melbourne’s west.

Dr Erin O’Donnell, a water law expert at the University of Melbourne Law School, said given the prices would still be regulated, it would be difficult for private companies to extract value from the services, and the money gained from the lease would amount to only about 5% of the debt held by the state.
“I wouldn’t even classify it as a sugar hit – it’s smoke and mirrors,” O’Donnell said.
“This will not make a significant dent in the debt that Victoria holds, and we are compromising the future of our water resources 90 years into the future.”

O’Donnell said Victoria already required corporations to pay significant dividends to the state government, with strict controls over pricing. It means there is no profit to be realised for private owners while also delivering the same quality of services, she said.

“Victoria has some of the lowest water charges of anywhere in Australia and the idea that there is unrealised profit that could be safely stripped out without compromising those services is a total furphy – I can’t say it any clearer.”

O’Donnell and Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the school of civil engineering at the University of Sydney, both pointed to the UK privatisation of water services in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher as an example of how it can all go wrong.

The privatisation has been described as an “unmitigated disaster”, with hopes the Burnham Labour government will renationalise the utilities following years of declining services, and rivers polluted by private operators.
Khan said the UK’s services were privatised without guardrails around pricing or minimum standards of services.

“Practically every single river in England now has sewage contamination in it,” he said. “That’s the sort of situation that we need to make sure that we avoid because obviously private players are only going to be there if there’s a profit to be made.”
Victoria’s Labor state minister for the environment, Jaclyn Symes, pointed to the UK system and said it resulted in bills going up by 40% and “left wildlife swimming in a toilet”.
Khan said the NSW government’s privatisation of Sydney desalination plant could be a model that would work.

“It’s price regulated. It has requirements around managing water quality and they put drinking water straight into Sydney’s distribution system,” he said, adding it also has requirements from NSW Health and the state’s environmental protection agency.

Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert Prof Richard Kingsford warned the privatisation could have disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including the wetland in the Western treatment plant at Werribee.

In 1983, the site was listed under the Ramsar convention as an internationally significant wetland, and more than 300 species of bird – including many threatened species such as the orange bellied-parrot – have been recorded there.
“It’s absolutely one of the more important wetland systems,” Kingsford said.
“I think it’s becoming increasingly important because we’ve had more wetlands drying up, less flooding and, particularly in dry times, it provides dependable habitat.”
Kingsford said privatisation “would likely drive different ways of management that might actually not have any consideration for the environmental value of the system”.
O’Donnell said it was “extraordinarily disingenous” for the Liberal party to announce the policy less than two days before the election when many Victorians had already voted.
“I think there is a real concern there, in terms of the openness around their policies [and] this will have significant implications for things like a swimmable Birrarung [Yarra River],” she said.
A Victorian Liberal party spokesperson said the criticism was “another desperate scare campaign by Labor.”
“We are not selling Melbourne Water. It was Labor that had a plan to privatise Melbourne Water. What we are proposing is a lease. When you lease something you still own it.
“The proceeds will be used to reduce Victoria’s debt and interest bill.”
The proposal has already been thrown into doubt after One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, vowed to block it should the party hold the balance of power after the election.
The Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, also promised to “fight Jess Wilson’s privatisation agenda tooth and nail should her Coalition form government”.

items.title: Labor faces prospect of electoral wipeout in Victoria as voters turn to Liberals and One Nation
paragraphs: The Victorian Labor government is facing an electoral wipeout after 12 years in office as the state heads to the polls on Saturday.
Polling during the campaign has consistently pointed to a Coalition victory. The final Newspoll, released on Thursday, showed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two-party-preferred basis.

If replicated across the state, that swing would translate into 67 seats for the Coalition – comfortably above the 45 needed to form a majority government. The Liberals and Nationals currently hold a combined 29 seats.
But the scale of Labor’s defeat remains unclear. Some polls have suggested the party could fall behind One Nation into third place, with its primary vote only marginally ahead of the Greens.

“Right now, definitely, it’s going to be a Coalition government, but how Labor, the Greens and One Nation are going to go – that’s going to be a lot more chaotic,” said Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room.

Raue said One Nation’s prospects will depend heavily on which party it is competing against in each seat. One Nation is targeting 12 lower house seats. It will field candidates in all lower house seats.
In contests with the Liberals or Nationals, One Nation would fare “very badly” because about 80% of preferences from other parties would flow to the Coalition partners, he said.
“The places where they are likely going to be strongest are those outer suburban seats they could take off Labor,” Raue said.
“They probably couldn’t take them if Labor was in a stronger position. Labor is so weak right now that those areas can come into play.”

On Friday, Labor campaign sources said they were bracing for a “wild night”, with three- and four-cornered contests expected across the state. Internal research suggested the party could lose up to 10 seats to One Nation, prompting former premier Steve Bracks to urge voters not to abandon Labor.
One Nation’s state leader, Warren Pickering, tempered expectations, telling reporters on Friday: “We have effectively got one state member, anything more than that is a success. We have already won.”
Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a pollster with Redbridge, said Labor was at risk of losing more than 30 seats – a figure he described as conservative. The party currently holds 54.
“If they come out of this with 20 seats, it’s a really good result,” Samaras said. “Below that, without stating the obvious, it’s a massive problem.”

Samaras said Labor was likely to lose several regional seats, including Ripon, Bendigo East – held by former premier Jacinta Allan – Bendigo West, Eureka and Wendouree. The party could also lose seats across the Geelong region that it has held since 1999, including Bellarine, Geelong, Lara and South Barwon.

In Melbourne’s south-east, Carrum and Frankston were also at risk of switching from Labor to One Nation. Further out, Labor was not in contention in Bass, Hastings and Pakenham, where the contest was shaping as a fight between the Liberals and One Nation, he said.

In the north-west, Melton, Sunbury and Sydenham were also potential One Nation gains. Meanwhile, the Liberals are expected to pick up eastern suburbs seats including Ashwood, Bayswater, Box Hill, Glen Waverley and Ringwood.
The Liberals are even confident in the premier’s own seat of Niddrie and neighbouring Essendon.

Labor’s inner-city seats of Footscray, Northcote and Pascoe Vale were each a “coin toss” between the party and the Greens, Samaras said. But Greens sources are confident about the seats, as well as Prahran, which it lost to the Liberals at a 2025 byelection.
Samaras said the margins in many seats would be fragile.
“The Coalition is going to win 55 to 60 seats but someone only has to breathe in the wrong direction and they lose 20,” he said.
The premier, Ben Carroll, made his final pitch to voters on Friday, saying while Labor had “made some mistakes”, it was the only party on the side of workers in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis.

“We won’t fight against you. We won’t make cuts. We certainly won’t say one thing and then, after several million people have voted, then go and do another,” he said, in reference to the Coalition’s pre-budget costings on Thursday, which detailed a plan to privatise the sewage system.
The Coalition leader, Jess Wilson, called the poll a “a referendum on four more years of Labor”.
“Tomorrow Victorians have an opportunity to change the direction of the state we all love and we have the plan to get started,” she said.
If elected on Saturday, she will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.
Additional reporting by Bertin Huynh and Henry Belot

items.title: It’s the biggest ever month for video games – so why am I playing a title from 2006? | Dominik Diamond
paragraphs: I find myself on the wrong side of gaming history this month. I have zero zeitgeist. My takes are as fresh as something found at the rear of the fridge. I haven’t even played Grand Theft Auto VI yet, but we’ll get to that.

Worse, all month, the Nintendo sector of the gaming world has been going googly eyed over Zelda. The Ocarina of Time remake seems to have produced more joy than all the puppies in the world. But not for me. I have never liked Zelda. It’s like being a movie reviewer who doesn’t like Disney, or a vegan shark.

I have played the Zelda games, because #1 Child was into them, but not to any decent extent. Shallow Male Me back then felt that it was for little kids, and worried that testosterone would leak from me every time Link cut some grass with his sword instead of slicing something’s head off.

Determined to right this wrong, I made something of a misstep. While everyone else was trying to play Linkin Park on the ocarina in the new remake, I dusted off the Nintendo Wii that I rediscovered while moving house. In the disc slot lurked The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess, a cheaper alternative to spending 50 million quid on a Switch 2. Finally, I would discover the lure of Zelda.

The opening level was everything I feared. Link was running around looking for fish to give to cats. But the Wii control system made even this simple task hell. Walking along thin ledges with that diddly nunchuck and no 360-degree camera control is like being drunk on a tightrope. On a unicycle. After 10 hours of gameplay, I was still pushing the wrong button among what feels like an ocean of them.

It’s not all bad. The graphics are beautiful. The reveal of the Twilight World and accompanying lycanthropy is spectacular, and so existentially poignant it should be written in French. Wolf Link and his assorted moves are also terrific, or at least they would be with a different controller. (I really should have dug out a GameCube instead.)

But I was having a frustrating experience, far removed from the unbridled joy flooding my socials from people playing the OoT remake. Then I hit my first dungeon. And I remembered why I really disliked Zelda games: I hate dungeons. They are mazey mental torture prisons with switches, locked doors and repetitive puzzles. You must find a specific solution or you cannot continue. I am an open world guy! I want to have different ways to crack a nut, including a sledgehammer option.

While I tried to leap over tiny platforms to cross a lake of lava in the Goron Mines so that I could pull a chain to move a block to run back the way I came to get on a platform before it retracted, GTA VI came out. Grand Theft Auto is a game that I have loved in all its incarnations. I felt like the rest of the world was driving round in Ferraris while I was on a penny farthing.

Meanwhile, after dying in a dungeon, getting confused and going the wrong way, I finally found the door that led to the big boss. But I couldn’t open it because apparently I had not collected all three key shards. I could swear that I did! After a lot of backtracking, I returned to the boss door and attempted to save the game so that I didn’t have to go through this again, but instead my useless fingers slipped and I selected “quit game” instead of “save game”. When I loaded it up again, I had been returned to the dungeon’s entrance. I was profoundly depressed by this.

I just don’t get Zelda, at least not this one. Maybe I really should have spent all that money and tried the new Ocarina of Time. So why continue? Because I want to belong. I want to be part of this gigantic community that finds such joy in Zelda. That’s what so much of gaming is: connections with other people, from global Fortnite Discords to the Norwich Amiga Group.

We all want to be a part of something. Thankfully, there’s another huge thing going on in gaming, and it’s definitely more my speed: I fire GTA VI up and it is everything I hoped for. I am … home. I may never be part of the Zelda crowd, but right now we have two massive games dominating global culture, two huge communities of friends we haven’t met yet. How often has that ever happened?

items.title: NSW Labor is ‘trampling over party principles’ with preselections by captain’s call, members say
paragraphs: Labor’s New South Wales leadership has been accused of alienating members and undermining the democratic process, after multiple state election candidates were preselected by “captain’s call” instead of the rank and file.
The premier, Chris Minns, announced on Friday that commercial litigator Jade Tyrrell will be Labor’s candidate for the marginal Liberal-held seat of Lane Cove at March’s state election.
He confirmed the nomination is the latest to be sent to Labor’s national executive, a procedure which bypasses a preselection by branch members.

Guardian Australia understands that Labor’s candidate at the 2023 election, Ryde councillor Penny Pedersen – who reduced the margin of the previously safe Liberal seat by almost two-thirds – was asked not to nominate by Labor head office, in favour of another candidate, Vivienne Moxham-Hall, a former adviser to the health minister, Ryan Park.

After Moxham-Hall – who was subsequently endorsed by local members – withdrew her nomination this month, citing a change in her current workplace policy, Tyrrell has become the second candidate to be chosen for the electorate by party leadership.
A local Labor source said Moxham-Hall and Tyrrell were both highly qualified candidates, but local rank-and-file members had been “strung along” by head office.
“We’ve been trying to win this seat since 2011 and the first time we get close they say all of a sudden, ‘No, we’re imposing a different candidate,’” they said.
In recent weeks, Minns and the party’s organisational wing in Sussex Street have faced accusations of making “captain’s calls” on candidates in multiple winnable or Labor-held seats.

This includes the premier publicly endorsing candidates in seats without rank-and-file preselections, in some cases before the national executive had signed off on them. The candidates in 12 seats for March’s election have been sent to the national executive so far.

Under Labor party rules, the 21-member executive, which includes prime minister Anthony Albanese, can intervene over rank-and-file preselections to choose candidates. While other candidates can still nominate, a recommendation by NSW party leadership in one candidate’s favour is considered a fait accompli.
In the safe Liberal seat of Epping, the premier last week endorsed former Liberal staffer and councillor Tanya Raffoul as Labor’s candidate, a move which has drawn some internal anger.
Although another Labor member Benson Koschinski nominated against Raffoul, the national executive endorsed Raffoul’s candidacy in a unanimous vote.

Guardian Australia understands every member of the executive subbed out to allow proxy voters. NSW minister Rose Jackson subbed in for Albanese, while other proxies included staffers from the premier’s and senior NSW ministers’ offices.

One senior Labor source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters, said it was not unusual for proxies to be used when ballots were conducted on short notice, but others said it was highly unusual for every single member to nominate one.
Multiple senior branch sources said sending preselections to the national executive had become too regular.
One said it had become “the norm instead of the extraordinary”, while another said it was undermining Labor institutions.
“How does this help the health of the party?” they said.

In Terrigal, another marginal Liberal seat – and the only one held by the Coalition on the central coast – the deputy premier, Prue Car, on Thursday announced local high school principal Lisa Wicks as Labor’s candidate.
The party’s candidate in 2023, Sam Boughton, had been re-endorsed by members but recently dropped out following a family tragedy and has endorsed Wicks.
Guardian Australia understands that Wicks was first introduced to members at a branch meeting as a new member of the party on Sunday.

In a meeting with members at another local branch on Wednesday – the evening before the announcement – a senior member of Labor’s organisational wing said Wicks would be the party’s candidate after the preselection had been sent to the national executive without any other nominations.

One local member said some at the meeting accepted this, but others supported a preselection “in order for the rank and file to be given their say, after which we would probably have been satisfied with who had been chosen democratically, as is our right”.
A senior Labor party source said the unforeseen circumstances which led to candidates dropping out in Lane Cove and Terrigal had made the use of the national executive necessary.

On Tuesday, Minns said the preselection for Rockdale, a seat held by the sports minister, Steve Kamper, who is a close political ally, would be decided by the executive, following a similar announcement last week about another sitting minister Anoulack Chanthivong.
The intervention in Rockdale has drawn criticism from the former Labor upper house member Shaoquett Moselmane, who said he would have nominated for a rank and file preselection.
“Such action represents yet another example of a party leadership that is increasingly detached from the needs and aspirations of the majority of party members,” he said.
“It’s an act of trampling over party principles of fairness, transparency and honesty in preselection.”

Speaking alongside Tyrrell on Friday, Minns said he understood “concern and consternation about some of those processes”, but cited the threat posed by One Nation which is consistently polling a close second to Labor in NSW.

“I have to put the best team on the path, I have to put outstanding candidates, ones that have got deep connections with the local community, an element of the community that have traditionally voted maybe for a conservative candidate” he said.

Tyrrell, a Labor party member of 15 years, said she had grown up in Hunters Hill, which is in the Lane Cove electorate, and now lived in Waverton, which is in the neighbouring electorate of North Shore.

Guardian Australia understands Pedersen had been involved in monthly street stalls after the 2025 federal election success of local Labor member, Jerome Laxale, but that the party head office had asked for this campaigning to pause earlier this year.

In response to a series of detailed questions sent to NSW Labor head office and the premier, Guardian Australia was referred to comments Minns made at press conferences endorsing the candidates for Winston Hills and Wallsend, both preselections sent to the national executive.
Minns told reporters in Wallsend that Labor was “not running a charity” but a political party.

A Sussex Street source said if the candidates sent to the national executive were elected in March, there would be a “massive injection of talent in Macquarie Street”, including potential future ministers.
Pedersen and Moxham-Hall have been contacted for comment.

items.title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
paragraphs: Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles, external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases, external. Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

items.title: Five Gladiators will not return for new BBC series
paragraphs: Five Gladiators stars will not be returning to the BBC television show for its upcoming series, it is understood.
Athena, Comet, Bionic, Phantom and Cyclone will not be featured when the show returns in 2027.
A spokesperson for the production said the departing cast members "remain part of the wider Gladiators family" and are taking part in the ongoing arena tour, which comes to an end in December.
Gladiators relaunched on the BBC in 2024, having originally been aired on ITV from 1992 until 2000, and then on Sky between 2008 and 2009.
A spokesperson for Gladiators said: "We would like to thank our incredible Superhuman athletes for their contribution to the success and power of the Gladiators TV show.
"While they will not be appearing in Series 4, they remain part of the wider Gladiators family, and you can currently see them across the remaining shows in the UK Gladiator Arena Tour 2026."
Athena, real name Karenjeet Kaur Bains, 30, is a powerlifter and former track and field athlete, while Comet, real name, Ella-Mae Rayner, 31, is a former elite-level gymnast.
Cyclone is 25-year-old Irish powerlifter Lystus Ebosele.
Bionic is the alter ego of 30-year-old body builder Matty Campbell, while Phantom is Toby Olubi, 39, who competed for Team GB in the bobsled at the 2018 Winter Olympics.
The upcoming series is due to introduce the first celebrity Gladiator, former England rugby union international and Celebrity Traitors star Joe Marler, who will use the name Mauler.
In June, the BBC said the series will return in 2027, hosted by father and son duo Bradley and Barney Walsh.

A celebrity special will also be broadcast over Christmas, featuring Big Brother presenter and I'm A Celebrity campmate AJ Odudu, TV presenter Chris Ramsey, social media star George Clarke and comedian Sara Pascoe.

items.title: Meta whistleblower calls on Burnham to go further with ban on NDAs
paragraphs: The Meta whistleblower who made allegations about the social media company’s treatment of teenagers has urged Andy Burnham to go further in banning non-disclosure agreements, warning that tech insiders with concerns about AI development need to be protected.

Sarah Wynn-Williams, who served as the director of global public policy at Meta, then called Facebook, has been unable to talk about a series of allegations made in her memoir as a result of restrictions secured by the company.
The restrictions, which stem from a severance agreement Wynn-Williams signed after leaving Meta, mean she could face significant legal penalties for speaking about the company.

Giving the annual Orwell lecture in London, Wynn-Williams said she could not discuss her own case. However, she said NDAs had become a key weapon used by the powerful to keep “control over narrative”.

“The aim is not to win the argument,” she said. “The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures.”

She noted that NDAs appeared to have been used in the cases of both David Walliams, who faces allegations of sexual misconduct by several women, and Russell Brand, who was recently convicted of rape and sexual assault. Walliams denies the allegations against him.

“In both cases, there are reports of NDAs being deployed to silence women to ensure information that was clearly in the public interest was suppressed,” she said. “It may, allegedly, still be being suppressed.”

She welcomed the prime minister’s commitment to restrict the use of NDAs. Burnham said earlier this week that he was bringing forward changes to ensure victims of crimes or workplace harassment will have complete freedom over whom they can speak to, even if they have signed an NDA.

However, Wynn-Williams called on Burnham to go further by making the changes retrospective. She also called on the public to lobby for stronger action. “Change like this is hard,” she said. “And it is meaningful. It is an achievement that will impact people’s lives. But as the prime minister said, it is just the start.

“Tell your MP, your politically connected friend, your neighbour, it needs to go further. Make it retrospective, ban NDAs, allow people to speak. Even with this announcement, there will still be many with information that the public needs to know who are silenced.”
Wynn-Williams compared NDAs to the “memory hole” that George Orwell envisaged in his novel 1984 – a slot into which inconvenient documents are dispatched and destroyed.

She said action on NDAs was needed in relation to the rapid development of AI, to ensure insiders felt able to sound the alarm. “Parliaments, the press, the law – they’re all outside the building,” she said. “The people who know are on the inside. The researchers, the engineers, the ones who will say, ‘I was there. I know what I saw. I will warn’.
“They’re the ones we need to protect from the memory hole. But in order to get inside the building in the first place they needed to sign away their rights to speak.

“The technology industry has learned to buy silence by contract, the courts enforce the contract, and we are relying on those silenced by contract to warn us about its most dangerous product. That is the memory hole, installed in the place we can least afford it.”

Wynn-Williams made her allegations against Meta in a memoir, Careless People. However, under an interim arbitration ruling secured by Meta she is unable to speak about the book, which contains claims about Meta working with the Chinese government on censorship tools, and its negative impacts on teenagers.
She sat in silence on stage at the Hay literary festival in Wales earlier this year after taking legal advice, and is suing Meta over the restrictions it secured over her.
Meta strongly disputes Wynn-Williams’s book, saying it contains several false claims, and describes her legal case as a ploy to shift more copies.
“An NDA agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car,” Wynn-Williams said.

“It is signed by all types – from the C suite to the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips.”

items.title: Turn a gap on your shelf into a tiny Hogwarts Express with these LEGO and Revell book nooks
paragraphs: Revell's Tiny Adventures miniature is a little craft project for Harry Potter fans, combining wooden model-making with illuminated miniature design, that can sit on. shelf and cast a magical glow. Oh, and there's a 15% Black Friday saving on the Harry Potter Hogwarts Express Book Nook at Amazon.

I'm a sucker for miniature worlds, particularly ones that make you stop and look twice, or light up (anything that lights up). Book nooks have become a fun way to add a little personality to a bookshelf, turning the space between novels into a tiny window into another world. And if you're a Harry Potter fan, this Revell Tiny Adventures Hogwarts miniature is a particularly appealing example.
If you love book nooks, Harry Potter, and LEGO, then on Amazon, the LEGO Harry Potter Book Nook: Hogwarts Express drops from £89.99 to £59.99.

The kit is made from laser-cut wood, with a clever plug-in system, so there's no glue and no mess. The details are printed rather than painted, which keeps things neat. Don't expect a quick job, though; book nooks are like little puzzle kits (with instructions). The Revell range is fairly easy and aimed at everyone, but the more detailed ones have more pieces and are much, much bigger.

I made two book nooks and gave my dad one for Christmas last year; he loved it and spent a week making it. A week when he couldn't nail his hand to a bird table (it happened) or cut his leg with a jigsaw (true story). So, buy a book nook for less, have fun and keep dads alive.

After a 10-year, £437m transformation, the glorious cathedral-like Smithfields market is the new home for the Museum of London. Our architecture critic entered a world of jewels, axes, DJs and dog races and was astonished. Read the full story

London: Interior of the Rotunda at Ranelagh by Canaletto, 1754

One of London’s vanished wonders is magically preserved in this masterpiece of perspective painting by an artist better known for his views of Venice. The Rotunda gave 18th-century revellers at Ranelagh Gardens, Chelsea, somewhere to promenade when it was raining or cold outside. Canaletto captures the flirtations, gossip, games and fashionable posing under this spectacular structure in the mid-1750s. It’s a high class, consciously sophisticated urban haunt. There are tables to dine at, privately located in their own arched alcoves, and a full orchestra is playing. The building itself is richly decorated in the rococo style, with a relaxed mix of classical grace and gilded ornament. It looks very European: a grand architectural expression of the rational, science-inspired era known as the Enlightenment. This is not a distorted view of London by Canaletto, but a reminder that the British capital was seen as the Enlightenment’s leading city, its science, coffee shops, commerce and comparatively free speech and satire the envy of continental visitors. The orchestra might be playing Handel, for instance, who worked in London and whose Water Music and Music for the Royal Fireworks reflect the lifestyle we see here. National Gallery, London

items.title: Acer’s new handheld eats the Nintendo Switch 2 for breakfast – get £235 off now
paragraphs: If you're looking for a handheld console that ISN'T a Nintendo Switch 2 this Black Friday, then I've got the perfect deal for you. I love my Switch 2, but after testing out the new Acer Predator Atlas 8 for the last few days, I'm 100% a convert. It's £235 off over at Very in the UK right now, which is a steal price for anyone looking for a Switch alternative to PC gaming on the go.

The Black Friday deal I've found is on the model I currently have, and the cheapest configuration. You get a 120 Hz refresh rate, Intel Arc G3 processor, 16GB of RAM and 512GB of SSD storage, plus a gorgeous 8-inch display and Windows 11 installed.

The best part? You can bag an extra 10% off today when shopping with Very using the code BFSAVE, which brings the final price down from £999.99 RRP to just £764.10 (10% off £849) – a £235 saving!! We're not done yet either – gamers who buy the console and register their purchase via the Acer UK Offers portal can claim £265 in free loot/accessories and get a free copy of the mountain-biking title Mavrix, too.
I can honestly say, from the few weeks I've had with it, that my gaming experience feels so premium. Pair this with the Chizha Mount Ling 2 Pro Smart Creator Dock, and you're basically a pro gamer.
There are several big advantages of a handheld PC over a beefy gaming PC, as well as in comparison with more family-friendly consoles like the Nintendo Switch 2.
Despite what my headline says, it isn't necessarily about which of these consoles is the "best", as they're catered to 2 entirely different demographics.

I had never considered a handheld PC prior to getting the Atlas, given that I'm more of a cosy gamer. Animal Crossing, Pokopia, and Disney Dreamlight Valley have always been my comfort games, but knowing that I can play juicier titles like Jurassic World Evolution 3, Marvel Rivals, and even a bit of Death Stranding from the comfort of my sofa if I fancy is a luxury you can't put a price on.

I've had my PlayStation 5 for what feels like a decade now, but it's become something of a paperweight recently since my desk has been overtaken by work priorities and filming gear. While I did consider the PlayStation Portal, the reviews weren't really selling it for me.

Having a powerful handheld PC that I can pick up and move with me on the go means clutter doesn't limit my gaming time anymore. I can pick it up and put it down whenever without relying on a large monitor or being tied to a chair.

For portability, comfort, power, performance, and ease of use (no building your own PC from scratch), this console is five stars and worth every penny in my opinion. Sure, you can get rivals like the ASUS ROG Ally or Lenovo Legion Go for a lot less, but the Intel Arc G3 processor alone is revolutionary and currently the strongest PC gaming handheld silicon available.

items.title: Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
paragraphs: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Pedestrians shield themselves with umbrellas as they walk in the rain on Thanksgiving Day in New York, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Yuki Iwamura/AP hide caption

Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.

Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.

The Trump administration has banned asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and canceled thousands of pending asylum applications over the past nearly two years. Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.

A pop-up shop for "dots" a personal assistant agent at the OpenAI developers conference on September 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Sam Altman announced a new artificial intelligence personal assistant agents named "dots" to rival Meta's Muse. Heather Diehl/Getty Images hide caption
This essay was written by Stephan Bisaha, NPR's personal finance correspondent

I was at a book club recently, chatting with a small group, when someone from another circle asked what we were discussing. Driven by an instinct to instigate (perhaps a side effect of our earlier heated book talk), I said the "benefits of AI."

After some anti-AI sighs, I told them about a source whose AI agent saved him $50 without him even asking. A friend uses Claude for her retirement funding decisions. Others are turning to AI for holiday shopping.
New AI agents can now help buy gifts, from brainstorming to checkout. Would I trust AI with my own shopping? Apparently not.

Those cheap acoustic panels AI recommended? Only a good deal if I ignored how tiny they were. The griddle it suggested? Too big. Then I started worrying about how much of my personal data my AI assistant was collecting and eventually asked it to forget everything about me.
Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer guided me through another attempt for my book club's gift exchange.
I gave Meta's new AI agent, Muse, my requirements: a $25 cap for a Gen Z crowd and something that makes noise, per the organizer's request (way to stereotype the radio reporter).
Muse's suggestions? A karaoke mic and a plastic, yodeling pickle. I wasn't sold on either.

My next attempt with AI, though, might not be this holiday season. Instead I'm planning to buy a Tamagotchi for the gift exchange. Remember those virtual keychain pets from the '90s? A throwback to a time when you could take your digital companion shopping without worrying about your privacy.
"Weird Al" Yankovic Getty Images/Bob Riha Jr. hide caption

🍿 Movies: The holiday season is packed full of can't-miss films. These are 17 movies that you should see before the year ends.

📺 TV: Parks and Recreation star Amy Poehler and creator Michael Schur reunite for Dig, an ensemble comedy about a team of archaeologists caught up in a series of mysterious events after uncovering an ancient artifact in Greece.
📚 Books: Why settle for one book recommendation when you can get more than 300? Now's the time to browse this year's Books We Love.

🎵 Music: NPR Music's Stephen Thompson and Lars Gotrich join host All Songs Considered Robin Hilton to attempt to build a canon of music for giving thanks, spending time with loved ones and, of course, celebrating food. Check out their playlist here.

🍴 Food: A few years ago, Israeli American chef Alon Shaya spearheaded the Rescue Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, exploring food's role in World War II. He has compiled his stories and dishes in a new cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.

items.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
paragraphs: FILE - Actor Gerard Depardieu arrives to face trial for the alleged sexual assaults of two women on a film set in 2021, on March 24, 2025 in Paris. Aurelien Morissard/AP hide caption

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

items.title: Ambidestro clads coastal home in Brazil with rough local stone
paragraphs: Contrasting volumes of smooth plaster and rough local Morelo stone define this coastal home in Brazil, designed by local architecture practice Ambidestro.
Named Casa Los Cobos, the home is located in Xangri-Lá on Brazil’s southern coast, and was designed to make the most of panoramic views out over the sea from the rear of the site.
Set back from the road, a series of routes both through and around the home “reveal the landscape gradually,” including a path beneath a timber canopy and via a paved veranda screened by lush plants.

“The main opportunity was the merging of two adjoining lots into a single site that extends to the rear, where the landscape opens onto the water,” Ambidestro co-founder João Pedro Crescente told Dezeen.
The ground floor of Casa Los Cobos has been given over almost entirely to a single large living, dining and kitchen space, wrapped by service spaces and bathrooms.
Full-height sliding glass doors allow this space to be opened out onto a large sheltered terrace alongside a swimming pool, with a lawn that slopes down to a nearby waterway.

“The ground floor is free of partitions: living, dining and the entertaining kitchen are integrated and turned toward the greenery, accommodating everything from a weeknight dinner to a Saturday party,” Crescente told Dezeen.

“Between the living room and the water lie, in sequence, the veranda, the garden and the pool, which wraps around the house. The eye passes through these layers before reaching the backdrop,” he added.
Both the exterior and interior have been given contrasting finishes of rough Morelo stone and white plaster and paint, with the rear terrace framed by white-painted masonry.
This is complemented internally with bespoke carpentry in pale oak, including a floating timber bar supported by a concrete column that defines one edge of the living space.
“The intention was to use natural, local materials in light, warm tones repeated inside and out, making the transition between spaces almost imperceptible,” said Crescente.
“Moledo stone clads the facades and changes in appearance from morning to late afternoon. Other natural stones continue onto the floors and wet areas,” he added.
A skylit staircase leads up to the more compartmentalised first floor of the home, which contains six en-suite bedrooms, two of which open onto a balcony overlooking the sea.
To provide both shading and privacy from the road, sliding timber shutters can be pulled down over the full-height bedroom windows.

Other homes in Brazil recently featured on Dezeen include a home in São Paolo by Studio Arthur Casas featuring dramatic overhangs and cantilevers, and a low-lying dwelling by Sabella Arquitetura that is topped by a gridded timber roof.
