items.title: A bakery, a playground, a speaker’s corner … how a former Brussels car garage tore up the art gallery rulebook
paragraphs: ‘A cathedral of cars” is how the colossal Citroën garage in Brussels was described when it opened in 1934, conceived as a startling glass temple to showcase the streamlined wonders of the automobile age. It greeted the street with an immense curtain wall of glass that wrapped a monumental nave-like showroom, culminating in a curved art deco prow, which glowed like a crystal lantern by night.

Almost a century later, arts and culture have replaced cars as the great urban consumables of our age. Consequently, after a €230m decade-long transformation in collaboration with the Pompidou Centre, this gargantuan garage has been reborn as a palace of performance, dance, music, film, architecture and visual art. The original Parisian Pompidou was designed as a transformable cultural machine for the city; this place takes those urban ambitions to an even greater extreme.

“It’s a true city within a city,” declares Yves Goldstein, director-general of the Kanal-Center Pompidou, as he stands beneath the building’s soaring industrial roof, at the crossroads of two indoor streets where cars were once shuttled to and fro between the mechanics’ workshops. “We have a bookshop, library, restaurants, workshops, an indoor playground – and what other museum has at its heart a place where you can come to buy your daily bread?” He gestures at the bakery, which occupies a prime position at the crossing of the indoor streets. Visitors can watch bakers kneading dough through big picture windows, a spectacle that might be just as entertaining as the performance art in the black box studio next door.

Brussels may be the de facto capital of Europe, but it has shockingly never had a dedicated museum of modern and contemporary art, until now. With the momentous opening of Kanal, there is a slight sense of overcompensation. It occupies a 1.7-hectare city block on the banks of the Charleroi canal, in the northern fringes of the city centre, and contains 40,000 sq metres (half of which is freely accessible), making it larger than the original Tate Modern. As if the existing garage wasn’t big enough, three new buildings have been inserted into the complex, rising above the pitched industrial roofscape like supersized concrete sugar cubes, clad in veils of ribbed glass. One contains the five-storey art museum; another is the new home of Kanal Architecture, formerly CIVA, the city’s architecture centre; while the third houses an auditorium and offices. These cubic volumes plunge down into the factory floor, their walls of raw terracotta blocks mingling with the steel trusses, concrete beams and brick panels of the rambling Citroën pile.

“Our work is merely adding another layer,” says Stephen Bates, co-founder of London architects Sergison Bates, which teamed up with Belgian practice noAarchitecten and Swiss firm EM2N to form Atelier Kanal, winning the 2017 competition. “You’re never sure if you’re looking at something new or repaired.” In an unusual step, the collaborative team moved their office into the building, so their engagement with the existing fabric could be as hands-on as possible throughout.

Much of it was a process of invisible mending. The building’s 470-metre-long glass curtain wall facade has been meticulously replaced with thermally-efficient, slender laminated vacuum glass panels, set within the original (and pleasingly wonky) 1930s steel frames, avoiding clumsy new-look double glazing. “Re-use should be about drawing attention to the existing characteristics of the architecture,” says Bates, not “fixing” every detail. A lively colour palette, developed with artist Sarah Smolders, picks out particular features and helps to humanise what might otherwise be an intimidating scale. Patina is celebrated: the floor is painted with three coats, each a different colour, with the idea that these layers will be revealed with use.

A pre-existing first-floor mezzanine threads its way through the entire complex, providing elevated views down on to the expansive shop floor, accessed by processional vehicular ramps. It’s a “wandering space”, says Bates, that the museum hopes people will appropriate as they see fit. There’s an informal stepped stage, where Goldstein imagines the citizens of Brussels might spontaneously perform, as part of his quest to “abolish the boundary between the public space outside and inside”. With its endless ranks of steps, ramps and rails, it is a skater’s dream – if they’re allowed.

Quite how permissive the radical art garage will be in practice remains to be seen. One corner of carefully curated anarchy comes in the form of an intriguing indoor adventure playground by the British Turner prize-winning collective Assemble, developed with local school groups. Dark mounds of resin-bound rubber hint at the piles of coal once transported along the canal, as well as volcanoes and lunar landscapes, while soft boulders and movable ramps await a fleet of miniature wheelbarrows. “It’s a framework for children to create their own worlds,” says Assemble’s Emily Wickham. Her colleague Mark Gavigan adds: “We hope that how the children play might influence the institution as a whole.”

The theme of bottom-up, participatory city-making is central to the ethos of Kanal Architecture, too, a place that Goldstein describes as “a laboratory to dream and conceive the city of tomorrow”. Its opening exhibition, Right to the City – Right to the Future, takes a rather wordy look at Brussels’ role as an incubator of radical architectural activism. “The city has a traumatic history of modernisation, seeing major demolitions in peacetime,” says the centre’s cerebral director, Nikolaus Hirsch. “But this has made it a fertile ground for new spatial practices.” Exhibits range from fragments of Victor Horta’s art nouveau Maison du Peuple, senselessly demolished in the 1960s, to a “Fugitive Cartography” project mapping Black experience in Brussels, to the Right to Housing campaign, as well as lengthy manifestos printed out and stuck on the wall. It’s worthy stuff, but you’ll need patience.

There is a bit of a studenty feel to the whole enterprise, familiar from biennales, particularly in spaces like the “Salon”. This flexible room features a big silver tent and a hydraulic concrete table-cum-stage, another element that the museum imagines will become an impromptu speaker’s corner. Sockets in the floor “allow visitors to plug in a lamp”, says one of the designers. Others might camp out with laptops. Like any self-respecting 1960s squat, Kanal also has its own printing studio, where posters will be continually produced and pinned up around the building to advertise exhibitions and events.

“We won’t have any screens in the public spaces,” declares Goldstein. “We want it to be a refuge, where people can spend the day without looking at their phones. No QR codes either!” The quiet reading room is a delight, lined floor to ceiling with books and equipped with bespoke modular furniture, designed to be compatible with the OpenStructures system. “It’s a place to study, do your homework, or just hang out,” says Bates.

It’s impossible to take it all in on a single visit. Drop-in visitors can delight in the magnificent former car showroom, a 24-metre high glass vitrine, currently bursting with bouquets of gold letter-shaped helium balloons, an installation by Banu Cennetoğlu. Or head straight to the rooftop, where a free public terrace and bar give the feeling of floating on the deck of an ocean liner amid the city. Or splurge in the fine-dining restaurant, where you can enjoy a €95 six-course tasting menu on an 11-metre long pewter table, welded in situ, while looking down on the showroom with the feeling of a well-fed Citroën exec.

It hasn’t happened without a fight. Kanal has long been a subject of political scrutiny, and has come under fire locally for what its critics see as a costly and colonial partnership with the Pompidou Centre in Paris. Kanal is paying €2m a year for a five-year partnership – funded, like the building cost, by the Brussels capital region. Perhaps in response to the controversy, there is very little sign of the P-word in the building. Only one of the opening 10 exhibitions features works from the French institution’s collection, Goldstein is proud to note. The 350 items on loan include the likes of Giacometti, Picasso and Matisse, intermingled with works from Kanal’s growing Brussels-focused collection. Other opening exhibits touch on themes ranging from Belgium’s bloody history in the Congo, to collaborative weaving on a series of long open looms. An atmospheric seven-metre-high underground gallery plays host to a polyphonic soundscape – although this isn’t an industrial leftover, but a vast concrete basement dug out at considerable carbon cost. It would have been a serendipitous “found space” to uncover, a la Tate Modern’s Tanks, but excavating it from scratch, and fortifying it against the canal, seems perverse when there was so much space to play with upstairs.

This great surfeit of space, pregnant with potential, is Kanal’s defining feature. But it might also prove to be its weakness. It’s a lot to fill in uncertain times. Goldstein abruptly announced his resignation in May, after a decade leading the project, after government cuts to the institution’s promised annual budget. From 2028, the Kanal will need to find private donors, said a government spokesperson, “and, in time, become financially self-sustaining”. Museums can be too big. Just look at the twisted brick albatross of Tate Modern’s £260m Blavatnik extension, completed in 2016, much of which is now closed off to the public.

Public or privately funded, Kanal deserves to thrive. The architects have given this automotive temple a wonderfully imaginative second life, in equal parts radical and sensitive, crafting a dazzling fun palace of endless possibility.
Opens 28 November. Free + ticketed exhibitions.

items.title: ‘Crisis in empathy’: prison guard was watching TV while Aboriginal man was dying in custody, NSW coroner finds
paragraphs: The NSW coroner has found the death of an Aboriginal man in custody in 2023 was not only preventable but was “one of the most egregious deaths” she had investigated.
Corrective Services NSW has been recommended to overhaul officer training for self-harm responses, and ban officers’ access to TV and YouTube while on shift.
Tian-Jarrah “TJ” Denniss, a Wiradjuri man, took his own life on 5 August 2023 at Silverwater prison.

The 33-year-old was in the prison’s complex placement unit (CPU) for inmates at acute risk of self-harm. In his time in NSW, Denniss had 17 interfacility transfers, and had occupied more than 100 cells in his last year of life.

In her report released on Friday, the state coroner, Judge Teresa O’Sullivan, found it was eight minutes between when Denniss covered up the camera in his cell at 6.56pm and when a cleaner reported to correctional officers that Denniss was appearing to self-harm, and another four minutes until a correctional officer reached Denniss’s cell.
His cell was not opened for another seven minutes after that, and CPR was not commenced until after 7.12pm. Denniss was pronounced dead at 7.53pm.
At 6.53pm, Denniss had used the “knock up” system to contact correctional officers, and threatened self harm, to which a correctional officer replied: “Oh will you stop threatening me”.
An officer monitoring the cell was watching sport on the TV in the office at the time.

O’Sullivan said in her report the evidence “discloses a cultural crisis in empathy and professionalism” within Corrective Services NSW “where self-harm is treated as manipulation or a disciplinary matter, abusive language is used towards inmates” and officers in monitoring roles are distracted from their duties.
“I consider that not only was Tian-Jarrah’s death preventable but that it is one of the most egregious deaths I have investigated,” she said.

“There is a critical need to take the lessons from this case and improve practice and procedure across the custodial system in NSW so that the tragic circumstances of Tian-Jarrah’s death are never repeated.”

The report found officers thought Denniss was “just manipulating” because he had made two earlier self-harm attempts in the shift “which did not seem genuine”, and assumed he was “playing possum” and they risked being assaulted if they entered his cell.

O’Sullivan said if the fear was genuine, the danger of any surprise attack is diminished as more officers arrive at the cell, and any suggestion Denniss was “playing possum” for seven minutes was “implausible, to say the least”.

The coroner also found the 17 facility transfers and 100 different cells were “a significant factor undermining Tian-Jarrah’s wellbeing” and it was inevitable he would not be in an optimal state to receive and positively respond to mental health and behavioural interventions.

Among her recommendations, O’Sullivan has said Corrective Services NSW should issue directions “prohibiting the use of personal electronic devices, the viewing of movies, television, YouTube, social media clips, or other forms of entertainment while on duty in any post with observational duties”. She said the agency should also investigate use of blocks or firewalls to restrict access to entertainment.

Corrective Services was also told to review its policies and training for assessment of unresponsive or injured inmates, including in situations where they might be “playing possum” to ensure that such concerns to do not result in undue delay in welfare checks or cell entry.
Officers should be trained that the concept of “playing possum” must not operate as a static assumption, O’Sullivan recommended.
O’Sullivan urged the agency to implement the recommendations urgently “given the number of Aboriginal deaths in custody has never been higher”.
Managing coronial advocate, James Pendler, from the NSW Aboriginal Legal Service, said the findings showed “TJ wasn’t humanised in jail”.

“The call of the family is that the recommendations are implemented and that this is taken seriously, so that this doesn’t happen again, not just for Aboriginal people but for all people in custody,” Pendler said.

“TJ came into contact with the justice system from an early age and unfortunately was involved in the all-too-common spiral of in and out of custody and he was caught up in this system that wasn’t safe for him.”

items.title: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
paragraphs: Next up in Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.
Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation during the 2023 edition of Milan design week.
Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.
Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer Wearstler, who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.
“That refusal to treat craft and technology as opposites is going to matter more over the next 20 years,” Wearstler added.
As well as a shared love of ornament and the decorative arts, Wearstler also picked up on how Goti’s practice is informed by her background in robotics and machine learning.
“It’s amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail,” Goti told Dezeen.
Goti added that she was pleased to be recognised by a leading female designer, as her creative muses are mostly women and femininity plays a major role in her own practice.

“My work is very personal so of course there are a lot of references to being a woman,” she said, adding that she draws inspiration from well-known artists and designers such as Louise Bourgeois and Faye Toogood.
Goti spoke to Dezeen from Paris, where she currently lives with her partner, French filmmaker Vincent Staropoli, having recently relocated there from New York.

She was raised in Thessaloniki and received a diploma in architecture from the local AUTh university before completing a masters degree in Integrative Technologies and Architectural Design Research at Stuttgart’s Institute of Computational Design.

The move to New York came after accepting a research position at Pratt Institute, but during the Covid pandemic Goti realised that she missed making her own work, so began experimenting with found materials.

“I really didn’t know what I wanted to do,” she recalled. “But through my research at the university and the New York design community I realised there were other people working in a similar way, which encouraged me to stick with it.”

The initial collection was followed by projects made with glass, marble and, most recently, a series of furniture pieces featuring lacquered wooden surfaces that contrast with bell-like aluminium elements.
Goti explained that her work usually starts with research into a specific technique or a material that interests her, before she then applies her findings to the design of an object.
She said she finds this approach creatively fulfilling as it offers endless opportunities, though as someone early in her career it means there is no identifiable style associated with her work.

“I don’t usually have a form or a shape in mind when I start,” she said. “So the outcomes are very unpredictable. Because the collections all look different there isn’t anything people can point to and say ‘that’s clearly made by Kiki’.”

“In the long term I hope people will recognise my work because of its research-led approach,” she continued. “We need to take more time to understand other artists’ work and not judge everything based on a few images on social media.”
Decoration and ornamentation are recurring elements within Goti’s oeuvre, although she doesn’t want to be labelled as a maximalist.
“My work is sometimes very ornamental and sometimes it’s more minimal,” she added. “So there’s a gradient and the outcome is really determined by the process.”
Like many contemporary designers, Goti does not produce all of her own work, instead utilising a network of expert artisans to help bring her whimsical and deeply personal creations to life.
“I’m a very collaborative person and I think we can create better outcomes when we put our minds together with other people,” she said.
“My architecture background really helped me develop this collaborative mindset and I think one of the key things you learn as you get older is to be selective about who you work with.”

The collection she developed with Marble Sachanas (top) exemplifies this collaborative approach, applying Goti’s visionary and playful style to an ancient material sourced from a quarry close to her home town.
Goti met the company’s representatives during 2025’s Milan design week and struck up a conversation that led to them returning this year to exhibit the outcomes as part of the Alcova event.

Projects such as the marble pieces and the furniture she developed for Mexican gallery Toro Manifesto fall into the category of collectible design, which Goti pointed out is a consequence of their artisanal production rather than a conscious decision to make high-end, limited-edition objects.

“Everything nowadays is so expensive to make,” she explained. “If you want to make something that’s well-crafted you have to pay for the materials, the shipping, the labour and that causes the price to be high – it’s not the designer’s fault.”

The armchair, coffee table and sideboard were shown at the Collectible design fair in New York, but Goti said she would also be interested in working on designs that could be licensed and produced by a brand.
She is currently developing a collection of glass objects that will be smaller and more affordable than her large-scale Graces vessels, while retaining their exuberant aesthetic.

Alongside her personal projects, Goti also runs an interior design practice together with Staropoli called The House Special Studio, which combines her distinctive aesthetic approach with his cinematic vision.
The studio’s first completed project was the renovation of a compact Paris apartment, which reflects their desire to create spaces that feel fun, personal and lived-in.

Looking ahead to what the next 20 years might hold, Goti intends to continue experimenting with different materials and techniques, while attempting to document her design process in a more detailed and consistent manner.

She believes some designers, herself included, have reacted to the isolated experience of Covid lockdowns by working more with their hands and exploring new ways of collaborating, which she hopes will continue over the coming years.
“I feel we’re all craving crafts and handmade objects more than ever,” she said. “The more digital content we are fed, the more we are drawn back towards analogue experiences.”

“I think we all want more physical interaction with materials and with each other, as well as more intimate settings where we can come together and make things. That’s the kind of future I want to see.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.
The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

items.title: As a writer, I'm obsessed with reMarkable's paper tablets – and they're $100 off for Black Friday
paragraphs: If you'd asked me a year ago whether I wanted a 'paper tablet', I'd have told you to get out of town. What's the point? I've got an iPad, and I've got a notebook. Why would I need to combine the two? Fast forward to 2026, and I'm obsessed with the things. The best ones come from reMarkable, and several of its tablets are $100 off right now for Black Friday.

From the moment I tried the reMarkable Paper Pure a few months ago, I was sold. Aside from features like handwriting-to-text conversion, perhaps the biggest selling point of these tablets is the paper-like feel. And it really does feel real. The black-and-white e-ink display with its textured finish is a remarkable (sorry) replacement for paper, while intuitive editing tools like circling text to erase are genuinely useful.

Then I tried the reMarkable Paper Pro Move. This diminutive version of the tablet puts all of the benefits of the Pure into a smaller yet more premium package, with an aluminium design roughly the size of an actual notebook. This one has become my daily carry.
If you're looking for a more traditional tablet, take a look at our roundup of the best iPad Black Friday deals available right now.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Hawkins\Brown's temporary housing for homeless families in London is a UK first
paragraphs: Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London, the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK.
Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.
Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.
Intending to set a benchmark for temporary family housing in the UK, Hawkins\Brown aimed to create a welcoming building that eases the stress of families facing homelessness.
“Many of the families who come here are fleeing hugely painful domestic situations,” said Hawkins\Brown partner Nick Gaskell.
“The Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre aims to make a traumatic period a little more bearable by providing a caring, calming and uplifting environment for as long as they need it.”
Designed to be in keeping with the neighbouring buildings, the exterior of the U-shaped building is lined with striped bands of orange-toned bricks and pops of pale green metal sheeting.
A secure, landscaped courtyard with play space at the centre of the building helps bring natural light into the surrounding flats.
Inside, the apartments were designed to offer higher-quality living arrangements than typical temporary housing, with tall windows, underfloor heating and open-plan kitchen, living and dining rooms.

Community and family support spaces on the ground floor of the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre include a reception, visitor breakout areas, children’s indoor play spaces, communal laundries and staff facilities.

Based on the studio’s research into dementia-friendly design, Hawkins\Brown used colour zoning, visual landmarks, accessible graphics and high-contrast colours in the centre, aiming to make the space easy to navigate for residents and visitors of all ages and abilities.
Elsewhere in London, architecture studio HTA Design recently unveiled what it says is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.
In Ukraine, architecture studio Office for Future is working on plans to transform a school into temporary housing for families affected by the war in the country.

items.title: Denver Design District’s rebrand is the ultimate love letter to creativity
paragraphs: Denver Design District has unveiled a slick new brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination. A blend of design-focused goods, art, retail and food, the new identity marks a more accessible, culturally relevant district made for the masses.

While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's new identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness. Sleek, timeless and characterful, the new brand identity is the ultimate love letter to design.

Created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark. Representing the district's evolution, the 3 'Ds' motif compresses the bold letterforms by a third each time, making for a dynamic visual anchor.

To accomodate the brandmark, Wunder Werkz created DDD Standard, a bespoke midweight sans serif, to act as the district's display typeface. Equal parts "architectural and playful", it draws inspiration from Herbert Bayer's mid-century furniture forms. Paired with an iconographic system of silhouetted design products, clarity and cohesion flow throughout the identity with a confident authority.

“The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, Partner at Wunder Werkz. “Trade remains an important part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”

A rich colour system of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow contrasts the tans and greys of the district's buildings, bringing warmth and personality to the clean design. The result is a refined homage to design that feels accessible and unpretentious, without losing the slick essence of the design district.

“This project represents the kind of work we love most because it allows us to engage at every level, from strategy and stakeholder alignment through implementation and installation,” adds Hartman. “For us, that’s where the best work happens. Not when design is treated as an afterthought, but when it becomes the link between strategy, space and experience. The result is a brand that feels cohesive at every scale, from a website headline to a warehouse-sized building facade.”

“Denver Design District has always been rooted in great design, but our vision for its future is much broader,” says Dan Cohen, CEO of Denver Design District. “This rebrand isn’t about changing who we are, it’s about reflecting what the District is becoming: a more dynamic, connected, and welcoming destination for Denver and the entire Rocky Mountain region.”
For more creative inspiration, check out The Royal Albert Hall's majestic rebrand or take a look at the gorgeous McMichael rebrand that's a pure work of art.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
paragraphs: Pedestrians shield themselves with umbrellas as they walk in the rain on Thanksgiving Day in New York, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Yuki Iwamura/AP hide caption
A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.

More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.

Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.
Waves pound the Pacifica Municipal Pier after a portion collapsed during high surf and tides in Pacifica, Calif., Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Noah Berger/AP hide caption

Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.
And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.
"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.
"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.

On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.
Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.
Luke and Liam Laputka paddle their boat through floodwater caused by high tides, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, in Sausalito, Calif. Heather Diehl/AP hide caption

New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.

Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.

Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.

There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.
Saturday's parade will be Macy's 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade's executive producer, told NPR's Morning Edition's host A Martinez.

"Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated," Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.
"Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from 'beginning to end' can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months," said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.
Workers deflate a balloon after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026, in New York. Yuki Iwamura/AP hide caption
This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.
Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade's first inflated character: Felix The Cat.

Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.

The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.

The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.
The organization said the top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.
Kat Lonsdorf and Alina Selyukh in Washington DC and Kate Bartlett contributed to reporting.

items.title: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities
paragraphs: Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle.

He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”.

The list of suspects was fatter than a conspicuous stack of dollar bills: the Driver series; Crackdown; the decades-late game adaptations of The Godfather and Scarface; kid-friendly The Simpsons: Hit and Run; the even more kid friendly Lego City Undercover; hacker-thon Watch Dogs; the Hong Kong-based Sleeping Dogs; and the gang-focused and increasingly daft Saints Row series.

But when Rockstar’s GTA Online started hoovering up players and revenue in the wake of 2013’s Grand Theft Auto V, earning billions over the next 10 years, the clones began to die off – until recently. In a real, “Ah shit, here we go again,” moment, the Rockstar replicas have been returning like a bank thief chasing one last score. Fuelled partly by nostalgia, and partly by the 13-year wait for Grand Theft Auto VI, aspiring developers now have the tools to make their own free-roam stories set where they please.

Swayah doesn’t have to wonder what a GTA in a deprived northern city in England looks like any more – the 30-year-old self-taught game developer decided to make it himself. The Estate allows players to rob betting shops, deal drugs and generally cause chaos on the Brit-core streets.

The game’s low-poly models hark back to the scrappy nature of GTA III, Grand Theft Auto’s first jump to 3D. “I feel that in the PlayStation 2 era they were still learning the technology and hadn’t perfected it,” Swayah says. “I think it really helps that I don’t know what I’m doing and I’m figuring it out as I go, which lends itself to a gritty art style … I’ve only just made a Steam page and that was a learning curve.” Ideas for new features in The Estate often come from the fans he’s garnered thanks to viral promotional posts, but the mechanics are only added if he can learn how to do it.

The solo developer’s first game shares much of GTA’s irreverent satire of its setting. For Swayah’s game, this manifests in egging people’s houses, bouts of knock-a-door-run, and even Mancunian radio chatshows that he recorded with his friends.

Burak Akşahin, who’s 32 and from Turkey is the solo developer behind Alaturka, an open world action game set in 1970s Istanbul. Akşahin teaches people how to make games online, and created his project during live streams to encourage solo developers. “When I saw GTA III as a child I told myself: ‘This is the most graphically [advanced] game we can see. This is the top notch game.’ But if we go like 20 years ahead, we have even better technology,” he says.

After plugging away at Alaturka’s retro graphics, doner kebab minigames and Anatolian soundtrack for just under two years, Akşahin was delighted when the explosive trailer for his game went viral when it was released in September. He hopes that the game can help spread Turkish culture, which is often undersold to western audiences. As a period piece – with its moustaches, lumbering cars and gaudy shirts – it has much in common with the 1980s world of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

But the game also shares the rags-to-riches tales of many famed GTA protagonists, from the fresh-off-the-boat Niko Bellic to the reluctant gang member Carl Johnson. “You came to the city not because you want to make huge [amounts of] money,” says Akşahin. “You came to earn enough money to return to your home village to get married. So you start working as a doner apprentice… you find some risky shortcuts. You mess with the mob, you mess with the police.”

Yet another solo developer has brought GTA-flavoured chaos to Finland. In October, Pietari Niinimäki launched Helsinki Online, a browser-based sandbox built from real-world geography data and coded using AI. In it, players can socialise, control a goose, and even traverse the Finnish capital in a flying bathtub.

Niinimäki is not much of a gamer himself, and the 23-year-old’s initial idea of a bird-themed MMOG (massively multiplayer online game) set in digital Helsinki was a far cry from the criminality of GTA. But the important ingredients crept in: missions to complete; an open city to explore; a mini-map. Now, with properties to buy, vehicles to drive and players generally running amok, the game has become a kind of Scandi, hygge version of GTA: Online.

“It sort of makes sense as a genre,” Niinimäki says, “People immediately understand what you mean when you say that you made a Helsinki GTA.” But he is keen to keep his player base acting as upstanding as possible: “I’m intentionally not adding that much crime, violence, drugs, stuff like that.”

Another Finnish developer has added as much of all that as he can. In August, Henri Koskinen’s small studio Lohkare Games Oy released Last Drop, an unashamedly grim look at a fictional Finnish city in the 1990s. Just as GTA III drew its gangster credentials from films such as Goodfellas and The Godfather, Koskinen’s team were inspired by the work of Finnish film-maker Aki Kaurismäki. The game’s story is also shaped by the very real social impact of alcoholism in Finland. “All these stories are in the game and they are very personal. Our neighbours died by alcohol,” he says.

Traditionally, each new Rockstar release has ushered in a new way to think about games – a new standard to be envied, copied, or even challenged. Indie developers might not be able to match the billion-dollar budget of GTA VI, but Rockstar’s detailed depiction of Floridian life can still inspire them. The best approach for a GTA-alike, according to Akşahin, is to take things back to basics: where Rockstar has expanded realism and scope, smaller developers should focus on the chaotic gameplay that players fell in love with in 2001.

“I’m a technical person, so if I try to push cinematic cutscenes, I cannot do them well,” he says. “But that chaotic gameplay is much more immediately appealing for players. When you see two police cars flying over you as they start to shoot, you feel like, I want to play this game.”

items.title: Can luxury save Macy's?
paragraphs: Macy's flagship store in New York unveils its 2026 holiday display. Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images hide caption

Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."

As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.

"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
A shopper with a bag from rival Target visits Macy's in New York. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.

As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.

Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."
A mall visitor walks into a Macy's department store in Towson, Md. Stephanie Scarbrough/AP hide caption

Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.
"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."
Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.

"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.
Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.
"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.
"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."
One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.
But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.
"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

items.title: ‘It’s not helping’: calls for guardrails and regulations as AI use rises at US retailers
paragraphs: As millions of Americans begin holiday shopping this Black Friday, consumers and workers alike are already seeing how artificial intelligence is reshaping the retail landscape.

Anna, a cashier in a southern Oregon Walmart and leader with United for Respect, who requested to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, criticized the implementation of AI at Walmart and its effects on workers.

According to Anna, AI is used for human resources tasks such as scheduling, assigning attendance disciplinary points, and through a safety alert system that she says is often inaccurate and often pulls her away from customer service interactions.

“During the course of a day on a given shift, I will get at least 10 or 15 safety alerts on my phone. I can’t move on through the app until the safety alert’s clear.” she said. “It’s very annoying when you get them. I need to go over here to help this young lady who’s crying her eyeballs out because she needs a pregnancy test, and I can’t get in to get her pregnancy test because I have to clear a stupid alert.”

She explained she has to take a photo and upload it after completing a safety alert, noting alerts can often mistake a shadow, a sticker, or something else as an actionable item, or will be flagged to an associate when it is a maintenance issue.

“If there is something that I clearly see that is on the floor, I’m going to pick it up. I’m not that ignorant to not to pick it up, but I don’t need an AI telling me to do it,” she added. “It’s not helping. This thing is supposed to be working with us and to help us and things like that. I don’t see how this is, because it’s not.”
In September 2026, several hundred Walmart workers had signed onto an open letter calling for the company to put workers first as it rolls out the use of AI in stores.

Walmart investors overwhelmingly voted down a proposal for a report on how the Walmart workplace is being affected by AI and automation in June 2026. A Walmart spokesperson cited an internal June 2026 survey where 84% of Walmart workers claimed they were confident using digital tools.

“Walmart’s approach to AI is, and always has been, people-led and tech-powered,” a Walmart spokesperson said in an email. “We use AI to serve our customers and members and better support associates – not to replace their judgment, experience, or expertise. Like any technology, these tools evolve over time, and feedback from the associates who use them helps us continually improve the experience and build practical tools that are useful on the floor.”
The use and implementation of AI in the retail industry is expected to continue to grow, according to industry leaders.

According to a survey of 56 AI leaders at US-based retailers published in December 2025 by the National Retail Federation, most retailers have or are implementing AI in variety of uses, with plans to increase investments and implementation over the next few years.

Some 75% of retailers surveyed reported implementing AI tools for coding and app development, 73% for office productivity tools, 66% for cybersecurity and fraud development, 59% reported preparing or implementing AI for supply chain and warehouse operations, and 45% reported doing so for marketing and advertising.

As AI use is becoming more commonplace, labor leaders and advocates have called for guardrails and regulations to protect workers and consumers, and protections in collective bargaining agreements to ensure workers have a say in AI use and implementation in their workplaces.

“Without proper guardrails, AI systems have supercharged surveillance for both consumers and for the workers who make it possible for consumers to buy what they need or what they want for their loved ones for the holiday season,” said Crystal Weise, Policy & Programs Director at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute, a nonprofit labor hub started by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of unions in the US.

Weise noted surveillance of workers starts at the factories and warehouses where consumer goods are manufactured and distributed, to surveillance of consumers online and in stores, who have their shopping habits tracked and influenced by algorithms, and of workers, with these surveillance systems fueled by AI.

“We know that these surveillance technologies make jobs worse, and we know that it makes products and services more expensive. We need policies and collective bargaining agreements that stop exploitative surveillance,” she added. “We want to see humans in control of how shoppers and consumers are accessing the goods and services that they need.”

Weise said AI-fueled surveillance systems such as surveillance pricing, productivity quotas on workers, and monitoring dissent and workplace organizing efforts are already collecting reams of valuable data on workers and consumers, which is used to cut costs and drive up profit margins.

Shoppers may be subjected to AI before they even walk into a brick-and-mortar store, with several major retailers such as Macy’s, Target, Home Depot and Costco using automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and other retailers using AI tools to scale back Black Friday discounts and bolster their profit margins.

“We use this technology for limited, authorized purposes. Data is collected through ALPRs to prevent theft and fraud, help ensure security, and maintain the safety of individuals and our properties,” states Macy’s disclaimer notice on the use of the technology at some stores.

For workers, they may be subjected to AI from the beginning of applying for a job, such as at Amazon-owned Whole Foods, which uses an AI recruiting agent named Sage – the only way to apply for a job at the company, according to Whole Foods’ website on job applications.

Once in stores, customers and workers can be subjected to AI facial recognition technology, with major retailers such as Wegmans, Macy’s and Home Depot citing use of the technology, and customers’ are having their data collected by major retailers, such as Kroger, which archives data it collects on customers and sells it, according to a 2025 Consumer Reports investigation.

“We’re not anti-technology, but we are anti-dehumanization of the workplace,” said Stuart Appelbaum, president of the Retail, Wholesale, and Department Store Union and executive vice-president of the United Food and Commercial Workers.

Appelbaum argued AI can’t measure or be aware of life situations that should be accounted for in decisions related to discipline or job termination, and cited negative effects of algorithmic surveillance on workers.

“We’ve seen a rise in algorithmic surveillance, and it creates a pressure cooker environment. People are afraid to pause for a breath, or even to go to the bathroom, and for us, that’s really workplace harassment by algorithm,” he said. “Every worker deserves to have a human involved before any discipline takes place.”

He cited contracts the union has won at employers that include protections on how AI is used and implemented in workplaces, and emphasized the importance of being able to bargain over new technologies as employers are frequently using AI to try to lower labor costs and increase profit margins.

“A lot of retailers are using AI as an excuse to have fewer people on the shop floor,” Appelbaum added. “What you end up doing is diminishing the in-store experience, and I think that’s a huge mistake. Not only does it put pressure on the people who remain working, but it also, I think, isn’t good for the future of the store. Basically, we think the technology should be used to empower and strengthen retail workers, and I think that’s part and parcel of everything we negotiate.”

Fears of large-scale layoffs in the retail industry thanks to AI have yet to materialize. According to a July 2026 policy brief published by Stanford University researchers, AI’s impact on overall employment is “likely small” at the moment. But several firms have announced planned job cuts over the next few years, citing AI or AI investments as a leading factor, and new technologies, such as electronic shelf labels, are projected to result in job losses and increase prices for consumers.
In October 2026, Kroger announced plans to cut 3,000 corporate jobs over the next three years, citing the use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.

“These notifications are part of the corporate headcount reduction the company announced in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology,” said a Kroger spokesperson on the cuts.
The announcement came after the company was hit with a charge of $2.6bn in 2025 following its decision to shut down three automated robotic delivery centers, which Kroger did not comment on.

“As retailers feel the pressure from Wall Street to cut costs and pump up share prices, they’re turning to AI to do the dirty work,” said Milton Jones, international president of the United Food and Commercial Workers, which represents workers at around two-thirds of Kroger stores in the US. “Whether it’s AI-powered scheduling that slashes retail workers’ hours or surveillance pricing that raises costs for consumers, people are getting squeezed on both sides of the cash register.”

Bryan Wynn, national bargaining director for the United Food and Commercial Workers, said that investors are pushing for artificial intelligence investments at firms to cut labor costs, increase efficiencies, boost profits, largely without concerns for how these technologies impact workers and consumers.

He explained planning for these technologies has exceedingly become a concern in bargaining contract renewals and future union contracts, as retail employers are using AI for data collection and surveillance to influence and monitor the behaviors of workers and consumers, and to use that data to further increase profits.

“People should have a say in how AI and their data are used to change how they work and shop,” added Jones. “We need technology that works for our members, and all working people, not automation that steals their livelihoods.”

items.title: Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
paragraphs: First published in 1974, Dungeons & Dragons is now being embraced by a new generation looking for a screen-free hobby. Lauren Migaki/NPR hide caption
Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than 50 years.
In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10-minute piece on it in 1979.
More recently, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows including Stranger Things, a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream — a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.

"It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of 9- to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."

Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens, a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host events like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.
Rose Watson (left) with her brother, Leo Watson, Amos Slodounik and Benjamin Cho, are members of a D&D group hosted by Tweens Without Screens Sequoia Carrillo/NPR hide caption
"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.

In their most recent session, the group explored a cave and discovered a mysterious egg. Possibly a dragon egg? They didn't get a chance to find out! A low roll of the dice meant that instead of successfully stealing the egg, it crashed into pieces on the floor.
"It's like painting a picture in your mind," said Watson. She likes the in-person nature of the game. "A big part of it is getting together with other people and friendship and making jokes."
"And collaboration!" added her 9-year-old brother Leo Watson.
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
The players use pencils to fill out their character sheets and use books to look up questions about the game. Lauren Migaki/NPR hide caption
For fellow 9-year-old Amos Slodounik, it's about getting to try on a different personality.
"You can express yourself in different ways. You can be goofy and nobody will care," he said.

And for Benjamin Cho, also 9, the fun is in the imagination. He spent much of the session drawing elaborate tools and creatures for their game (a healing spider donut, for example). "I like D&D because there's a lot of items and things that you can make up."
Edited by Lauren MigakiAudio story edited by Lauren Migaki, Nirvi Shah and Nicole CohenAudio story produced by Lauren MigakiVisual design and development by LA Johnson

items.title: 12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
paragraphs: The risk for dementia, long thought to be an accident of genes or luck, can be cut with commonsense lifestyle interventions. Raquel Alvarez Tabernero/iStockphoto/Getty Images hide caption
Raquel Alvarez Tabernero/iStockphoto/Getty Images
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.
For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.

In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. And lifestyle changes, when sustained over time, can be a powerful form of prevention. Last year, a large clinical trial from the Alzheimer's Association, called U.S. POINTER, found that older adults at risk of cognitive decline who combined physical activity, healthy eating, cognitive exercises and social activity could protect brain health, thinking and memory.
So where do you start? One good place is a free, five-minute online tool called the Brain Care Score. You can take it with friends and family members as you gather for the holidays.
It was developed by Jonathan Rosand, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and his colleagues. It's now supported through the Global Brain Care Coalition.

"The Brain Care Score tells you how to reduce your risk of brain diseases in the future, especially dementia, stroke and depression," Rosand says. "And it tells you what you can do to live a longer, more flourishing life."
The score covers 12 factors in three areas. The higher your score, the lower your risk. Those factors are:
According to the coalition, the tool, "wasn't built to label risk. It was built to give people options and to show them that small changes made today can matter years from now."
High blood pressure might seem like a heart issue, but it's one of the biggest risk factors for dementia, and many people don't know their numbers.

"The higher your blood pressure, the more stress on your blood vessels," Rosand explains. "The more stress on your blood vessels, the more they break down over time," and the more they break down, the more likely they are to block or rupture. He says high blood pressure can increase the risk of stroke and dementia.

That's why the first step in calculating your score is to know your numbers: blood pressure, blood sugar (measured as A1c), cholesterol and body weight. You can ask your healthcare provider, check your patient portal or use a blood pressure cuff at a pharmacy. If you've been prescribed medication for high blood pressure, he says, taking the medicine is one of the most important things you can do.

What if you take the quiz and don't love your number? The whole point of knowing your score is to use it as an assessment, a place to begin and a way to strategize about what changes you can make to your daily lifestyle habits. There's no need to overhaul your life.

In an analysis of real-world data from thousands of adults, each one-point improvement in the Brain Care Score was linked to up to a 4% lower risk of dementia, stroke or late-life depression. And even people who change their habits late in life can benefit.
The key is to pick one change that feels doable, such as:
Researchers say one healthy change often leads to others. Better sleep, for example, can make it easier to exercise and eat well, so the benefits can multiply across the score.

One part of the score that surprises people is the value placed on relationships and purpose. A 2025 study found that people with a higher sense of purpose were about 28% less likely to develop cognitive impairment.
That means joining the class or the volunteer gig you've been putting off can be considered a form of brain care.
You can retake the quiz over time to track your progress, and you can share it with family and friends. Healthy habits can be contagious.

items.title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
paragraphs: A view of the border wall at the U.S.-Mexico border near Somerton, Ariz., on Oct. 18. Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.
The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.

The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.

"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.

Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.
But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.

Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.

In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.
The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.

If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.

"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."

Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.

One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.

Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.

"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.

But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.
An undocumented immigrant prepares to be deported on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flight bound for El Salvador on Dec. 8, 2010. John Moore/Getty Images hide caption

In an effort to curb asylum applications and alleviate a crushing backlog of cases for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Trump administration is urging ICE attorneys to terminate asylum claims by convincing immigration judges that an application is incomplete or that a person can't substantiate their claims. Or the administration could argue what it did in ZG's case: that he could apply for asylum in a third country.
It has proved to be a highly successful strategy for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has so far canceled thousands of pending cases.

Narayanan said experiences like ZG's reflect how Trump's changes to immigration courts have all but eliminated due process rights, including evidentiary hearings, clearing the way for summary removals. They also show how new guidelines are designed to limit a judge's autonomy. Recounting the events of the motion to end ZG's claim, Narayanan said the immigration judge told the court that his hands were tied.
"He was basically like, 'OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case and I'm not allowed to consider this,'" Narayanan recalled.

According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued so far during the second Trump administration — a sharp increase when compared with the 30 immigration-court-related memorandums issued during Biden's four-year term.

The administration has also been aggressive in its pursuit to remake the immigration court bench, purging more than a hundred experienced immigration judges. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago, told NPR that immigration courts across the country have become unrecognizable.
"Everything is different now," said Peyton, who was fired via email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench.

During Trump's first year back in office, nearly 40% of immigration judges were fired or resigned. Nearly all of them have been replaced with what the administration calls "deportation judges," who critics say are ideologically aligned with the president's immigration agenda and keen to rubber-stamp asylum denials and expedited removal orders. That shift, plus Trump's previous appointees, has overhauled the immigration bench. Now more than half of immigration judges are Trump appointees.

Of those new immigration judges, very few have experience working on behalf of migrants. About two-thirds of them come from a homeland security or military legal background, according to an essay in The Yale Law Journal by Geoffrey Heeren, an immigration law and policy professor at the University of Idaho. He wrote that "only about eleven of the new [immigration judges] have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience."

In her previous role, Peyton was part of the immigration-judge hiring-and-training team with the Justice Department. She now practices immigration law representing asylum seekers and appears before the same judges she helped train. In those instances, Peyton said, she feels a bit more at ease because she knows the quality of the training they received. But when she argues cases in front of unfamiliar hires, she said, she's often dismayed.

"There is no doubt in my mind, when I have the misfortune to appear before them, that they don't know the immigration law so much and they don't care that they lack the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team," Peyton said.

She added: "The vast majority have not been taught the process of evaluating a case, but rather the shortcuts to make sure that these procedural roadblocks come up, to make sure that the noncitizens are stripped of their due process."

items.title: Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK
paragraphs: An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.
The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

“We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”
The team ordered the pizzas using the Papa John’s AI agent, which had been given permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.
Papa John’s AI agent was set to work with a strict mandate established with Lloyds, including a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared.
Simoneschi said the test was the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits.

“This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it,” he said, referring to the annual online sales discount day. “At the moment plenty of us are already using AI to write up the shopping list. I think next year the agent will buy gifts on our behalf. Agents will do shopping on our behalf, will manage our finances, and will help us understand and compare complex products. This idea that they can really help us to sort out a lot of different aspects of our lives is a little bit like having an assistant available to millions of consumers out there.”
However, Simoneschi said consumers would still need to make informed decisions about how they used AI agents for making purchases.

“I think good [personal] judgment still applies, of course,” he said. “It does require control and supervision, and we need to make sure that the underlying technology is fit for purpose, while enforcing the highest possible security standards.”

He added that if there was an error or mistake in the order process, such as the agent ordering the wrong product, consumers would still be protected by existing rules and regulations covering buyers’ rights.
Earlier this week the FCA issued a warning to financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations.
“The reason we are testing with regulators in this sandbox is to really understand all the aspects of the technology ahead of its mass adoption,” he said. “This is a great place to start.”
Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, which launched in the UK on Tuesday, can also make purchases online. Unlike TrueLayer, Muse makes payments using a customer’s bank card.
