items.title: Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
paragraphs: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Joe Milton III (14) runs against the Dallas Cowboys in the second half during an NFL football game in Arlington, Texas, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Julio Cortez/AP hide caption

ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them.
That 50-yarder was the first of two long touchdowns for the Philadelphia duo against the quarterback's former team, and the start of quite a comeback.

Milton, who was Dak Prescott's backup all last season, threw three touchdowns and ran for another one in a 39-38 win Thursday in his third start for the Eagles, who signed him off the Dallas practice squad on Oct. 16.

"The guy's a rock star. ... True example of being cool, calm, collected, and just keep playing the next play, no matter what the outcome," said Eagles tackle Jordan Mailata, who was then asked about the long TD passes. "We've seen it in practice a couple of times. The oohs and aahs were still there, but not as much. It was just like you know he can get that throw done."

After 50- and 45-yard touchdown passes to Smith, Milton ran 15 yards for a score in the fourth quarter and threw a 24-yard TD to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left before Philadelphia lined up for a 2-point conversion. Milton connected with Smith in the end zone, but a holding call against Mailata wiped out the tying score before another try was broken up at the goal line.

But the Eagles (4-7), who were down 31-10 early in the third quarter, got one more chance after sacking Prescott on fourth-and-1 for a nine-yard loss to their 48 in the final minute. After a couple of short completions to Smith and a pass interference call against Dallas, Jake Elliott kicked a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left.
Milton, signed by the Eagles about the same time they were determining that Jalen Hurts' season was over because of diagnosis of blood clots, completed 21 of 31 passes for a career-best 331 yards.

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Joe Milton III (14) runs to score a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys in the second half during an NFL football game in Arlington, Texas, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Julio Cortez/AP hide caption

"You never know when your opportunity is going to come. You never know, when, where, how. The only thing you can do is just prepare yourself," Milton said. "That's just the main thing I did. There wasn't a day where I was in a Cowboys facility and I didn't take notes. I didn't let a day go by where I didn't ask a question. So just being prepared for the moment and I mean, it showed up when it needed to. ... Really trying to hold my emotions in up here. Just thankful for the moment."
While he was sacked five times, and the Cowboys defense had him on the run throughout, Milton made several big plays out of the pocket.

On the 50-yard TD late in the first half, Milton rolled to his left and was in front of the Cowboys sideline when he threw back toward the center of the field — the ball was in the air more than 60 yards before Smith caught it at the goal line. Milton then looked toward the Dallas bench and made some seemingly good-natured gestures with a huge smile on his face.
"Can't even remember doing that, but it was just kind of in a moment," he said.

Then late in the third quarter, while rolling to his right toward his sideline, Milton threw deep to an open Smith, who after the catch had to take only a few steps into the end zone to complete the 45-yard score. Smith had 11 catches for 200 yards.
Milton's quick sprint down the sideline on his touchdown run got the Eagles within 38-30 with 9:09 left.
"He played his butt off. He played really good, made some throws that only he can make," coach Nick Sirianni said. "He played an outstanding game, super composed throughout."

After appearing in four games for Dallas last season, Milton lost his backup role to Sam Howell in training camp this year. But Milton stayed with the Cowboys on their practice squad until getting signed by their NFC East rival.

Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (4) embraces Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Joe Milton III (14) after an NFL football game in Arlington, Texas, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Julio Cortez/AP hide caption

The Eagles lost their seventh game in a row, 19-11 to the New York Giants in Milton's first start Nov. 8. After a bye week, they won 19-16 last Sunday over Pittsburgh, when Milton got them in range for a field goal and a two-score lead with four minutes remaining and then converted a third down in the final minute that allowed them to run out the clock.
Only one of Milton's regular-season appearances for the Cowboys was at AT&T Stadium, in a 34-17 loss to the Los Angeles Chargers last Dec. 21.

His third start Thursday was only his eighth regular-season game in the NFL after appearing in nine preseason games — six for the Cowboys this season and last, along with three for New England in 2024 after the Patriots drafted him in the sixth round that year.

items.title: Rachel Whiteread punctures 2027 Brit Award trophy
paragraphs: Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year’s Brit Awards trophy, a silver sculpture covered in holes to “expose the interior of the statue”.
Since 1992, a different creative has been selected to design the handheld trophy for the UK music industry’s annual Brit Awards.

Essex-born Whiteread has designed the statuette for next February’s ceremony, which is her interpretation of the annual trophy depicting Britannia, a helmeted warrior that is a traditional symbol of Britain.
The result is a minimalist silver statuette cast in resin and covered in holes to draw attention to the inside of the trophy.
“I exposed the interior of the statue, as an artist would do with their music,” said Whiteread.
The artist then handpainted the nickel-plated trophy in a silver hue.
Whiteread is known for casting everyday architectural forms, such as staircases or sheds, in materials including plaster and concrete to showcase their negative space.
She explained that when designing the Brit Award, she wanted to put her own spin on the recognisable trophy.
“I saw this as a natural extension of my work – to continue to celebrate and recognise British art and creativity,” said Whiteread.

“Art and culture are under very real threat,” she continued. “So I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year’s trophy and standing together as artists, whether from music or the visual arts.”
The Brit Awards will take place on 27 February 2027 at the Populous-designed Co-op Live arena in Manchester, where the ceremony was held for the first time at the start of this year.

To mark the awards’ departure from London, where it was held consecutively before 2026, British fashion designer Matthew Williamson designed an amber trophy to reference Manchester’s worker bee city logo.
Other former trophy designers have included British architect Zaha Hadid and British-Indian artist Anish Kapoor.

items.title: People are making their own art from GTA VI, and it's really quite beautiful
paragraphs: We've seen the GTA VI Easter eggs, we've admired the best GTA VI brand reactions and we've dived into the history of the Grand Theft Auto logo. Today, let's turn our attention to the artists.

I don't mean the artists who made the game – we've already interviewed Rockstar Games' art team about GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI. I mean the players who are turning their passion for the game into art of their own.

I hesitate to say "turning GTA VI into art" because it already is art. But there are players who are using the game's vast world as a creative medium for their own expression, whether through in-game virtual photography or capturing scenes from the game in other media.
There's nowhere near enough space here to mention all of the people who are making art from the game, but here are just a few examples.
GTA VI's Photo Studio, available from the pause menu, provides adjustable camera settings such as aspect ratio, aperture, and depth of field and lighting controls for in-game virtual photography.

Players can frame shots, hunt for the perfect lighting, compose scenes, and capture images that resemble fashion, street, documentary or landscape photography. Photo Studio even has filters and post-processing effects, so you don't need to take your shots into the best photo editing software like Photoshop.

The dedicated PlayStation in-game artist Photo.in.game (above) shows that creating art in photo mode is about much more than taking a simple screenshot, demonstrating their editing process for a shot of Jason and Lucia at sunset.

The Cone Studio has been sharing multiple daily shots from GTA VI taken not with the in-game Photo Studio but with a real-world Sony Alpha Nex 5n. Using a low shutter speed and some curves and hue filters in post, they're creating some evocative shots that feel drenched in nostalgia.
There are phones in GTA VI, and phones can shoot hyperlapses. So Fons de Haan has done just that: a hyperlapse made only using Jason's in-game phone.

Australia-based Kindred Cameras (above) has been bringing in-game shots of the GTA VI's stunning environments into the real world by printing them as Polaroids. Anyone unfamiliar with the game might never connect this piece of art to a controversially violent game franchise.
I made an oil painting of Jason stealing a mobility scooter in GTA VI https://t.co/ei0axkXs72November 25, 2026

The artist Cayde (above) is painting scenes from GTA using oil paints. Again, the use of physical media brings the game into the real world. His subjects so far have included Jason stealing a mobility scooter and Cal and Jason snuggling. He's been painting some scenes live on Twitch. Check out his website.

GTA VI is an incredible achievement that sets a new bar for game graphics, and it also has a very distinct aesthetic, so it's perhaps only natural that it would inspire players to create their own art.

As I said, this is just a sample of how people are finding inspiration int the game. There's also the traditional fan art, design and brand concepts, which perhaps deserve a post all of their own. Let me know in the comments if you've spotted some more good examples.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: 'I wouldn't be here today without you': Student's praise for man who stopped train attacker
paragraphs: Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.
Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."
Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."
Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.
"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."
She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.
"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.
Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.
"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.
During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.
Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.
Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.
Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.
He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.
The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.
"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."
Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.
Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.
Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.
On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.
As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."
Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.
She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

items.title: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
paragraphs: Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser.

The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site.

The Environment Agency – which is also threatened with abolition by the de facto deputy prime minister, Louise Haigh – objected in addition to the flooding risk at the site, which is on a high-risk flood plain, expressing concerns people would not be able to take safe refuge in the event of a deluge.

Haigh this week blamed quangos, including Natural England, for blocking development and indicated both bodies could be scrapped with their responsibilities handed to ministers or devolved. Ministers are pushing for the construction of AI datacentres across the country as key to growing the UK economy.

Hundreds of AI datacentres are planned, with more than 300 waiting in the queue to connect to the electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand – almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK. But they face considerable environmental and sustainability issues over their high energy use, pollution, encroachment on protected habitats and emissions from fossil fuel power stations many want to install while waiting for grid connections.

To side-step local democracy, the government is allowing datacentre developers to use the nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIP) regime, with the secretary of state acting as the decision maker.
But Natural England has expressed concerns to ministers about the rollout of datacentres, urging caution and a precautionary approach.

In a response to the government’s draft datacentre national policy statement, Natural England said AI datacentres were a relatively new development type whose full environmental impacts were still being understood.
It highlighted the potential impact on rare and vulnerable species from overabstraction from waterways to meet datacentres’ demands.

Government sources denied the objection to the datacentre at Avonmouth or Natural England’s stance on taking a precautionary approach to their widespread construction had influenced Haigh’s announcement of their possible abolition.

But Craig Bennett, the chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the government’s threatened abolition of Natural England was a worrying sign of an attack on environmental regulation. “Regulatory arm’s-length bodies like Natural England are set up to implement the law of parliament,” he said. “If we want decisions made about nature on the basis of science rather than the very last private corporate or vested interest that a minister has spoken to, then we have independent arm’s-length bodies like Natural England.”

Earlier this month Natural England advised Bristol city council that the datacentre could cause “disturbance and displacement” to rare and vulnerable bird species within the Severn estuary special protection area, just 600 metres away. Another protected site, Hallen Marsh, was only 270 metres away but had not been accounted for by the developers when assessing noise pollution, Natural England said.

As well as the flood risk, the Environment Agency said the developers had not provided any information on the level of water use, and the risk of pollution from land contamination to controlled waters. More than 4,000 people have objected to the datacentre’s construction.
Bristol council said the proposal was “likely to give rise to significant environmental effects” and it wanted the developers to carry out a full environmental impact assessment.

Mary Stevens, an AI campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said: “Natural England was doing its job brilliantly here as an independent adviser. I would have no confidence if this was a government minister doing the work because they would not be acting independently to protect nature.”

Rivington Energy, which is developing the datacentre, said: “We acknowledge the feedback received from the Environment Agency and Natural England and welcome the opportunity to continue working constructively with all consultees throughout the planning process.

“While substantial environmental and technical assessment work has already been undertaken, additional studies are being prepared in response to comments received and will be submitted as part of the ongoing planning process.
“We … are now preparing a detailed environmental statement to support the next stage of project assessment.”

The Wildlife Trusts have launched a petition to save Natural England, saying the current body and its predecessors have been vital protectors for wildlife, land, water and sea across England since the 1940s.

A government spokesperson said: “Datacentres are essential to our economy, but their development must protect the environment and benefit local communities. Developers must meet planning requirements, with local authorities assessing environmental impacts, and then deciding on local applications.”

items.title: ‘If the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?’ Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday
paragraphs: They promise to find the best Black Friday deals, source Christmas gifts and find the ingredients for a romantic dinner.
This week’s UK launch of the Muse AI assistant by the owner of Facebook and Instagram promises to transform how we shop – and how retailers make money.
Meta has teamed up with high street names including Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s, JD Sports and Currys for what the Silicon Valley firm claims is a seamless, secure and time-saving tool.
“From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you,” Meta said.

But for companies that have painstakingly transformed from bricks-and-mortar retailers into online emporiums, AI agents pose risks as well as opportunities. Will AI agents kill window shopping, ignore vast online ranges and send shoppers straight to the checkout? Will retailers be forced to discount heavily to stand out? How do they avoid being steamrollered by Silicon Valley tech titans in commercial negotiations?

John Roberts, the founder and chief executive of online electrical goods retailer AO.com, said the impact of AI agents – at present – was “relatively low” but their use as shopping assistants was clearly “a direction of travel”.

He said AO was positioning itself to get recommendations from AI agents in the same way it generally attracted customers, by offering decent prices and good service, which was winning good online reviews on sites such as Trustpilot.
“We need to work out how we are the best option for whichever AI agent you use,” Roberts said.

Working out where to invest is a challenge. Some smaller firms are almost ignoring the developing channel, waiting to see how and where it might go. However, holding back on involvement with the developing technology – such as online shopping in the early noughties – has killed off brands in the past.

Sharon Iles, a senior apparel analyst at the analytics and consultancy firm GlobalData, said those brands that have chosen to partner with Muse would get an early view of how people shop, what they bought through an AI agent and which products got recommended, which could help brands make their listings more visible.
But she said retailers “must continue to prioritise their own channels to protect what an AI agent cannot replace”.

If agents bypass retailers’ websites, said Iles, this could mean companies “miss out on the impulse items that shoppers often add while browsing”, while those selling more complex items such as apparel could find issues with the choice of fit and sizing, “which could lead to higher return rates”.
“Retailers’ own channels should remain the core of their business, and they must give consumers more reasons to shop directly,” she said.
Retailers including Sainsbury’s and Tesco have used their loyalty schemes and websites to build sizeable businesses that monetise customers’ data and sell advertising space to brands.

However, retailers cannot ignore the agents. Muse has proved successful in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

UK residents may be more cautious about agentic technology than those across the Atlantic, but the technology is entering the mainstream. This year, a third of people planning to shop during Black Friday sales intend to get help from AI – up from 19% last year, according to a recent YouGov poll.

To fans, the likes of Muse or rivals such as Google’s Gemini or ChatGPT’s Dots can be a personal secretary helping organise the boring details of life, but to others they are an untenable busybody, parsing their personal data and monetising it.

For Muse to work as Meta envisages, it not only needs access to your email, calendar and shopping apps but details of relationships on apps such as WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, your preferences and even your financial and health information.

Sainsbury’s suggests its customers can “tell Muse about their week” and the AI agent will help build a shopping list to provide for dinner parties, different dietary requirements or suggest menus and recipes.
Mark Given, the chief technology and marketing officer at the supermarket chain, said the retailer was “starting carefully, listening to customers” and using what we learn to keep making it better”.
“AI can be genuinely useful, taking on routine tasks like checking offers and building the basket, and helping customers find great value and inspiration more quickly,” he said.
In the UK, Muse must ask for your approval before making a purchase or sending an email, while a separate “security agent” checks the AI tool’s actions against the permissions you have granted.
Meta said Muse had no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods, and it did not share users’ conversations with advertisers.

However, almost half of shoppers using AI (48%) are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations, according to YouGov. Rival research firm Kantar found only 23% trusted a chatbot’s recommendations.

Meanwhile, some retailers are territorial about which AI agents get to trawl their data. Amazon has blocked AI agents from its store, although it is reportedly in talks with Meta about allowing access. Last year, Amazon sued the AI company Perplexity over its shopping feature that automates placing orders for users.

Research from the advisory firm KPMG highlights consumer caution. It found just 12% of those planning to shop during Black Friday – a largely online sale event in the UK – intended to use an AI tool (such as prompting ChatGPT or Gemini) specifically to find deals, slightly lower than the 15% using it last year.

Linda Ellett, the head of consumer, retail and leisure at KPMG, said trust would remain an important factor for shoppers and, while some would be happy to give access to their data to “make life easier” and enjoy the ability to “have a chat with an agent” to organise tasks, others would be much more cautious.
With about 70% of shopping still taking place in stores, and more than that in many categories, AI agents have some work to do to kill off the high street.
Brands made familiar through advertising, a store presence or social media content will continue to be important.

Most consumers use AI as only part of their search, to compare prices on kitchen equipment, home electronics or food, for example, or seek recommendations on complicated products such as electronics or supplements.
The advisory firm OC&C said: “For now, AI often helps shoppers validate a choice rather than create an entirely new preference.”

Mark Howell, the director of European retail at Rithum, an e-commerce firm that works with Asos, M&S, Aldi and Shein, said: “Retailers aren’t going to be comfortable handing checkouts entirely to bots until questions around responsibility and liability are resolved.

“Agentic commerce is both real and overhyped. The technology is clearly going to become part of retail, but the legal and commercial realities are much more complicated than people acknowledge. In Europe especially, retailers are asking a simple question: if the bot gets it wrong, who’s liable?”

Retailers and brands said that AI agents were having only a tiny influence on shopping behaviour but most larger businesses already had teams ready to support “generative engine optimisation” (GEO) tactics. These include: making sure they appear in Reddit forums, an important source for some platforms; ensuring AI models can access correct and more detailed product information in text as well as photographs; and responding to reviews on Google or Trustpilot.

While some have suggested that the use of AI agents could diminish the power of brands and loyalty schemes built up by companies with advertising and paid-for search, Roberts suggested agents might well be influenced by these factors.
The AO boss said that if an agent could see there were better deals via a loyalty scheme, then the technology could act as “an accelerant to membership not something that bypasses it”.
In future, industry insiders believe, ChatGPT, Amazon, Meta and Google are likely to try to monetise their AI platforms with some form of paid search or featured ads.
“I am pretty sure agents will start clipping the ticket from an advertising perspective,” said Roberts.

items.title: Council to set London's highest littering fines
paragraphs: People caught littering or illegally dumping waste in a north-west London borough are set to face higher fines as the council steps up its efforts to tackle persistent fly-tipping.
Harrow Council has approved plans to increase penalties for littering, breaches of Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) and the most serious fly-tipping offences.
Penalties for littering will rise from £500 to £750, with a reduced penalty of £300 available for early payment - the highest to be introduced in the capital under a new national maximum cap.
The penalty for breaching a PSPO will increase from £100 to £500, while a new £5,000 penalty will be introduced for the most serious fly-tipping offences.
The changes follow an increase in the maximum penalties available to councils under government rules.
The highest fly-tipping penalty will only be used in cases involving "aggravating factors", such as hazardous waste or repeat offences.
Other factors include the dumping of multiple bags, whether the waste affects vulnerable people, and whether it was dumped by a business for financial gain.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting where the proposal was approved last week, councillor Pritesh Patel said: "The reason for these changes is that the government has increased the maximum penalties available to councils. This gives us an opportunity to strengthen our response to environmental crime.
"Most people do the right thing, but there is a minority that don't, and it is important that the consequences are meaningful and encourage prompt compliance and resolutions."

items.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
paragraphs: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.
“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

items.title: "We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism" says curator of Geoffrey Bawa exhibition at Vitra Design Museum
paragraphs: As the Vitra Design Museum hosts Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses, the first major retrospective of the Sri Lankan architect in over 20 years, co-curator Johan Deurell explains why the ‘tropical modernist’ label has confused Bawa’s legacy.
Geoffrey Bawa is one of Asia’s most prolific 20th-century architects, known for projects such as the Bentota Beach Hotel, the Kandalama Hotel and his own houses, Number 11 and Lunuganga.
Bawa’s work is often described as tropical modernist, as it is seen to blend Western modernist principles with Sri Lankan vernacular traditions and materials.
But Deurell said he and his co-curators deliberately stayed away from this label, which was coined by Western architects and scholars and is closely associated with British colonialism.
“We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism,” he told Dezeen.
“It comes with so much baggage. But it’s also not the most useful tool to discuss Geoffrey Bawa’s work with.”

As one of the Vitra Design Museum’s in-house curators, Deurell oversaw the show with Shayari de Silva, chief curator for the Geoffrey Bawa Trust, and Ikko Yokoyama, a senior curator at M+ in Hong Kong.
The exhibition offers a broader understanding of Bawa’s legacy, highlighting qualities that set him apart from the modernists.
For instance, it highlights how his buildings worked with existing landscape conditions.
“He built with nature rather than against it,” Deurell said.
“Modernist site planning often involved clearing the land, rather than having buildings like Kandalama Hotel, which snakes its way around a rift.”
The show also spotlights the sustainability of Bawa’s designs, in terms of both ecology and socioeconomics.
His buildings harnessed the skills of local craftspeople and were built with locally sourced materials. They also featured climate-conscious strategies for shading and ventilation.
This approach is particularly relevant today, said Deurell, as the building industry faces the reality of a climate crisis.
“His ideas on landscape and ecology was really at the forefront,” the curator said. “He had a holistic approach to architecture and he built with nature in mind.”

The exhibition features a scenography designed by Lina Ghotmeh, who was named Dezeen Awards’ Architect of the Year 2026. It contains over 250 exhibits, including drawings, models, archive photography and furniture.
Among the highlights is a new photography series by Iwan Baan, capturing 11 of Bawa’s buildings as never seen before.
Drone photography offers a look at Bawa’s Number 11 house and University of Ruhuna from above, while other shots show people occupying the Lighthouse Hotel and Bentota Beach Hotel.
Furniture on show includes a mix of original Bawa designs and versions of well-known modernist pieces remade with local materials.
As Deurell explains, these were not intended as copies. The originals were not available in Sri Lanka at that time, so Bawa simply commissioned replicas for use in his interiors.
Standouts include a version of the Barcelona Chair by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, with a welded iron frame and stripy upholstery fabric designed by Sri Lankan designer Barbara Sansoni.
“Bawa collaborated with artists throughout his career, ” said Deurell, pointing to long-standing collaborations with Ena de Silva and Laki Senanayake as well as Sansoni.

“All of these artists ran their practices as social enterprises, so they would employ villagers and train them in a craft,” stated the curator. “It shows the social consciousness within his practice.”
Drawings bring another dimension to the exhibition. Highly detailed maps, floor plans and sectional drawings emphasise the relationship between building and landscape.
Although these drawings were mostly produced after the buildings were completed, they offer an insight into the architect’s mindset.
Deurell points to a quote by Bawa, where he talks about landscape elements as being part of “the total picture”.
“They are just as important as the architecture itself”, he said.
All archive material is courtesy of Geoffrey Bawa and Lunuganga Trusts.

Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses is on show at the Vitra Design Museum in Weil am Rhein, Germany, from 26 September 2026 to 28 February 2027, before a run at M+ in Hong Kong from June 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design exhibitions around the world.
Photography is by Iwan Baan unless otherwise indicated.

items.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
paragraphs: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

items.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
paragraphs: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”
