items.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
paragraphs: Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.
In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."
Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.
"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.
"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.
But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.
Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'."
He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".
However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.
"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."
Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).
Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.
Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.
He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.
"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

items.title: Killer frogs and rat-murdering fairies: the macabre cards Victorians sent at Christmas
paragraphs: Chestnuts roasting on an open fire. Rosy-cheeked children singing carols in the snow. And a dead rat suspended over a fire by a group of fairies wearing the skins of its murdered family. Merry Christmas to you!

The phrase “Victorian Christmas”, to many people, conjures up sentimental images of warmth and good will. But the Victorians themselves held a view of the festive period that could be much darker – and weirder.

A new set of genuine historic cards that have been reproduced for sale by English Heritage is a reminder of this macabre and darkly humorous view of the festivities, offering season’s greetings that are anything but cosy.

A robin – that cheerful figure of festivity – lies dead and cold on the ground, under the slogan: “A Joyous Christmas to You.” Another stands triumphantly on the breast of a turkey it has just murdered, knife and fork in hand, in an offbeat parody of the tale of George and the Dragon: “Cheerful Good Wishes – Always a knife and fork for you”, reads the motto.

Perhaps the oddest image of the set depicts a dead frog lying spreadeagled on the ground with a tiny dagger in its chest, while its fellow frog killer – for some reason wearing trousers and a waistcoat – escapes with a bag of loot. Nothing says “A Merry Christmas to you” like frog theft and murder.

Peter Moore, a curator of collections and interiors at English Heritage, said the twisted Christmas images emerged during the mid-19th century, when the seasonal card industry was expanding rapidly, driven by advances in print technology and the growth of the postal service.

“As sending Christmas cards became increasingly popular, publishers competed for customers with unusual, eye-catching and sometimes downright bizarre designs,” he said. “Many of these illustrations play with the uncanny, depicting animals behaving like people in scenes that could be humorous, absurd or unexpectedly violent.”

They also echo the darker and more subversive traditions of the winter festival, said Moore. From the Roman festival of Saturnalia to the Welsh tradition of Mari Lwyd, where wassailers went door to door with a horse’s head, to the Catalan “caganer”, a figurine posed as if defecating that is placed in nativity scenes, “a lot of the alternative folklore traditions across Europe come from the idea of winter being dark and cold and threatening, a time to think about death and redemption,” Moore added.
Some of the imagery may have made more immediate sense to the Victorians than it does today, said Moore, with the dead robin as an intriguing example.

“Robins became associated with Christmas through their connection with Victorian postmen, whose red uniforms earned them the nickname ‘robins’,” he said. “Some historians have also suggested that the bird carried religious symbolism, with a popular Christian tradition holding that the robin’s red breast was stained with Christ’s blood as it sought to comfort him on the cross.”

The rat-murdering fairies, too, while deeply odd today, would have been less alien in a culture in which stories of elves and pixies were wildly popular. That image is captioned, “With the compliments of the season” and, Moore said: “It’s so hard to say if there’s any kind of irony there. This is a visual culture and history that isn’t really recorded, so we’ll never really know how people responded. I’d love to be able to go back in time and ask people what they made of it.”

He had been unable, similarly, to find any fable or potential inspiration for the festive frog murder, but said it was probably intended as a pantomime-style scene. “The dagger is very theatrical, don’t you think? It has got the weird air of a froggy version of a Shakespearean tragedy.”
The limited edition cards are available – alongside more traditional festive cards – at English Heritage gift shops.

items.title: Victorian hospital conversion in Edinburgh named Scotland’s best new building
paragraphs: An old Victorian infirmary transformed into an educational space by UK studio Bennetts Associates has won the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland for 2026.

Named the Edinburgh Futures Institute, the project involved refurbishing the Category A-listed structure, originally designed by Scottish architect David Bryce, and integrating new teaching and work spaces for the University of Edinburgh.

The Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) said the award jury praised the project for its “modern, welcoming, clever and stimulating” design that successfully blends “Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation”.
“The Edinburgh Futures Institute stood out for its civic generosity, scale and ambition,” said RIAS president Libby Heathcote, who is associate director at Reiach and Hall Architects.

“Balancing loyalty to David Bryce’s diagram with creativity in introducing bold new interventions is a remarkable achievement, blending historic Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation,” she continued.
“The result is a modern, welcoming, clever, and stimulating place that people want to work in and return to.”
Central to Bennetts Associates‘ redevelopment was the restoration of the building’s existing fabric, which was at risk of dereliction after being vacated in 2003.
Updates to the existing structure included reopening an original clock tower and public plaza, as well as the restoration of original wards and 150-metre-long corridors.
Across its five floors, flexible teaching and work zones were added alongside new public areas such as exhibition space and a 450-seat event hall below ground.
The Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual prize named after Scottish architect Andrew Doolan, who passed away in 2004. It recognises buildings of all typologies.

The Edinburgh Futures Institute was chosen as this year’s winner ahead of two other adaptive reuse projects. These have each been featured in a series of videos produced by Jim Stephenson and published by Dezeen and RIAS to showcase the shortlist.
The other two projects shortlisted were the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by London-based Studio Octopi and the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture.

Previous winners of the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland award include the Union Terrace Gardens by Stallan-Brand and LDA Design and the Burrell Collection museum by John McAslan + Partners.

items.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
paragraphs: Powerful storms threaten Thanksgiving travel across North America
ByAna FaguyJames FitzGerald and Sareen Habeshian
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.
Flight delays are affecting travel for more than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. More than 400 flights in the US have been cancelled so far on Thursday.

Another 1,900 flights into, out of, or within the US have been delayed, tracking site FlightAware said. The FAA previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.
Meanwhile, thousands are without power, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.
FedEx aircraft sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
On Wednesday New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency, as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked all runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.

The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travellers in the country over Thanksgiving, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.
Watch: Man and dog narrowly escape powerful king tide in Oregon
Has your region been affected by the adverse weather?

items.title: Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now?
paragraphs: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?
ByPeter Hoskins and Osmond ChiaBusiness reportersReporting fromSingapore
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.
Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.
From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.
In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.
That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.
For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.
It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.
That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.
"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".
Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.
On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.
Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.
"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE, external. The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.
But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.
The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.
The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.
For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.
In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.
In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.
Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."

However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.

Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.
Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.
Jensen Huang signs a Taiwanese banknote for a visitor at Computex 2026 in Taipei

This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.
Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.
Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks.
"Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank.
Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets.
Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat.
Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry.

"I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.
"The story is not over yet... Jensen coming back is probably the biggest, baddest return ever. The question is what will happen next?"
Additional reporting by Benny Lu, BBC Chinese

items.title: Floating nature islands installed in parks as Glasgow Games legacy
paragraphs: The islands are made up of recycled plastic materials, including drinking water pipes, to create buoyancy and are held together using marine-grade stainless steel.
They are then topped with a lightweight clay aggregate, called leca, into which the plants are inserted.
The aquatic plants include a mix of evergreen and flowering native species such as marsh marigolds, water forget-me-nots and ragged robin.
Their roots underneath the islands provide shelter for aquatic wildlife.
The location, in the middle of the water, also provides nesting spaces for birds, which would be largely free from disturbance.
Local schools and "friends of the park" groups are helping with the planting and maintenance.

Games organisers say sustainability is an important delivery factor with all competition venues powered by renewable electricity and electric or hybrid vehicles making up two thirds of the transport fleet.
Glasgow 2026's head of sustainability, Selina Donald, said the city council had been looking at creating floating islands but did not have the funding.

"I really saw the pride in all the parks, the pride in the green spaces, the pride in the natural environment across the city," she said. "And so really, for us, it was a way that we can celebrate and support that."

items.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
paragraphs: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

items.title: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
paragraphs: Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".
"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.
However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.
Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.
UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald told the BBC that the sharp rise in flu cases was happening earlier compared to last winter and previous flu seasons.

"Flu is very, very unpredictable and we don't know what the flu season will look like until it has unfolded," she said, adding that although last year's flu season arrived early, it peaked at "moderate levels".
She said it is not known if this flu season will go on for longer, or peak higher, but urged people to get vaccinated, saying said thousands of people die from the flu every year.
However, flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practice good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.
Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.
Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.
But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible have taken up the offer.
School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.
McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.
"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives".
This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.
The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.
As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.
This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.
Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.
A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

items.title: Documentary about Ukraine wins International Emmy; producer cites ‘unvarnished’ look at war
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
A documentary by the British channel Sky News about Ukrainian defenders, "24 Hours in the Kill Zone," has won an International Emmy Award.

In an interview with VOA, the film's producer Azad Safarov said, "We managed to show people during the war. It’s not about the shelling or the gunfire. It’s about the human story of the war — what ordinary people go through. After all, the majority of our service members come from civilian life."
Safarov is also a co-founder of the charitable foundation "Voices of Children."

The film captures a single day on the front line, as captured by a film crew in October 2025. The documentary team embedded with the 4th Battalion "Freedom Force" of Ukraine’s National Guard, the "Rubizh" Brigade.

The International Emmy is one of the most prestigious awards for television content produced outside of the United States, and it provides an opportunity to draw attention to Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Safarov says it has become more difficult to keep Ukraine in people's minds as the war has dragged on. "While everyone wanted to help at the beginning of the war, now one has to fight to capture that attention." He said he wanted to bring "the viewer into that space" and "allow them to feel what it’s like to be a soldier worrying about a fellow comrade-in-arms."

One of the film’s primary objectives was to highlight how Ukrainians go to extraordinary lengths to extract their fellow soldiers from even the most hopeless situations. In one instance, the film crew witnessed a six-hour rescue operation that involved Ukrainian personnel — and even a Russian prisoner of war.

Safarov said one of the aspects of the film that surprised the crew was how Ukrainian soldiers treat their wounded. He said the crew "had never before seen a commander remain on-site until the very end of an operation — until the soldier was successfully rescued. And believe me, this wasn't staged for the camera; these were genuine emotions."
Safarov recalls a particularly poignant moment when, back at headquarters, they watched in real time as a Ukrainian soldier checked the pulse of a wounded warrior.

"And at that moment, there is absolute, total silence. No one speaks. Then I hear the commander ask again, 'Check one more time.' They tell him, 'He’s not there.' He repeats, 'Check again, check again.' It’s chilling — you can truly feel how deeply he cares for his brother-in-arms. They had a whole host of missions and tasks that day — destroying the enemy, engaging targets, but everything else faded away. They were entirely focused on this single moment. When the commander gives the order to check— to turn on a flashlight immediately — and then they all let out a breath of relief... when there’s a response from the wounded man — it’s just..."

"It’s an incredible moment," says the film’s producer. "You realize that Ukrainian soldiers ... don’t treat their men like cannon fodder; they do absolutely everything in their power to bring them back. The commander told me later that it’s painful and difficult for him to look into the faces of the families of his fallen comrades and try to explain things. He feels the responsibility entirely on his own shoulders. That’s why, during the 22 hours or so we spent there, I never once saw him go to get some sleep."

Safarov says that while filming, he couldn't maintain journalistic objectivity; instead, he was genuinely rooting for the life of the wounded Ukrainian defender. "We need to be there to show the truth; we need to be there to document this moment. And I am very glad that we managed to do this — to show our people in action, to reveal the human side of this war.

“Because in every command post, every stronghold, and every trench, there are people— ordinary Ukrainians — who, due to Russian aggression, are currently forced to be away from their families, their jobs, and their civilian lives."

items.title: Slow internet? The best wifi extenders and mesh systems to boost your home network – tested
paragraphs: Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office.

Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home.

Extenders are cheap and cheerful, but often only extend your wifi coverage to one area. A mesh system, working properly, should cover your whole home. I’ve tested the best of both to find the fastest, most effective and most affordable ways to boost your wifi.
Best value wifi 7 extenderTP-Link RE225BE
Best mesh wifi system for all-round coverageTP-Link Deco BE68
Best wifi extender for gaming and high speedsAsus ZenWiFi BT10

I’ve spent more than three decades reviewing technology, covering PCs, printers, laptops, tablets, games consoles, projectors and more. In that time, I’ve also tested more than my fair share of network extenders, mesh systems, network storage devices and routers. I know what to look for in terms of features and performance, as well as ease of setup and use.

I tested 11 wifi extenders and mesh systems from the leading manufacturers, covering as many different product types and budgets as possible. Each product was set up for real-world testing in my three-bedroom, two-floor home. It’s a tough testing ground for wireless products, with an unusually wide floor plan that makes it hard to push a wifi signal to one side of the house, especially with thick interior walls and glass doors getting in the way.

I installed and configured each mesh system or extender and added any satellite units. I then ran bandwidth tests using network-testing software to see how fast data could pass back and forth between a wifi 7 laptop and a second laptop, connected via ethernet cable to the router. I also ran file-transfer tests to check connection speeds. Tests took place in the two most troublesome wifi locations in the house: the dining room, where I often work, and an upstairs room used as an office.

In addition to these tests, I streamed 4K video from YouTube to check for signs of an erratic signal or buffering, and streamed games from a PC running Steam, a gaming platform. Testing network products can be frustrating and demoralising since there’s nearly always something that doesn’t work the first time. Blasting demons to bits in Doom: The Dark Ages helped keep me sane.
After testing, all the products were either returned to their sources or donated to InFocus, a charity that supports young people with vision impairment and complex needs.
What we loveFantastic wifi speeds and coverage; easy setup; good value
What we don’t loveFeatures locked away behind subscription, advertised in-app

Amazon’s premium mesh system can give you high-speed wifi 7 just about anywhere across your home, without too much fuss or expense. You can buy the router unit solo (£209.99 at the time of writing) or with one or two satellites, with each slim white unit standing at 18cm. The Eero app handles setup and configuration, and the mesh can run across the 2.4GHz, 5GHz and 6GHz wifi bands, with a combined theoretical bandwidth of 10.8 gigabits a second (Gbits/sec), rated BE10800, although Eero lists a more realistic 3.9Gbits/sec maximum.

Why we love it It’s extremely easy to set up. The simple-to-follow instructions in the app offer advice on where to place the satellites, and information on what devices are connected to which satellite, as well as the amount of bandwidth they’re consuming. Each unit has two 5-gigabit ethernet ports (5GbE), making this system future-proof, too.

The three-unit setup was super speedy in both test rooms, with the fastest file-transfer test recorded in the office and dining room. Wifi 7 speeds peaked at 854Mbits/sec in the dining room and 755Mbits/sec in the office, and neither 4K video nor game streaming showed any sign of lag or buffering.

It’s a shame that … the most useful security features and parental controls are locked away behind an Eero+ subscription for an additional £9.99 a month or £99.99 a year. And you’ll be reminded of this at every opportunity in the app.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7, 3.9Gbits/sec Bands supported: tri-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHzPorts and sockets: 2 x 5GbE ports, 1 x USB-C power port
What we loveFantastic wifi speeds and coverage; easy setup; good value
What we don’t loveFeatures locked away behind subscription, advertised in-app
What we loveNot exactly speedy, but reliable and steady
What we don’t loveSetup could be easier with clearer instructions

There’s nothing fancy about this basic wifi 6 extender. It doesn’t push the frontiers of performance, even by wifi 6 standards, with a maximum speed of 1.6Gbits/sec. As far as features go, there’s just one 1GbE port. However, it’s affordable and does a good job of extending wifi coverage to distant rooms. And for that, it’s a simple, cost-effective pick.

Why we love it Placed strategically in a nearby wall socket, the EAX12 delivered solid and reliable wifi 6 coverage in both the dining room and the upstairs office. Speeds aren’t anything to write home about, but were perfectly respectable, peaking at 218Mbits/sec in the dining room and 201Mbits/sec in the office. Once set up, it just got on with the job, with no unexpected dropouts. I was also surprised by how well it handled 4K video streaming and cloud gaming, as long as other devices on the network weren’t streaming and gaming at the same time.

It’s a shame that … there’s a mismatch between Netgear’s quick setup guide and the actual setup routine, with no QR code to be found on the extender itself. Luckily, setup is more straightforward if you install the app and follow the instructions in there.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX1600, 1.6Gbits/secBands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHzPorts and sockets: 1 x 1GbE
What we loveNot exactly speedy, but reliable and steady
What we don’t loveSetup could be easier with clearer instructions
What we loveSolid mid-range performance; simple setup
What we don’t loveDoesn’t reach maximum wifi 7 speeds

The RE225BE supports the latest wifi 7 standard, but doesn’t cost as much as the high-performance models. That’s partly because it’s a dual- rather than a tri-band extender (read more about this in the buying guide below), with speeds of up to a maximum 3.6Gbits/sec across the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands. The pricier RE405BE offers speeds up to 6.5Gbits/sec. Still, 3.6Gbits/sec isn’t to be sniffed at, and is more than enough for today’s wifi 6 devices, while leaving headroom for future laptops and smartphones.

Why we love itTP-Link has mastered easy setup, and following the instructions in the app, you’ll have this extender up and running in minutes. In my tests, it was noticeably faster than the wifi 6 models with my wifi 7 laptop, with speeds of 279Mbits/sec in the dining room and 278Mbits/sec in the office. Coverage was excellent in surrounding rooms, 4K video streamed flawlessly to the dining room, and I could kick demons around in Doom without any dropouts or lag spoiling the party. Considering its price, it offers impressive value and enough performance to see you through your next few device upgrades.
It’s a shame that … there’s only a 1GbE port rather than a faster 2.5GbE port, but that’s only likely to matter if you’re connecting a high-end desktop PC or laptop that supports the faster standard.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE3600, 3.6Gbits/secBands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHzPorts and sockets: 1 x 1GbE
What we loveSolid mid-range performance; simple setup
What we don’t loveDoesn’t reach maximum wifi 7 speeds
What we loveEasy to set up; great coverage and speeds

TP-Link’s two-unit wifi 7 mesh system nearly scooped the overall prize. It delivers tri-band wifi 7 performance with a theoretical 14Gbits/sec speed across all three bands, while each unit has one 10GbE port for connecting to your router, one 2.5GbE port for PCs or consoles, and a 1GbE port for other devices. This should more than cater to any device upgrades you make in the next five to 10 years.

Why we love itOnly the Eero Pro 7 matched TP-Link’s hassle-free setup, while TP-Link’s app offers more features and fewer irritating prompts to subscribe for extras. The compact, cylindrical design is simple, stylish enough and easy to tuck away. Although I tested the two-unit system, coverage and performance came close to the three-unit Eero and Orbi setups in my most distant test rooms. I hit it hard with 4K video, game streaming and online gaming – and it handled it all without breaking a sweat.
It’s a shame that … it’s not as fast as rivals for close-range connections, and there are some intrusive ads in the app.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE14000, 14Gbits/secBands supported: tri-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHzPorts and sockets: 1 x 10GbE port, 1 x 2.5GbE port, 1 x 1GbE port, 1 x USB
What we loveEasy to set up; great coverage and speeds
What we loveStrong performance and superb features; subscription-free
What we don’t lovePricey; underwhelming at long range

This two-unit, tri-band Asus mesh system is another serious contender. The square-fronted units look a little chunky compared with the TP-Link and Eero models, but with a combined theoretical bandwidth of up to 18Gbits/sec, it’s hard to complain. It’s also packed with features, including dual 10GbE ports and a 1GbE port per unit, built-in security tools, a USB port for shared network storage, and a truly comprehensive app.

Why we love itThe Asus system has all the tools and features an enthusiast could hope for – and all the performance you’d want to make the most of the UK’s fastest fibre connections. It’s ludicrously speedy at close range, and testing it with 4K video and full HD game streaming isn’t really enough to stretch it. More advanced features and parental controls are accessible through the app or the browser-based interface, and you don’t need to pay extra to use them. The powerhouse spec makes the Asus a good investment for the future.

It’s a shame that … speeds and coverage at long range weren’t quite up there with the Eero and Netgear Orbi setups, especially in my distant upstairs office. You can buy a three-unit system, but it costs more than £900.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE18000, 18Gbits/secBands supported: tri-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHzPorts and sockets: 2 x 10GbE ports, 1 x 1GbE port, 1 x USB
What we loveStrong performance and superb features; subscription-free
What we don’t lovePricey; underwhelming at long range
For more, read the best gaming chairs for every player
What we loveSuperb speeds and rock-solid coverage
What we don’t loveUnits are too big and too expensive for most homes

Netgear’s three-unit mesh system makes an intimidating first impression, with each of its black and dark-grey towers standing nearly 30cm tall. And it has the performance to match, beating the Eero, Asus and TP-Link systems in some tests and matching them closely in others. When I checked coverage around the house, it was hard to find a spot where signal strength dropped below 80% to 90%, and the app and the browser-based interface provide access to a huge range of settings and features.

With one 10GbE port and two 2.5GbE ports per satellite unit, plus an additional 10GbE port on the main unit for the WAN, the Orbis are ready for the fastest fibre broadband connections and anything else you might want to plug in. Plus, they have a combined theoretical bandwidth of up to 27Gbits/sec across four bands – 2.4GHz, two 5GHz and 6GHz bands – with one 5GHz band dedicated to the “backhaul” connection for the mesh. That’s arguably more bandwidth than most homes could realistically use, making regular wifi 7 routers look puny.

It didn’t make the final cut because … two units cost nearly £900 at the time of writing, with three at nearly £1,600. I struggled to connect one of the satellites, and the speeds don’t quite justify the premium for all but the most demanding tech-heads.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE27000, 27Gbits/sec; bands supported: quad-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz (x2), 6GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 10GbE port, 2 x 2.5GbE ports on satellite units, 2 x 10GbE ports, 4 x 2.5GbE ports on router
What we loveSuperb speeds and rock-solid coverage
What we don’t loveUnits are too big and too expensive for most homes
What we loveEasy to set up and super cheap for wifi 6
What we don’t loveSpeeds can’t keep up with the competition

There’s much to love about this budget wifi 6 extender. It’s super-cheap – you could pick it up for less than £30 at the time of writing – and it still gives you up to 1.5Gbits/sec wifi over the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands. It’s easy to set up using the Mercusys app or by pressing the WPS button on the extender and your router. The smart signal indicator also makes finding the best position straightforward. Performance won’t match pricier setups, but I had no issues streaming 4K video or spreading demon guts around the scenery in Doom: The Dark Ages. Basically, it does the job.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s cheaper than the Netgear and TP-Link extenders, but also significantly slower. Speeds topped out at 137Mbits/sec in the dining room and 140Mbits/sec in the office. It’s a decent wifi booster for now, but it could hold you back in a few years’ time.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX1500, 1.5Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 1GbE port
What we loveEasy to set up and super cheap for wifi 6
What we don’t loveSpeeds can’t keep up with the competition
What we loveGood value wifi 7; decent coverage for smaller homes
What we don’t loveDual-band rather than tri-band; unimpressive speeds
Best for: a more affordable wifi 7 mesh setup

This Devolo wifi 7 mesh is the cheapest three-unit mesh system I tested, and its compact router and satellites – smaller than the average paperback in height – also make it one of the least obtrusive. Unlike most budget wifi 7 systems, it has a BE6500 speed rating, meaning wireless speeds are about as good as they get with two bands. You can switch the system to use a combination of the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands or the 2.4GHz and 6GHz bands. This leaves you with a conundrum if you want to run existing wifi 6 kit at a decent speed, as they’ll be stuck on the slower 2.4GHz band if you want to run wifi 7 devices on the 6GHz band. Still, it gives you scope to switch as wifi 7 support improves.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found it difficult to position the satellites to achieve a good balance between fast connections to the router and a decent signal in my two test rooms. The result? Underwhelming speeds, particularly in the upstairs office where I couldn’t push the speed over 168Mbits/sec (I could get up to 877Mbits/sec at close range, though).
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE6500, 6.5Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, or 2.4GHz and 6GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 2.5GbE port, 3 x 1GbE ports
What we loveGood value wifi 7; decent coverage for smaller homes
What we don’t loveDual-band rather than tri-band; unimpressive speeds
What we loveFast wifi 7 connection speeds
What we don’t loveExpensive for a dual-band extender

The RE405BE offers a speed boost over the RE225BE above, particularly if your phone or laptop supports wifi 7. It’s still a dual-band extender, but its BE6500 rating means a bump to 5.76Gbits/sec on the 5GHz band and 688Mbits/sec on the 2.4GHz band. This isn’t just a difference on paper: bandwidth peaked at 408Mbits/sec in my upstairs office and 326Mbits/sec in the dining room. The four-aerial design – which makes it look weirdly like a robot roast chicken – ensures a good signal in nearby rooms, while the 2.5GbE port makes it a great match for high-speed PCs, media servers and wired networks. It could also double as a wifi access point for a fast wired network.
It didn’t make the final cut because … it was almost twice the price of the RE225BE at the time of writing, and the speed increase isn’t really worth it unless you’re a gamer.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE6500, 6.5Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 2.5GbE
What we loveFast wifi 7 connection speeds
What we don’t loveExpensive for a dual-band extender
What we loveGood wifi 6 connection speeds
What we don’t loveUnreliable connection at long range

Devolo’s wifi 6 extender is a little faster than its Netgear and Mercusys rivals, offering up to 2.4Gbits/sec on the 5GHz band and 574Mbits/sec on 2.4GHz. The compact unit has a single 1GbE port, while the front LEDs double as a status indicator and a wifi signal meter to help find the best position. I had some issues connecting the Repeater 3000 using Devolo’s Home Network app, but once up and running, it provided useful info on connected devices and bandwidth usage.
It didn’t make the final cut because … I couldn’t get it to connect to my main test network, and it struggles to maintain a good connection at a distance, rendering its speed advantage almost moot.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX3000, 2.97Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 1GbE
What we loveGood wifi 6 connection speeds
What we don’t loveUnreliable connection at long range
What we loveThe fastest wifi 6 extender tested
What we don’t loveConnection drops; expensive for old tech

The most unusual extender in my test, this one looks more like a compact router than a traditional plug-in unit, thanks to its separate power supply. That gives it more room for internal aerials and two 1GbE ports, while offering greater flexibility over placement. It was noticeably faster than every other wifi 6 extender I tested, with excellent signal strength in nearby rooms. In fact, it was faster in my office than some wifi 7 mesh systems. It sailed through my gaming and video streaming tests, too.
It didn’t make the final cut because … in everyday use, it sometimes lost the connection to the router, and it’s comparatively expensive.
Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX5400, 5.38Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 2 x 1GbE
What we loveThe fastest wifi 6 extender tested
What we don’t loveConnection drops; expensive for old tech

While they both improve wifi range, extenders and mesh systems do slightly different things. An extender (or repeater) works with an existing router, extending its wifi signal to a room or an area in your home. It receives packets of data from your router or the device you’re using, then repeats them to the router or device at the other end. This can reduce connection speeds, but you can get a solid connection in areas where you wouldn’t otherwise.

A mesh system replaces your existing router or works alongside your broadband provider’s router, using one or more satellite units placed around your home to create a single, seamless wifi network. These units communicate with each other to find the most efficient route to send data between your devices and the router, helping extend coverage throughout your home. The downside? Mesh systems are considerably more expensive than a simple extender.

A new wifi standard is introduced every few years as the industry works to stay ahead of the demands of newer devices and faster internet connections. Routers, extenders and devices such as smartphones, tablets, laptops and games consoles gradually adopt each new standard, ideally before the next one arrives. Wifi 5 is still usable, but it’s a bit old-hat these days and will limit newer devices, particularly with broadband speeds of 100Mbits/sec and above. Wifi 6 is faster, better at longer range and now supported by most new devices, making it a good fit for connections below 1Gbit/sec.

However, internet connections are getting faster, and we have more devices competing for bandwidth. That’s where wifi 7 comes in, offering more capacity for busy homes and support for the fastest internet speeds.

There are two things we should make clear, though. First, your wifi doesn’t determine your internet speed – that’s down to your provider, the connection infrastructure in your area, your service package and the router it supplies. Better wifi can remove bottlenecks between your devices and that router, but it can’t speed up the connection itself. Second, older devices will still work with newer wifi standards; a wifi 6 laptop will still connect to a wifi 7 mesh system, but it won’t make the most of the available speed and bandwidth.

There can be incompatibility issues between manufacturers in some instances, but otherwise yes. Wifi standards are backwards-compatible, although you’ll be limited by the slower connection speed between the extender and the router. However, this isn’t a problem with mesh systems, where the main unit connects to your existing router through a cable and creates a brand-new wifi network. Speeds may be limited if your existing fibre router only has a gigabit ethernet connection or you have a relatively slow fibre broadband package. A mesh or extender can make the most of what you’ve got, but it can’t make your actual broadband faster.

Gigabit ethernet (GbE) ports are now standard on most mesh systems and extenders, providing a fast wired connection to your router and a way to add wired devices, such as a desktop PC or network storage, to your network. Faster 2.5GbE and 10GbE ports are useful if you have ultrafast fibre broadband above 1Gbit/sec, or a high-end gaming desktop PC that supports those speeds.
USB ports can also be handy on mesh systems if they allow you to hook up an external hard drive or SSD, and to share files between PCs or other devices connected to your network.

Most wifi 5 and wifi 6 networks run over two frequencies or bands – 5GHz and 2.4GHz. This gives them more bandwidth to work with than they’d have over a single band, and also means that some devices can use the 5GHz band, which is less congested and less prone to interference. The wifi 6E and wifi 7 standards went one better by adding a third 6GHz band (though, strangely, not all wifi 7 routers or extenders support this). This doesn’t have the same range as the 5GHz or 2.4GHz bands, but there’s even less congestion, and it can be really speedy at close range. You get increased capacity, giving more devices more bandwidth to work with.

What’s more, in a mesh network, the third band can work as a “backhaul”, passing data between the different nodes on the network while keeping the other two bands free for connecting your devices. Those devices aren’t then competing for the same resources, and can connect at even higher speeds.

Tri-band networks, then, are faster, but you might not need that fast a network, especially if your real bottleneck is your fibre broadband connection speed. Also, there may not be a difference at long range. Think of tri-band as a nice-to-have for maximum performance, but not an essential if you’re on a budget.

Most routers or mesh systems are able to run more than one wireless network at once, and many use this ability to offer a guest network or a dedicated network for your IoT (Internet of Things) devices. That makes sense, as many smart lightbulbs, security cameras or appliances don’t receive regular updates, and a hacker might use them to get a foothold on your network and see what mischief they can do from there. Also, keeping all those devices on a separate network means they’re not clogging up your main network with unnecessary traffic. You may need to enable additional settings to properly isolate them.

It’s a similar idea with guest networks. You can offer them to visitors, with their own network name and password, but they can’t see or start investigating any laptops or devices that you have hooked up to your main network. Plus, this usually preserves bandwidth for your devices, and stops a guest hogging it all with video streams or massive downloads.

Sites and stores such as Back Market, CeX and Amazon Resale sell customer returns or preowned products. If they’ve been reset and prepared for a new setup, they’ll be perfectly fine so long as they’re compatible with your network and still receive security updates. I’d still steer clear of older wifi 5 systems and extenders, though; wifi 6 mesh systems should have plenty of life in them yet.

Extenders and mesh systems can be recycled like most other electronic products, either through local collections or recycling points. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to reset the device before disposing of it, and check that the reset has completed successfully. While it won’t store personal files, it may retain your wifi settings and network passwords, which could be misused.
For more, read the best gaming chairs for every player and best 4K wireless TV streamers for more choice – with no aerial required

Stuart Andrews is a journalist with more than three decades of experience in computing and consumer tech. When he’s not messing around with PCs, laptops and projectors, he’s trying to tame his post-apocalyptic garden with the latest cordless gadgets. Likes arty movies, walking and devices that just work; hates things that won’t connect to his home network. This round of testing may have affected his blood pressure and increased his snack consumption

items.title: China extends suspension period for its ban on export of critical minerals to US
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

China has extended for another two months its suspension of a ban on exports of several critical minerals to the United States, a move analysts say roughly aligns with the timing of the current U.S.-China trade truce.

China’s Ministry of Commerce said Tuesday that from November 28 through January 27, 2027, it will continue to suspend its ban on U.S.-bound exports of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials, which are used in semiconductors and defense systems. It also will keep on hold stricter reviews of graphite exports to the United States. Other export controls on the minerals remain in place.

U.S. officials have repeatedly described critical minerals as a national security priority and urged world economic powers to diversify their supply chains to reduce reliance on China for critical minerals.

Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the Indo-Pacific Program at the Washington-based German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Voice of America in an email that she reads this "as an extension of the suspension of US-specific restrictions, not an elimination of China's export-control regime... General licensing requirements remain, and the separate prohibition on exports to US military users or for military purposes remains in effect.”
Glaser added that “The extension approximately aligns the expiration date with the expiration of the tariff deal. It is only for two months.”

China introduced the export controls on certain “dual-use items” to the U.S. in December 2024. The move was widely seen as retaliation for then-President Joe Biden’s expanded restrictions on exporting chip technology and equipment to China.

China imposed export controls on seven rare earth elements in April 2025, as trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies escalated following President Donald Trump’s announcement of global reciprocal tariffs. Beijing broadened its rare earth restrictions again in October of that year.

After President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, in late October 2025, the two leaders reached an understanding on trade issues. The following month, China announced a one-year suspension of the export-control measures.

Earlier this month, as some of the pauses were due to expire, China’s Commerce Ministry announced a two-month extension. The ministry’s notice on Tuesday extended the suspension of several restrictions outlined in the original 2024 announcement, which had been set to expire Friday.
Washington and Beijing have been negotiating to extend the current trade truce, which is set to expire on January 10, 2027.

On Wednesday, Washington announced plans to levy new tariffs on major trading partners over excess manufacturing capacity, with China facing a 20% tariff. He Yadong, a spokesman for China’s Commerce Ministry, said Thursday that China asked the U.S. to return to the “track of resolving disputes through dialogue and consultations.” He added that China “reserves the right to take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”

President Trump met again with President Xi earlier this month in Shenzhen, China, while attending the APEC summit. Xi is expected to meet again with Trump in December when he travels to Miami for the G20 summit, which would mark the fourth face-to-face meeting between the two leaders this year.
