items.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
paragraphs: Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.
It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.
The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.
“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.
The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.
A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”
That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.
Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

items.title: Dozens of court cases in England and Wales affected by undisclosed AI use in 2026
paragraphs: Undisclosed AI use has affected more than two dozen court cases this year, prompting judges to complain about AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, an investigation has revealed.

Proceedings where judges have been forced to deal with lawyers, police officers and claimants misusing the technology in 2026 include a high court dispute between tax lawyers marred by what the judge called “unacceptable” use of “generative AI hallucinations” and references to nonexistent cases.

Another involved a police officer in a grievous bodily harm case who used AI to write a witness statement so it would maximise the attacker’s sentence and “make a judge … weep”. A barrister in a $21m (£16m) high court dispute between two Nigerian oil companies made an argument based on a ruling – supposedly by a senior judge – that had been entirely invented by a hallucinating AI, leading the judge to warn of “the dangers of relying on the product of AI without verification”.

The spate of cases in which problems with AI tools have occurred in 2026 – at least 25, according to a trawl of published judgments by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism shared with the Guardian – comes despite a series of warnings from senior legal figures about the danger of the technology when used to cut corners and build cases. Brett Dixon, the president of the Law Society, told the Guardian AIs producing verbose case documents, particularly when non-lawyers represent themselves, is also taking up more of judges’ time, undermining efforts to clear court backlogs.
“You go from three pages from a lawyer … using human judgment to a rambling 60 pages from a commercial AI,” he said.

Last week, the supreme court judge Lord Sales also said the supreme court was growing “increasingly concerned” about AI and highlighted fears the technology could leave the legal profession deskilled.
“The danger is not simply that the machine gets the answer wrong,” he said. “The greater long-term danger is that human beings gradually lose the ability to know whether it has got the answer wrong.”

Cases affected by AI this year often involved people representing themselves, but also legal professionals increasingly using the technology to accelerate research, save time and increase earnings. Earlier this month the problem hit the Crown Prosecution Service when one of its lawyers cited an imaginary legal precedent.

Among the cases so far in 2026 a senior insolvency judge, Mark Mullen, discovered a junior solicitor had relied on an AI chatbot to research a point of law and took its invented quote from a fictitious statute. The judge examined the AI chat logs and discovered it had produced “nonsense” and warned in his judgment “AI has the potential to be wholly unreliable”.

In another case, the court of appeal dismissed an application for a convicted criminal from Derbyshire to challenge a four-year prison sentence for crimes including grievous bodily harm. The man had pleaded guilty after smashing his way through a glass patio door with a shovel to get into a house where the mother of his children had barricaded herself with a friend and her child. He threatened them with a large kitchen knife, fled and in the process broke a police officer’s shoulder.

The investigating police officer created a victim personal statement (VPS) by uploading a transcript of the mother’s interviews to Microsoft’s Copilot AI and prompting it “to achieve the highest sentence and the most tear-jerking VPS to make a judge or reader weep when reading”.
After the officer was removed from frontline duty the appeal court judges warned that “that no police officer should ever prepare a witness statement of any kind in this way”.

“We have seen how vulnerable the court system is to the introduction of AI,” said Brian Flanagan, associate professor at the school of law and criminology at Maynooth University. “It is always going to be very tempting and people will continue to produce fabricated authorities and that’s pretty serious.”

Last month, the Civil Justice Council recommended that witnesses of fact in civil cases must sign a declaration that their statements had not been prepared through the use of an AI tool that had generated or influenced its substantive content – including facts, reasoning, arguments and opinions. The CJC’s working group, led by Sir Colin Birss, the second most senior judge in England and Wales, also highlighted the urgent need for guidance on the use of AI by non-lawyers who are representing themselves in the courts – known as litigants in person.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the growing use of AI in our courts and we’re taking steps to ensure any use of the technology is safe, appropriate, and properly controlled. That includes boosting the support given to courts through additional judges, legal officers, modern case management systems, and remote hearing technology.”

items.title: Government's antisemitism adviser opens investigation into BBC
paragraphs: The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.
Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."
The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".
The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".
The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".
Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019, external, said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".
"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".
"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."
The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.
He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".
His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".
Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".
He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".
He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS, which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.
The Guardian recently reported, external that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.
"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.
"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.

"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."
Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.

The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.

In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".

Last September, the BBC's broadcast of Bob Vylan's controversial set at Glastonbury broke editorial guidelines in relation to harm and offence, with the corporation's complaints unit ruling that some comments could "fairly be characterised as antisemitic". The band denied being antisemitic.

items.title: "Europe's largest museum development" opens in 1930s Citroën garage in Brussels
paragraphs: Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.

The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.

Claiming to be “Europe’s largest museum development”, Kanal – sometimes referred to as Kanal-Centre Pompidou – hopes to provide space for people to gather to enjoy visual art, performance, dance, music, film and architecture.
Opening to the public on 28 November, the canal-side building was originally built in 1934 as a garage and showroom for the car company Citroën.

Atelier Kanal aimed to keep the industrial character of the building by implementing a “light touch” approach, restoring most of the building fabric, repairing and upgrading parts where needed, and replacing other parts to improve climatic and acoustic conditions.
The garage’s former showroom, a modernist curved glass building with 20-metre-tall interiors, was converted into a gallery space topped with a publicly accessible rooftop.

“Rather than a spectacular gesture, our proposal offers an attitude of ‘radical optimism’ – open and non-prescriptive, spontaneous and instinctive – much like the spirit of modern progress in which it was created,” said Atelier Kanal.
“The interior is a fine example of elegant industrial engineering, while the glass facades clearly express early modernism,” it continued.
“Our ambition has been to trust the building as we found it, embracing its industrial character and many layers of use.”

Three new buildings were added inside the existing structure, including a four-storey volume with a basement level that contains art galleries, and another volume housing a 378-seat auditorium and the Kanal offices.
The third volume is the new home for Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, Kanal Architecture, which was formerly known as CIVA.
Rising nine stories on the north-east side of the campus, across from the art galleries, the structure includes exhibition spaces, a library, archives, research centre, bookshop and workshop spaces.

Architecture collective Assemble designed an indoor playground on the first floor of the museum, which features playscapes informed by volcanoes, planets, and piles of coal that were once transported on the canal.
Elsewhere in the building are a library, bookshop, rooftop bar, restaurants and an in-house bakery.
Kanal’s year-round programme of exhibitions was developed in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou art museum in Paris.

“Kanal invites citizens, organisations, collectives and communities to appropriate and inhabit large parts of the building, for production, performances, events, informal gatherings or simply to spend time,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The museum extends beyond curated art, becoming part of the city and its fabric,” it continued. “In this sense, Kanal departs from the traditional museum and instead offers a place for civic gathering, responding to the growing absence of shared public spaces in our cities today.”

Other museums that have recently opened in historic buildings include the London Museum, located in a transformed Victorian market building, and a bank in Santander that was transformed into the Faro Santander museum.
Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

items.title: Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
paragraphs: In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of new materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

“A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” said De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”
“It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.
According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.
“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” said De Cooman.
“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

Several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a new hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.
“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”
“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.
“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings,” says Wes Degreef.
“I think we were very surprised that the idea of working with a certain bioregion and its materials is something that we forgot in Europe.”
“Some of it still exists, but you really have to search for it. And with earth materials, for example, those crafts don’t exist anymore in Belgium. So we had to do it; we became the craftsmen.”
Sure enough, the scale of the projects involving BC Architects & Studies & Materials – whether they are engaged as architects or as craftspeople – is growing.
“In the beginning, we were just like young, crazy people who are doing these weird things on Belgium,” said De Cooman.

“There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.”

In Brussels, BC Architects & Studies & Materials worked alongside EVR-architecten to convert a former barracks into the Usquare Feder university district, the materials for which were sourced in part by the dismantling of several neighbouring buildings.

With numerous other residential and office projects in the works – including a new bioregional materials hub and workspace in the centre of Brussels, Stadsatelierdeville, that will be its future office.

If it at times felt like BC Architects & Studies & Materials were up against the world, it is projects like La Magasin Électrique, which was a finalist for the 2026 Mies van Der Rohe Award, that reveal a growing international network who share their outlook, one that De Cooman is quick to credit with a lot of their own success.
“I think the dial is shifting, but I don’t think it is us who did it,” said De Cooman.
“There are all kinds of practises, organisations, material developers, and so on, who see a different construction sector – it’s a wave, a societal shift.”
“We’re very happy about it, but it’s broader than our practice. The construction sector is very conservative and we’re not there yet at all.”
Degreef adds that external social and economic pressures have also had a hand in forcing change to some degree.
“After Covid and the impacts on material prices, the gap between contemporary materials and the materials we want to promote is not so big anymore.”
Asked if there is a particular type of building that represents a dream project, however, they remain resolutely focused on processes and systems.
“I think, for us, it’s not in the buildings itself. It’s not what we build, but how we build and how everybody needs to build.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.
The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

items.title: RSHP centres cantilevered office building Sąvaržėlė around glass atrium
paragraphs: UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.
Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.
The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes new public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton said.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”
Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

The building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio said “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.
Sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.
To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.
In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.
RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

items.title: Veruschka: Striking images of one of the world's first supermodels, who has died aged 87
paragraphs: Veruschka was a distinctive presence on the covers of magazines like Vogue and Life in the 1960s and 70s
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.
She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary, external described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."
She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.
Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.
Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.
She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute, external.
"She worked with Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, and Valentino, but also immersed herself in avant-garde photography projects in which she painted, staged, and deconstructed her body.
"Veruschka was never just a model – she was an artist, a boundary-pusher, a rebel. Her work is considered a feminist precursor to performance art."

items.title: Carlo Ratti and AI assistant to curate Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism 2027
paragraphs: Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.
Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.
However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.
What Ratti has revealed so far is that he plans to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.
Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.
“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” says Carlo Ratti.
“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.
“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”
Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.
Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.
The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.
“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore new possibilities,” said mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.
At the time, Ratti said, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.
The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

items.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
paragraphs: The phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.
“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”
Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.

In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia, which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.

On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”
Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.

Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing: “GPU Jesus has risen.”

Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.

Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT. On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”
While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.

The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded: “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.

Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.

Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying: “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”

And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”

Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.

Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.

“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”

Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.
“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.
In a separate statement, Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.
“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

items.title: "How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"
paragraphs: In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

The last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

Having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.
Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience
“How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers.

These were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question who defined them, whose interests they serve, or whether they should exist at all. They are commissioned to make products more sustainable without questioning production volumes, or improve services without examining the policies that make them inaccessible.
I often say design is a series of well-informed decisions. Every object, building and service emerges from decisions about resources, labor, budgets and the conditions of life.
Designers participate in these decisions, although they rarely control all of them. So where does their power begin and end?

Imagine a design studio commissioned by a city to address extreme heat in a low-income neighborhood. The brief requests solar-powered cooling shelters and shaded public spaces, with a fixed budget and deadline.

During research, the designers discover that the proposed shelters would be too far from elderly residents most vulnerable to heat, while existing community centers could accommodate cooling facilities at a lower cost. What should they do? Follow the brief, collect their fees and pretend their hands are tied? Refuse the commission, leaving another studio to complete the work, perhaps feeling rebellious for a moment?

There is a third possibility. They could show the city why its proposal would fail to reach its intended beneficiaries and present an alternative within the same budget. Working with residents and community organizations, they could identify accessible locations, compare costs and demonstrate how the alternative better meets the city’s objectives.
The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client

Here we see a tangible expansion of design as a civic responsibility. Designers can use their expertise to bring communities into decisions that affect their lives, improving outcomes while sharing decision-making power.
And if the city insists on its original proposal? The client controls the budget. A junior designer acting alone may have little negotiating power.

But a studio can incorporate community research into its contracts before work begins, negotiate a paid investigation phase and require the client to review evidence and alternatives before approving the design. Of course, this doesn’t guarantee agreement, but it makes critical inquiry a recognised part of the commission.

Design is a practice of applied imagination: understanding interconnected systems to intentionally shape the conditions of life. In this example, designers would examine the relationships between urban planning, public health, housing, energy and community governance. Their value lies partly in identifying what the original commission overlooked and developing viable possibilities with the people affected.

Thanks to the work of people like Victor Papanek, Tony Fry, Ezio Manzini and Arturo Escobar, by now it’s well understood that design has the capacity to shape the world but remains complicit in ecological and social destruction. The challenge today is to translate that knowledge into professional authority, economic leverage and meaningful participation in the decisions that will determine our collective futures.

Likewise, advocates of participatory design have long argued for involving people affected by design decisions. The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Meeting these challenges requires rethinking design education. Designers need to learn to investigate the historical conditions behind a problem, understand ecological and economic relationships, and work alongside communities to develop alternatives.

Design can shape community-owned infrastructure, food systems and forms of local governance as well as products and buildings. These are tangible fields of work requiring collaboration and shared authority.
We should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone

Of course, clients may refuse evidence, and insecure workers cannot always risk confrontation. Already there is too much pressure on Gen Z to save the world; we should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Studios, educators and commissioners must create paid roles and decision-making processes that give designers genuine influence. What if, for example, investigating the risks and assumptions behind a brief became an essential professional service, one that designers were commissioned and compensated to provide?

I keep thinking about those students at SVA, afraid of being considered difficult. We have taught them how to execute decisions without adequately preparing them to participate in making them. If designers are to take responsibility for their role in shaping the systems that govern our lives, they need a say in the decisions that produce those systems.

In the near future, success would mean residents gaining influence over where public money goes, with designers helping turn their priorities into lasting changes in public planning. This is design as a civic responsibility, and a meaningful distinction from machines optimized to execute instructions. To design possible futures, we must grow the agency designers hold, and the collective power they can help communities to build.

Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian designer, artist, writer, educator and speaker based in New York City, whose work focuses on climate issues and social justice. She is the founder of Slow Factory, a non-profit education and research platform that teaches about regenerative design. Her writing has appeared in The Cut, Vogue, Elle, Refinery29 and New York Magazine, among others. Her first book, A Woman Is a School, was published in 2024, and her upcoming book, Designing Possible Futures, is due for publication in 2027.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: Lucy McRae creates replicant birth bags for Blade Runner 2099 show where "violence and femininity coexist"
paragraphs: Los Angeles-based artist Lucy McRae has created tactile, custom-made designs for sci-fi mini-series Blade Runner 2099 that veer away from the traditionally cold and metallic aesthetic of the films.
The show, which premiered on Wednesday on Amazon Prime, is the latest in the Blade Runner universe and follows Cora, a human fugitive played by actor Hunter Schafer.

She goes undercover as a replicant – a synthetic human – blade runner with veteran replicant Olwen, played by actor Michelle Yeoh, to track down a runaway carrying a secret that could destabilise the city.
McRae joined the production in 2022 as the official futurist of the show, after showrunner Silka Luisa saw her previous work exploring the relationship between emerging technology and human biology.

Her speculative work on body futurism later became direct visual references for the show and McRae was asked to speculate on human consciousness in 50 years’ time, with a specific focus on memory, bio-engineering, replicants’ sensuality, sex and family.
“I created a world-build of those questions, through scale models, building concepts through physical materials,” McRae told Dezeen. “These ideas begin to transpire within the show.”
McRae designed the film’s birth bags, which are incubator-like sacks used to birth or transform replicants.
She also made the crèche set, the facility and replicant birth system that support the birth bags, as well as a skin polymer traction machine that was used for healing the protagonist Cora.

McRae also designed the material and colour palette for replicants, which includes pipes, quilting and industrial materials that fit the interiors of Olwen’s spacecraft and the padding around the traction machine.
The birth bag is a new iteration of McRae’s Compression Cradle, a project presented at the 2019 Milan Triennale exhibition Broken Nature.
It was a machine that offered a simulated hug to a person craving intimacy using an inflatable device.
In Blade Runner 2099, the design scale expanded dramatically, with nine vertical Compression Cradles created inside the Tyrell building where they functioned as birth bags in the show.
McRae often describes herself as a “body architect”. At Future Sensitive, the art-research lab she leads, her work revolves around using the body as a means to speculate on the future.

A few of her recent projects have explored what McRae calls the touch crisis – the idea that, with the rise of technology, digital devices might start to vie for human affection, and physical contact with other humans might suffer as a result.
Her Heavy Duty Love, for example, created for the Venice Architecture Biennale 2021, imagines a machine replacement of a parent’s embrace in a world where humans are grown in artificial wombs.
With The Future Day Spa, meanwhile, she presented a machine that could replace human contact altogether.
McRae’s says her focus on material tactility – such as creases, wrinkles, and squishy textures – adds a femininity to the show.
The series is built on the sci-fi intellectual property that followed from the original 1982 film and its aesthetic was historically labelled as metallic, cold, slick and masculine.
“The physicalisation of the work I do, the texture, achieves the femininity the show was after,” said McRae. “It’s an absolute masterpiece where both violence and femininity coexist.”
She also believes that by domesticating science and rendering technology malleable and wet, it creates a positive future that feels within human grasp and participation.

“It feels positive because it feels within my grasp. I feel I can participate and I can contribute,” said McRae. “Whereas if it’s a future that doesn’t look or feel or belong to something that I understand, then it feels like it’s a closed door.”

The designer said her work for the series, and in general, aims to focus on plausible futures rather than pure fantasy, while raising open-ended questions and encouraging audiences to navigate uncertainty with hope.
“What’s important for Silka and for my work is that anything I’m dealing with is never fantasy,” said McRae.
“I think physicalising possibility allows us to wear it, touch it and be able to get close to something that is far away but then allows us to see if it’s a fit, see if it belongs.”

“What I’m trying to do is create opportunities for people to ask these questions themselves and for me to not answer them. It’s going to be open-ended and unanswered because we don’t live in a world where one answer or many answers fit.”

items.title: DJ gets lucky after finding lost Daft Punk mixtape
paragraphs: DJ Ralph Lawson rediscovered a tape that Daft Punk gifted him in 1997

Daft Punk have become household names after storming the charts with One More Time and Get Lucky - with an intimate set in 1990s Leeds lingering in the memories of attendees. Now, those recollections have been reignited by the discovery of a lost mix by the French electronic duo hidden for several decades.
"It all started when I opened a show for Daft Punk in 1997," says Ralph Lawson, standing on the top floor of the Mint XL club in the city centre.
The 2,500-capacity venue is empty aside from staff testing out a staggering number of lights, bouncing off the spotless floors.
It is a far cry from Ralph's first clubs when he started DJing back in 1991.
He is a co-founding resident DJ at the legendary Back to Basics club - a DIY house music event that became one of Europe's longest-running club nights, hosting global stars until sunrise.
Mint evolved from an intimate Leeds club into festivals, large-scale productions and the new Mint XL club
Ralph is holding up a digital audio tape (DAT) - a discontinued method of recording high quality audio. On its side are the handwritten words: "Daft Punk Mix Feb '97."
"Daft Punk got so big so quickly, they were on such big stages at festivals that they did not really DJ," remembers the music producer.
The French pair were rapidly rising to fame when they were booked for Back to Basics, but they were pipped to the headline slot by drum and bass pioneer Goldie.
Daft Punk were on their rapid rise to stardom when they visited Leeds in 1997, but did not top the bill
By the time the night arrived, Ralph recalls "there were queues around the block".
Despite accidentally jogging one of their records during the set, Ralph got on well with both Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo - even if the latter only uttered a few words to him.
"I would not say I was best mates with them, but I could get on a guest list," says Ralph.
Whatever their relationship, it was strong enough that Daft Punk sent Ralph a gift in the post - an hour-long mixtape for his radio show on Kiss 105 FM.
This is the only picture Ralph has of Daft Punk playing their DJ set in Leeds
After it was played out on air, Ralph forgot about its existence for decades. He finally rediscovered it during a root around in some old storage boxes, but there was a problem.
"I took it out and there were two bits of tape hanging out."
Despite being in a dry studio, mould had found its way in.
When Ralph tried to play the tape it immediately ripped
Spurred on by his social media followers begging for him to salvage the mix, Ralph found a company that preserves tapes in Bristol.
"The problem with DAT is that it is incredibly fragile," says Adrian Finn, from Greatbear, one of the people tasked with fixing the broken tape.
He estimates the team spent hours across multiple weeks on this "difficult job", carefully disassembling the tape, repairing the rips and getting rid of the mould.
"It's nice to make people happy through this kind of restoration work," says Adrian, who admits he was dancing around "a little bit" while listening back to the mix.
"I thought it was good and glad it played back with hardly any errors."
Adrian Finn from Greatbear in Bristol was one of the people tasked with fixing the mixtape
Back at Mint XL in Leeds, Ralph cannot help but grin as he recounts attempting to play the mix for a second time.
"I was literally floored," he laughs, toppling over in delight once the kick drum blasted out of his speakers.
Ralph had no idea what the first track of the hour-long mix would be, so when it was one of his favourites - Everybody Dancing by the late American DJ Romanthony - he knew it would be "very special".
Ralph dropped to the floor in celebration when he heard the tape for the first time
It is the "rawness" of the vinyl mix - complete with crackles and impressive manual transitions - that Ralph adores.
"It's a testament to the times," he says.
"Not as polished as things are now, where people can see precisely how in time they are and have visual cues."

While the discovery may be a success for the nostalgia and memories of 1990s clubbing, Ralph also hopes the tape and the meaning behind it will inspire the next generation of DJs, music curators and artists.
"I want them to think, 'I could get behind the decks or find the next Daft Punk and put them on at our night', and there's the space for them to do that in Leeds."
Will another French electronic music duo stop by in Leeds on their way to global stardom? Who knows.
But producers like Ralph are adamant that the city's famous club scene can easily foster many more like them.

items.title: Elon Musk pledges to give two SpaceX shares to every child in the US
paragraphs: Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, has pledged to give every child in the US two shares in SpaceX, the space ⁠and AI company he ​runs, worth a total of almost $18bn.

In a brief post on X, the social media platform that he owns, Musk said children will receive one share from the company itself, and one from him personally. SpaceX announced earlier on Wednesday that it would ​contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock ‌to every currently active Trump Account, and that ‌Musk will match the number of shares it donates.

The Trump account program was designed to give every American under 18 a stake in the stock market, to help build wealth from an early age. The White House said last month that it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly $18bn.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s own donations would also be linked to Trump accounts.

In a separate post, Musk said the company shares will be transferred next ⁠month, with his own to follow later. “The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” he wrote.

In October, Musk, whose net worth is around $824bn, announced his intention to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. “This will be the first of many,” he said in a post on X at the time. As of June, he held about 6.42bn shares ​in the company.
Most of Musk’s philanthropic efforts have been conducted via the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds around $16bn in assets.
In October, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell ⁠and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under ​the Trump account initiative.

Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently detailed their sharply different approaches for sharing the spoils of the AI boom. Anthropic, which went public earlier this month, ​said it would commit 5% of its ​shares to a new fund for the “public good”. The company said this initiative, worth around $54bn at current prices, would give it ​more flexibility and scale to ‌make donations for the benefit ​of humanity.

Other major, long-running philanthropy ventures include those of Berkshire Hathaway chair emeritus Warren Buffett, who is reported to have given away $60bn, with the intention of doing the same with most of the rest of his $150bn fortune.
The Gates Foundation has distributed more than $100bn since its founding in 2000, with some of that fuelled by donations from Buffett.

items.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
paragraphs: FILE - Elon Musk listens as President Donald Trump speaks during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace, Oct. 8, 2026, in Washington. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."

"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.
Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."
"It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.
He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

"You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.
The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky."

"The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."
Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said.
Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

items.title: Gig evacuation quarantine was traumatic, fans say
paragraphs: Some Don Toliver fans who were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live arena after an unknown substance was released have said they were "quarantined for six hours" and threatened with arrest if they did not remove all their clothing.

Jordan, 33, from Scotland, said he and his brothers were among 88 people who were taken for decontamination after the incident at the gig on Sunday night, and it "felt like I was being taken hostage".
He said they had asked for medical help at 22:15 GMT and were taken to the Etihad Stadium, where they were made to change into paper suits, and stayed until 04:45 on Monday.
"It was so traumatic," Jordan said. Greater Manchester Police declined to comment.
The force has not confirmed what the substance was and there have been no arrests.
A woman was taken to hospital, with 88 other people reporting symptoms, including coughing and chest pains.
Dry decontamination was carried out by North West Ambulance Service (NWAS), GMP said.

NWAS said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution" in line with "advice taken from national scientific advisors based on the situation".
Molly, 19, said she was separated from her friends due to her gender which made her feel "alone".
"We were allowed a screen around us, it was all women in there, we had to literally strip down to our bra and knickers and put on a suit and slippers," she said.
"We had to put [our clothes] in a plastic bag and it got taken away.
"We were told 'I hope you've not got anything expensive as you might not get it back'."
She added: "There was no ABC of what was happening. It was just, 'you have to take your clothes off' but there was no further information."
Charlie said: "It was invasive, you had to wipe yourself down, wipe down your phone.
"Everything goes in a bag, But it was a mystery. No-one was telling us what was going to happen."
At about 04:30 the friends said they were given their clothes back and they were able to leave.
College student Archie Grime, 18, from Accrington, Lancashire, said he was also quarantined after the concert.
"It was burning and painful and I couldn't see or breathe," he said.
He said he and his friends sat "doing nothing for hours" while waiting to be released.
Archie said when the group were told they could leave the Etihad, he was able to get a lift home - but noted others were left "stranded" without transport plans.
"A friend's mum took us home," he said. "We were lucky though, a lot of people were stranded.
"They told us to walk back in the thin suits in the cold and to take our clothes home to be washed."
Police said the cordon was lifted at Co-op Live on Tuesday night, as the investigation continues.
The force said the substance release may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue.
